Name: Hybrid vs Remote: All About Each Work Environment [2026]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: More and more businesses are moving from 100% in-office work to hybrid and remote setups.
Post body:
More and more businesses are moving from 100% in-office work to hybrid and remote setups.

The question is: which of these options is best for your business?

In this post, you’ll learn all about hybrid vs remote work. You’ll get the advantages and disadvantages of each, plus examples from companies that have made the shift to one or the other.

Quick Summary:

  • The hybrid work model is flexible, with employees splitting their time between working remotely and working in the office. Employees are often free to set schedules based on individual work needs, productivity, and company goals.
  • The remote work model lets employees work from anywhere. Fully remote teams don’t use a shared office or workspace.
  • Whether to shift to a hybrid or remote work model depends on your business goals, your ability to maintain the level of quality your customers expect, and how you can support your employees.

Hybrid vs remote: all about each work environment

Hybrid work means splitting the workweek between the office and a remote location, while remote work means doing the job entirely away from a shared office. That single distinction drives most of what follows.

In the hybrid work model, employees work both remotely and from the office, often setting their schedules based on their own or the company’s needs. For example, the need to access materials or meet in person for collaboration will bring them in.

The remote work model lets employees work from anywhere. Employees who are fully remote don’t use an office or shared workspace.

Now that you know the basics, here’s a closer look at each of these work models.

Hybrid work model

The flexibility of the hybrid work model has made it the default for people who can work remotely. Gallup puts about half of remote-capable US employees in hybrid roles, with fully remote and fully on-site splitting the rest. Roughly half of all full-time US employees hold a job that can be done at least partly from home.

Hybrid work types

There are different naming conventions for the various hybrid work arrangements, but in general, there are four main types:

  • office-centric
  • flexible
  • remote-friendly
  • remote-first

The best option depends on how much flexibility you can offer based on your business type and goals. Shifting to a hybrid work model makes sense when you can hold your quality and productivity standards.

Here’s a brief rundown of each hybrid work type:

Office-centric

The office-centric model asks employees to work in the office for most of the week. Managers usually set this out in hybrid work policies.

Employees may still have some flexibility over their in-office hours and which days they work from home each week.

Flexible

The flexible hybrid model lives up to its name. The time employees spend working in and out of the office is largely up to them.

Remote-friendly

Remote-friendly businesses set clear guidelines on when and how employees work remotely. For example, employees may not be remote on certain days of the week, or certain tasks can’t be done remotely.

Remote-first

The remote-first model lets most employees work remotely most of the time. On some occasions, they still gather in the office for the moments that matter.

Any of these hybrid models can be applied company-wide or to a single department. If you need a physical presence to sell your product or provide your service, some workers won’t have the choice. But roles in HR or accounting, for example, can often shift to hybrid.

If you want to find the right hybrid work model for you, take this short quiz.

Advantages of hybrid work

Hybrid businesses get some clear benefits over fully remote work, including the following.

  • Better work-life balance. Setting their own schedule (here’s an example template) lets employees work during their most productive hours. They adjust as needed to attend to their personal lives or schedule appointments.

Flexible hours rank as one of the top benefits employees name, and they’re tied to higher job satisfaction.

That’s good for mental well-being, and for employers, it means stronger engagement and more workplace integrity.

  • Better engagement and collaboration with colleagues. Employees who spend part of their week in the office get the proven benefits of in-person communication.

Gallup also finds that being in the office two to three days per week produces the best outcomes for employee engagement and well-being, and reduces burnout and job hunting.

  • Access to office materials and workspaces is another perk of hybrid work. Good hybrid offices give teams places to meet in large groups, talk one-on-one, and do focused work at individual desks.
  • Higher productivity. Many studies show that productivity holds up or improves when people have flexibility in where and when they work. Read more about that here.

Here’s a fuller list of the most prominent hybrid work advantages.

Disadvantages of hybrid work

While the hybrid model has real benefits, there are trade-offs to plan for. The three most common hybrid work challenges are:

  • The transition can be tricky. Moving to a hybrid model from a traditional office or a fully remote setup takes work. You have to balance new work patterns and ride out early productivity swings, which is easier with the right software.
  • Onboarding gets harder. It loses the spontaneity and ease of in-person interaction, so you need a more structured, well-planned approach.
  • Meetings are harder to run. Running effective meetings with both in-person and remote participants takes effort. Remote employees have to be equally involved and heard, which is easy to get wrong in a hybrid setting.

Here’s a fuller article on the most important drawbacks and challenges of hybrid work.

Going hybrid also means paying to maintain an office. That includes the physical location plus the furniture, materials, and utilities to keep it running.

If you already have an office space and you’re planning to go hybrid, that can still save you money in the long run.

Working out how much office space you need requires knowing who is in the office and when.

Without the right tools, this is no small task. With OfficeRnD Workplace’s space management software, you can see what’s being used, what’s not, and where you can cut facilities costs.

Here’s an example of a business that shifted to hybrid.

Hybrid company example

Microsoft runs a hybrid model, giving employees options around their work site, location, and hours.

The company rejects a one-size-fits-all workday and commits to flexible work for the long term. Many other companies have made the same switch.

Hybrid work suits many companies, but you might wonder whether a fully remote workforce would fit your business better. Here’s what that looks like.

Remote work model

Like hybrid, remote work has held a steady share of the workforce.

The fully remote work model lets employees work from wherever they choose. Remote employees don’t use an office or shared workspace.

Around 3 in 10 remote-capable US employees are fully remote, a share that has held roughly steady since 2022.

Remote employees are sometimes called work-from-home (WFH). That’s technically true, but people with remote jobs can work from anywhere in the world.

If you’re thinking about going fully remote, there are benefits and drawbacks to weigh.

Advantages of the remote work model

Remote-only businesses have some distinct advantages.

  • Remote employees have the most flexibility over their schedules. Given the choice, most employees who can work remotely want flexibility. McKinsey found that when people are offered flexible work, they take it.

Remote employees typically set schedules for when they are most productive and to suit their personal lives.

  • Businesses with a mostly remote workforce cut or eliminate office and overhead costs. No physical location means no rent or mortgage, monthly utilities, furniture, or office supplies. Check this article to see if remote employees actually save you money.
  • A remote team gives you a much larger talent pool. You can recruit broadly because you don’t have to hire locally.
  • One study found a boost in creativity among remote workers. Their ability to shape their own jobs led to performance improvements.

Disadvantages of the fully remote work model

Here are the drawbacks to weigh before going fully remote:

  • Collaboration can be harder with reduced (or no) in-person contact. Video calls and virtual team building activities give people face-to-face time, but scheduling them is tough, especially across time zones. Remote employees are also harder to engage.

Fully remote colleagues miss the “water cooler” conversations too, which makes it harder to build and strengthen working relationships. Gallup’s own data shows fully remote workers report higher stress and lower thriving than hybrid or on-site workers, so distributed teams need deliberate connection built in.

  • Boundaries are harder to hold without deliberate intent. When work tools are always within reach, remote team members can struggle to set and keep work hours.
  • Remote businesses carry higher IT security needs across a distributed workforce. There are more risks to account for, and the cost of preventing breaches can be significant.

Here’s an example of a company built around a remote workforce:

Remote company example

Zapier has been remote since it was founded. The founders couldn’t afford office space or line up their work schedules at the start.

As the company scaled, they found they could hire whomever they wanted, keep a quality product, and keep customers and staff happy while staying fully remote.

Understanding the differences between hybrid and remote work is the first step. The second is deciding which model fits your business.

Hybrid or remote: which is best for your team?

Here’s what to weigh when deciding whether to move your business to hybrid or fully remote work.

What makes sense for your company and industry?

Start with your mission, goals, and objectives. Who are you, and what do you want to accomplish?

Will teams do well in a remote setting? Can you keep a quality service or product if you make the shift?

Set your budget and decide whether a physical office makes sense. Some roles or responsibilities need an onsite presence, and some services need a physical location to deliver.

Look at your talent pool. A remote workforce gives you access to the best available talent because you can hire from anywhere. Consider which parts of your business could go hybrid or remote and still do well.

How will you support hybrid and remote workers?

Both hybrid and remote work models can deliver a positive workplace experience.

Think about how you’ll keep people engaged, whether they’re fully remote or in the office part of the time. For instance:

  • Set clear channels for communication, such as email, chat, and video calls.
  • To support a hybrid setup, consider deploying hybrid work software that handles the tedious job of booking office resources like meeting rooms and desks.
  • Give remote teams real chances to collaborate, in person or remotely.
  • Create ways for hybrid and remote workers to give and get feedback, ask questions, and raise concerns through surveys, project management tools, and regular check-ins.
  • Factor in your customers. Can you keep customer service high when teams work remotely?

What do your employees want?

Take your team’s preferences into account where you can. More and more people want flexibility to get a better work-life balance.

Many businesses find productivity holds up or improves when workers pick the location that works best for them.

If you’re leaning toward hybrid, use strategies for boosting engagement, like strong communication and real interpersonal connection.

Remote or hybrid: what do the studies show?

The data points to a durable middle ground rather than a swing to either extreme. Among remote-capable US employees, Gallup puts about half in hybrid roles, roughly 3 in 10 fully remote, and 2 in 10 fully on-site. Those splits have held steady since 2022, with only small recent shifts toward fully remote and fully on-site.

The strongest evidence on productivity comes from a randomized controlled trial of 1,612 employees, led by Stanford economist Nicholas Bloom and published in Nature in 2024. A two-day-a-week hybrid schedule had no measurable effect on performance, promotions, or output, and it cut attrition by about 33%.

Remote work brings flexibility and better work-life balance, but also risks like burnout and weaker coworker connections. Hybrid tends to balance the two: the collaboration of the office with the flexibility of working from home.

Choosing between hybrid and remote comes with trade-offs. Once you’ve settled your top priorities, the right model gets clearer.

If hybrid is the way to go, OfficeRnD Workplace makes it easier to run. OfficeRnD Workplace is a hybrid workplace product that handles desk booking, room booking, and collaborative scheduling, so in-office and remote teams can see who’s in and plan around it.

With OfficeRnD Workplace, you can build collaborative workspaces where both people and work do well.

Name: Book, Work, Thrive: The On-Demand Space Revolution
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: The world has changed quite a bit in the last few years. Even one of the slowest and most conservative industries, commercial real estate, has changed. It’s not that the CRE industry is all about innovation and experimentation. It was forced to change and become more flexible.
Post body:
The world has changed quite a bit in the last few years. Even one of the slowest and most conservative industries, commercial real estate, has changed. It’s not that the CRE industry is all about innovation and experimentation. It was forced to change and become more flexible.

We all know that the office buildings as we know them are a dying breed. The workplace though is thriving! It’s the traditional office building that is dying. The modern workplace is developing and adapting to the new needs of working professionals.

The new workplace is all about providing outstanding space to work, collaborate, and all in between, bundled with exceptional additional services.

From day passes and short-term collaboration spaces to mid and long-term offices. From meeting and event spaces to food & beverage and concierge services. From gym and wellness services to daycare for kids. The list of great services that are now part of the modern workplace is endless.

That’s amazing for those who use the space. At the same time, it’s a huge operational and technological challenge for the people managing the space – landlords, coworking, and flex space operators alike.

How do you enable and streamline booking of on-demand spaces and services at scale?

  • How can you maximize bookings revenue?
  • How to offer a great booking experience?

Let’s explore how we can streamline this!

Coworking Booking Platform for On-demand Spaces

One way to approach the challenge is to rely on a best-of-breed booking platform, specifically built for flex spaces. Stepping on a solid foundation will allow you to unlock all screens and let users book on-demand space whenever they need one.

Imagine a user who wants to book a desk for a day or a meeting space to brainstorm with their team for a couple of hours.

Let’s examine all the places where a user may search and book a space or a service:

Resident Bookings (Members Area)

On average, 70-90% of all bookings that a typical coworking and flex space facilitates in a given period of time are done by residents of the space – members/tenants. That’s why, when you’re considering how to optimize your booking process, you should arguably place a bigger priority on your existing customers and community!

Member Portal

Arguably, your top priority should be to allow your member community to book any type of on-demand space and services easily from an easy-to-use web portal.

Most of your bookings will always come from your existing community (members, tenants, etc). That’s why you should provide an outstanding booking experience to your members, first.

Usually, all on-demand booking platforms, such as OfficeRnD Flex, offer a built-in Member Portal that comes with a lot more community features too.

Mobile App

Next in line is offering a great booking experience on mobile. On average, about 10-15% of your bookings will come from the mobile app (if available). This is a big enough percentage point to invest in an outstanding app.

Whether that’s an existing member or a new user, people should be able to easily find and book spaces whenever they need them.

Feature-wise, the mobile app is not very different from the member portal. It should offer a simpler, mobile-friendly interface to interact with the workplace and book the right services.

Some of the best on-demand booking platforms also offer out-of-the-box white-label booking apps for iPhone and Android.

Non-Resident (External) Bookings

As mentioned, on average, 70-90% of all bookings in a typical coworking space are made by the residents of the space. The rest of the bookings are coming from external users (non-resident bookings). Although 10-30% doesn’t sound like a big number, it’s usually a very considerable revenue. Most coworking spaces are very successful at driving growth and additional revenue by offering meeting rooms to external users.

For example, corporate executives might be gathering for a brainstorming session and prefer to do it outside of their HQs and they end up booking space in a nearby flex space.

Public Website

Most of the time, the person making a booking will go to a vendor they know and trust. They will open their website and either try to initiate the booking directly from the website, or, call the space and initiate the booking over the phone.

Either way, the booking should be recorded in a system with all details, including the additional services that the person requires, such as coffee, croissants, and other F&B products. In many cases, there’s a contract that needs to be generated and signed for the booking. Then, usually, an invoice should be generated too and a payment to be processed. Most of the time, this process can be fully automated by the core booking platform.

The best solution for this use case from a user point of view is to build a direct integration between the public website and the booking platform. Essentially, you should build simple listings into the main website. This will ensure:

  • Great (native) booking experience for the user
  • Single source of truth about all data points, such as resources, prices, availability, etc.

A simpler solution is to offer booking checkout pages on a sub-domain, usually, part of the member portal. These are often offered by the on-demand booking platforms as part of their offering.

Aggregators and Marketplaces

Next in line in terms of popularity when it comes to booking spaces for on-demand usage is through aggregators, marketplaces, listing sites, and other space networks. There are many flavors and great marketplaces out there, such as LiquidSpace, Tally, DeskPass, Instant Offices, Upflex, Gable, Coworker and so many more. Some of them are very local, others are more global networks. Some of them are focused on enterprise customers and others are mostly focusing on freelancers, digital nomads, and solopreneurs.

They can be great channels to generate more bookings and drive additional revenue. However, managing them all is really challenging. You have to add and keep your inventory up to date, as well as synchronize the real-time availability of space.

Using a well-integrated booking platform can help with that by directly integrating with some of the most popular marketplaces, like LiquidSpace.

Global Distribution (GDS) and Broker Systems

Another channel you can receive external bookings from is the so-called Global Distribution Systems (GDS). Historically, these were very important software solutions that enabled transactions between travel industry service providers, mainly airlines, hotels, car rental companies, and travel agencies. Nowadays, they are serving as a way to distribute your inventory to multiple channels that can drive additional bookings and reservations.

It’s a very new concept for commercial real estate. It has been developing more rapidly in the last few years due to the increased demand for flexible spaces. A few examples out there are Syncaroo and Valve.

Furthermore, we can also add the Broker Distribution Systems to the same category. For example, Valve is a great tool to drive bookings via brokers.

The best-of-breed flexible space booking systems, such as OfficeRnD Flex, are also integrated deeply with such systems.

Maps, AI & the future

One of the most exciting channels that are still not developed in the coworking and flexible workspace industry is booking directly through Google Maps and the like.

For most hospitality venues we can directly search on the map, find the right place for us, check its availability, and book it directly, such as restaurants and hotels. However, you still can’t do that for desks, meeting spaces, and other flexible workspace products. Surely, you should still have a really well-maintained and polished profile on Google Business so that people can find your space on the map. Hopefully, we will see the ability to book directly from the maps soon!

Of course, another future-looking option to book will be directly through AI chat platforms, such as ChatGPT and Google Bard. It’s inevitable that this will come soon! It will be really nice to have an AI helping you find the perfect spot for your next board meeting or customer meeting in NYC.

Your booking platform should be able to tightly integrate with these chat systems so that you can securely receive bookings directly from there.

In Conclusion

To wrap it up, high-quality on-demand booking platforms can streamline your channel management, help you improve your space utilization, and generate more revenue from your flex space assets.

The evolution of commercial real estate towards more flexible, dynamic, and user-friendly spaces represents a significant shift in how we view and utilize work environments. The key to successfully navigating this change lies in leveraging advanced booking platforms like OfficeRnD Flex. This platform not only simplifies the process of managing and booking on-demand spaces but also enhances the overall experience for both space managers and users.

Name: 14 Key Principles Of Good Calendar Invite Etiquette [2024]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Effective communication and time management are essential for personal and professional success. One often overlooked aspect of this is calendar invite etiquette.
Post body:
Effective communication and time management are essential for personal and professional success. One often overlooked aspect of this is calendar invite etiquette.

Properly managing and responding to calendar invitations can significantly improve not just your productivity but also your relationships and work-life balance as a whole.

In this article, we’ll explore why calendar etiquette is important and present a comprehensive set of principles and best practices to help you navigate this important aspect of the modern workplace.

Quick Summary:

  • Good calendar invite etiquette helps to streamline workflows and promotes professionalism in the workplace.
  • Calendar invite etiquette best practices can be broken up into three main groups: for sending invitations, for employees, and for employers.
  • Virtual meetings for hybrid work environments come with specific etiquette protocols.

Why Is Calendar Invite Etiquette Important?

Calendar invite etiquette plays a key role in helping you maintain a well-organized schedule and build positive relationships in both personal and professional settings.

But more than that, practicing good meeting invitation etiquette demonstrates your professionalism and capability in the workplace.

Here are five additional reasons why using the right calendar invite etiquette is essential:

It Shows Respect for Others’ Time

One of the fundamental principles of calendar invite etiquette is respecting other people’s time. Sending and responding to invitations promptly demonstrates consideration for the schedules and commitments of your co-workers.

It also prevents frustration and wasted time and helps create an environment of mutual respect and professionalism.

It Leads to Better Time Management

Properly managing your calendar invitations can help you manage your time efficiently. Plus, by maintaining an organized schedule, you can allocate your time effectively and reduce the risk of making double bookings or missing important appointments.

It Boosts Productivity

Establishing norms for scheduling and confirming appointments helps to minimize disruptions. You’ll experience a reduction in unnecessary back-and-forth communication, for instance, which can provide you with more productive hours in the day.

It Strengthens Employee Relationships

Calendar etiquette can also help you build — and maintain — positive relationships in your work environment.

Clear and respectful communication regarding appointments and meetings demonstrates reliability and builds trust in your professional and personal life.

It Minimizes Stress

Managing calendar invites in an organized manner can reduce stress. Knowing that your schedule is well-coordinated and you’re not likely to miss important events or meetings can give you a more relaxed and focused mindset.

Now that we’ve discussed the importance of using proper calendar invite etiquette, we’ll explore a comprehensive set of key principles to guide you in this aspect of time management and communication.

Calendar Invite Etiquette: 14 Fundamental Principles

Below are 14 principles that, taken together, set the stage for appropriate calendar invite etiquette.

We’ll start with the general etiquette of sending out calendar invitations, followed by best practices for employees and employers.

Best Practices for Sending Calendar Invites

Here are seven general practices for sending out calendar invites:

1. Use Clear Subject Lines

Use descriptive and concise subject lines when sending calendar invites. This helps the recipients quickly understand the purpose of the invitation and the nature of the event so that they can prioritize their time and prepare accordingly.

When creating a calendar invite, compose a subject line that clearly conveys the purpose of the invitation. Avoid vague or generic titles, like “Meeting” or “Appointment.”

Instead, use descriptive phrases, such as “Marketing Team Weekly Review” or “Client Presentation Planning Meeting.”

A company leader or supervisor could also use clear phrases such as “All Staff Mandatory Meeting at Noon Today” or “Important Planning Session at 3 pm Today (Tuesday) for the Entire Team.”

2. Include the Essential Details

Make sure that your calendar invites include all the necessary information for invitees so that they can prepare effectively and contribute meaningfully to the meeting or event.

Specifically, include the following important details in the body of the invitation:

  • Date and time: Specify the date and the start and end times of the event.
  • Location: Clearly state whether the meeting is physical or virtual. If the former, include the meeting location or address, and if the latter, provide a link or the relevant dial-in information.
  • Agenda: Outline the meeting’s main topic(s) or objective(s). If different participants are expected to contribute to or lead portions of the discussion, add their names and indicate how much time is allocated for their segments of the meeting.
  • Preparatory materials: If the participants need to review any documents or other resources beforehand, attach them or provide links if they’re downloadable.

3. Include All Relevant Parties

Make sure that all individuals who need to attend or have a stake in the meeting are included in the invite to prevent misunderstandings and keep everyone who’s part of the team or workgroup informed and engaged in the discussion.

For recurring team meetings, create an email group you can go to consistently. Make sure to update the group if team members move in and out.

For meetings that only happen once in a while, consult the notes from the most recent one to remind you which coworkers were invited.

For new meeting topics, use your contact list or the organization’s directory to make sure no one is accidentally omitted.

4. Respect People’s Scheduling Preferences

Be mindful of others’ scheduling preferences and time zones when sending invites. For instance, avoid scheduling meetings during lunch breaks or outside of regular working hours unless there’s clear direction and authorization for such unorthodox meeting times.

Time zone differences are a potential pitfall as well, so use the features included in your calendar tool to display multiple time zones.

Needless to say, respecting coworkers’ scheduling preferences minimizes disruptions in their busy days caused by inconvenient meeting times. It also makes it much likelier that the participants you invite will fully and freely engage in the discussion.

5. Confirm the Invitees’ Availability

An important feature of invite etiquette is to double-check whether the prospective participants can attend the meeting at the date and time you have in mind.

This extra effort on your part to confirm their availability beforehand reduces the likelihood of last-minute scheduling conflicts, rescheduling, or no-shows.

Use your calendar tool’s scheduling assistant or a similar feature to check the invitees’ availability. Tools like Microsoft Outlook’s scheduling assistant or Google Calendar’s “Find a time” feature can be helpful in this respect.

Your company can also use a meeting room booking feature that includes the option of checking people’s availability.

For example, the hybrid work management software OfficeRnD Workplace integrates with Google Calendar, thus making it possible for employees to book meeting rooms directly from Google Calendar. Meeting room booking is also available from the Google Chrome extension.

If the meeting is essential, but scheduling conflicts arise, reach out right away to the participants to find an alternative suitable meeting time. That way, no one’s own task scheduling will be held up or messed up by unsolved conflicting meeting invites.

Here are some killer Google Calendar tips:

6. Send Invitations in Advance

Send calendar invitations well in advance whenever possible, especially for significant events or important meetings. This allows participants to plan their own schedules accordingly.

Another benefit of advance notice is that it gives invitees time to adequately prepare and reduces the potential for scheduling conflicts. It also shows that you value people’s time and other commitments they may have.

In general, provide at least a few days’ notice for routine meetings and more extended notice (2–4 weeks or more) for important gatherings.

7. Communicate Changes Promptly

If the meeting day or time needs changing, promptly communicate those changes to the invitees to minimize confusion and disruptions and make it easy for them to adjust their plans.

Use your calendar tool to send update notifications to all original invitees. Make sure the subject line of the email invite shows that this is not a reminder but an update or change.

Be specific about the change you’re making, such as a time change, location change, topic change, or cancellation.

Meeting Invite Best Practices for Employees

Next, we’ll look at how each individual employee can practice better meeting etiquette in terms of both responding to invitations and best practices for making sure the meetings they attend will be productive and enjoyable.

1. Respond Promptly

When you receive a calendar invite, a prompt reaction helps the organizer finalize plans quickly and avoid unnecessary delays.

Use your calendar tool’s response feature to communicate your availability. If you have to decline, it’s helpful to add a note as to the reason, such as “I’ll be out of the office that day” or “I’m no longer part of that workgroup.” A detailed response gives the organizer the information they need to reschedule or cancel the meeting.

If you are unable to attend a meeting, but it’s important that you’re part of the discussion, promptly propose an alternative time. If appropriate, include a message with your response to give the host more details.

2. Follow Virtual Meeting Etiquette

Virtual meetings have their own meeting etiquette due to the technology used during these gatherings.

The right virtual meeting etiquette contributes to productive and respectful interactions in remote or hybrid settings. It helps maintain the quality of communication and collaboration and keeps the meetings congenial.

Good virtual meeting etiquette includes the following:

  • Muting your microphone when you’re not speaking
  • Using video cameras as much as possible or when appropriate so that fellow participants can make visual contact
  • Looking into the camera
  • Minimizing distractions in your office or home office environment (if your background could be distracting, consider setting up a blurred background or a pleasant background image, like a forest, clouds, or a beach).
  • Using a clear system for participants to indicate they want to speak, such as raising a virtual hand or typing a comment or request in the chat box

In addition to making those adaptations for a virtual environment, follow the same principles of courtesy and professionalism that you would in an in-person meeting.

3. Be Punctual

Whether the meeting you’re attending is physical or virtual, joining on time shows respect for others’ time and sets a positive tone for the interactions to come. It also helps meetings stay within their scheduled times.

Make it a habit to start and end meetings as scheduled. If you anticipate being late, notify the facilitator or participants in advance. If you are the person who set up the meeting and you’re arriving or starting late, make sure to adjust the meeting duration accordingly.

4. Regularly Review, Declutter, and Block Out Focus Time on Your Calendar

Start each day by reviewing your calendar to make sure you are prepared for your upcoming meetings and tasks.

Here are some helpful tips:

  • Use focus blocks: Block specific time slots on your calendar for different tasks to give yourself a structured and productive workday. Dedicate blocks of “focus time” to let your co-workers know you aren’t available to meet for non-urgent projects.
  • Use scheduling software: The right workspace management and scheduling tools can help teams collaborate easily in the office. With OfficeRnD Workplace, teams can easily book conference rooms for meetings, reserve desks, and create hybrid work schedules.
  • Declutter your calendar: Regularly remove or reschedule non-essential or outdated events to keep your calendar organized and easy to navigate.
  • Customize your calendar: It’s helpful to use color coding to categorize the events and appointments in your calendar so you can quickly and easily see what’s happening in your day.

Good categories to color-code include “work-related,” “personal,” “urgent,” and “deadlines.” Another color-coding method is to assign distinctive colors to projects. For instance, you could use yellow for planning sessions and green for budget meetings.

Calendar Invite Best Practices for Employers and Supervisors

Lastly, employers can take some helpful steps to make good calendar invite etiquette easier for the entire workforce. Here are three suggestions:

1. Use the Right Calendar Tools

Using universally recognized tools simplifies the scheduling process and minimizes potential compatibility issues.

It also accounts for better accessibility and a better user experience, especially for less tech-savvy individuals.

If you want to level up the calendar and scheduling tools you’re already using, OfficeRnD Workplace easily integrates with Microsoft Teams, Outlook, and Google Calendar.

2. Encourage Shorter Meetings

We’ve all heard about Zoom fatigue. Many employees feel like too much of their time is wasted in pointless meetings.

For this reason, company leadership would do well to encourage staff to hold shorter meetings or eliminate face-to-face meetings entirely in favor of email exchanges or chats.

If a meeting is important, consider the complexity of the topics to be discussed when you set the meeting’s duration.

For the most accurate assessment possible, map out the meeting agenda in detail and dedicate a realistic period of time to each item.

You can also reduce meeting fatigue by avoiding scheduling meetings back-to-back. Be considerate of your coworkers by leaving an adequate amount of open space in everyone’s calendar.

3. Find the Right Platform for Virtual Meetings

In remote work environments, virtual meetings are the norm, so make sure that all participants have easy access to the virtual meeting platform you’ve selected and understand how to use the available features.

Select a platform that has the presentation and interaction features you need. Think of features such as co-presenting, screen sharing, and virtual whiteboards.

If you’re the meeting organizer, familiarize yourself thoroughly with the chosen platform’s features so you won’t be thrown for a loop when it’s time to show your screen or lead a discussion.

Taken together, these 14 points of calendar invite etiquette will make a big difference in how your invitations are received and responded to and how well your meetings will proceed.

Calendar Invite Etiquette in a Hybrid Work Environment

Not surprisingly, the rise of remote and hybrid work environments has brought significant changes in how calendar invites are used and managed.

Understanding the nuances of calendar invite etiquette specific to remote and hybrid work settings will help you adapt to this shift.

Here are some key considerations, etiquette tips, and best practices for hybrid meetings:

1. Consider Time Zone Differences

In hybrid or remote work settings, team members are likely to be spread across different time zones. So, considering each participant’s time zone is especially important when scheduling hybrid meetings.

Use your calendar tool’s time zone feature to display meeting participants’ respective time zones and select meeting times that accommodate everyone as much as possible.

Being mindful of time zones shows respect for your colleagues’ work-life balance and minimizes your likelihood of scheduling meetings at inconvenient hours.

2. Record Meetings

It’s not always possible to get an entire virtual team together since time zone differences and personal schedules can prevent real-time attendance for some of the intended attendees.

One way to counteract this is to download a notetaker app or bot that automatically records your meetings and generates a transcript. Another is to audio or video-record the meeting.

Before launching into a meeting recording, make sure your recording practices are in line with company policies.

Equally important, always announce to the participants that you are starting a recording so that everyone can be mindful of their word choices and tone.

Share the recording with the participants shortly after the meeting ends to allow those who couldn’t attend to catch up quickly and those who did attend to review key discussions.

3. Follow Up with Key Takeaways and Action Items

Email follow-ups are particularly valuable in remote work environments where face-to-face communication may be limited.

In your follow-up email, summarize the key points, action items, and deadlines that were discussed during the meeting.

If you recorded the meeting, include a link to the recording and let the relevant individuals know how long the recording will remain available.

4. Master Asynchronous Communication

Since remote and hybrid employees can’t always communicate in real-time, mastering asynchronous communication is essential for productivity. It allows team members to manage their time effectively and prevents an overload of virtual meetings.

Not all discussions require meetings. Some can be handled perfectly via chat or email. So, evaluate each discussion topic to make sure it’s worth calling a virtual meeting for.

Build Calendar Invite Etiquette into Your Hybrid Workflow

Calendar invite etiquette is a fundamental aspect of effective time management and communication.

With these principles and best practices, you can create a more efficient, professional, and team-minded workplace for yourself and your colleagues.

Author: asen-stoyanchev

Post body:
Since the pandemic reshaped where people work, the office stopped being the only place work happens. Millions of people now split their week between home and a workplace, and the conversation has moved from whether hybrid work is viable to how to run it well. That’s where hybrid work advantages come in.

Hybrid work is a model where employees split their time between a workplace and a remote location, usually home, instead of being in the office five days a week.

Many people have grown used to working from home and aren’t eager to give it up, especially when it means better mental health and more time with the people they care about.

At the same time, some employees feel isolated and disconnected when they work fully remotely. For them, collaborating and being around colleagues carries real value.

Hybrid work gives you both. Below are the advantages worth knowing, backed by current research from Gallup, Owl Labs, and Stanford.

Free bonus: Watch this exclusive webinar where industry experts discuss the top workplace trends and what's coming next. It includes a free resource you don't want to miss.

What are the most important hybrid work advantages?

Gallup’s research puts numbers on it. The biggest advantages Gallup found are improved work-life balance, more efficient use of time, control over hours and location, less burnout, and higher productivity. Gallup also notes the top challenges of hybrid work show up far less often than the top advantages.

1. Improved collaboration

Remote work has clear perks, but communication and collaboration can suffer when people never meet in person. Microsoft’s research found collaboration takes a hit when employees work only remotely.

A hybrid workplace gives employees room for brainstorming sessions, team meetings, and discussions that save time, lift productivity, and build a stronger company culture.

In our article on hybrid vs remote working, we explain that a lack of in-person collaboration is one of the main downsides of fully remote work.

2. Higher productivity and employee satisfaction

Getting people together out of their homes drives both productivity and creativity. Noise and distraction are the usual objections to returning, and you can design around them. An activity-based approach is worth exploring in a hybrid workplace.

Tailored zones for focused work have a proven record of lifting productivity. The office neighborhoods concept is one example of that in an office setting.

The evidence backs the model. In Owl Labs’ 2025 State of Hybrid Work report, 90% of hybrid workers said they’re just as productive or more productive in a hybrid setup, and 69% of managers said hybrid or remote work has made their teams more productive.

Options for focused work plus time to collaborate with teammates support employee well-being and a healthier company culture.

3. More opportunities for continuous learning

Give your employees the chance to build skills that help the organization. It’s a genuine perk for people who work hard, and it builds community.

For onboarding or training new colleagues, mixing office and home time can make the process easier. On-site courses also work well for team building.

As a related read, check out our article on quotes about hybrid work.

4. Socializing with colleagues

Sharing a physical space with coworkers carries new value, especially for remote employees. Part of our team at OfficeRnD prefers coming in more often because home has too many distractions. As mentioned, we set up office neighborhoods where people can concentrate on deep work.

Employees tell researchers the days worth commuting for are the ones spent with the team. When Owl Labs asked where people feel most productive, they pointed to the office for collaborating (55%), meeting new people (56%), and being mentored (52%). Being together in person still matters.

5. Improved mental health

Isolation takes a toll. Working fully alone can deepen loneliness, dull social skills, and worsen symptoms of depression for some people.

On the other hand, interacting with others seems to boost mental health and productivity for many.

The keyword is balance, and it’s one of the hybrid work advantages every hybrid work influencer keeps returning to.

6. Flexibility in the hybrid workplace

Flexibility has become one of the perks candidates weigh most heavily. In Owl Labs’ 2025 report, 40% of workers said they’d start job hunting if flexible work were taken away, and another 22% would expect a raise to make up for the lost flexibility. Keeping talent now means offering flexibility.

Hybrid work serves both sides. Companies keep a physical space where culture takes shape, and people get to work partly from home while still coming in.

Adopting a hybrid policy also keeps communication open about how work happens. As an employer, you have options:

  • Require your employees to be in the office a set number of days per week (for example, 2 mandatory days)
  • Ask employees to work in the office most of the time while allowing occasional remote work
  • Make remote work the norm, with the option to come into a physical office.

The right setup often depends on the role. Either way, hybrid models give both employer and employees plenty of room to arrange work around real life.

7. Better work-life balance

One of the strongest hybrid work advantages is improved work-life balance. A well-designed workspace gives people the flexibility they need.

Team members don’t have to pick office or remote. They get both, without choosing between work and personal life or losing hours to a daily commute.

Gallup’s data supports this: most hybrid workers say the arrangement improves their well-being and their productivity. Over the long run, that satisfaction is what keeps people, which still matters in the years since the Great Resignation.

8. Access to wider talent pools

Working from one office with no remote option limits you. You can only hire from your immediate area.

With a hybrid setup, you can hire talent internationally. Diversity has been shown to improve the bottom line for many businesses, and a flexible policy is a real advantage for your employer brand.

9. Building trust

The pandemic proved employees stay productive at home, and the data has only strengthened since. In Owl Labs’ 2025 report, 90% of hybrid workers said they’re just as productive or more productive, and 69% of managers agreed their teams got more done.

Hybrid work raises comfort levels on both sides. Employers can track productivity by building it into the organization’s OKRs. Employees get a better work-life balance. Trust runs both ways.

10. Reduced real estate costs

Space utilization and cost reduction are the employer-centric advantages. Hybrid work lets organizations shrink their office footprint and cut real estate spend. Some companies grew their teams over the past few years without buying more space.

OfficeRnD Workplace handles this. Our system helps you run hot desking, where you reduce the number of dedicated desks and use space only when it’s needed.

Fewer desks means lower overhead. That frees up resources for other uses and cuts the risk of common hybrid work mistakes.

11. The hidden gem of hybrid work: creativity through solitude

There’s an advantage that gets overlooked: the creative thinking that comes from quiet, solitary time away from the office.

Most discussion of hybrid work focuses on collaboration and connection. The solitary hours matter too, and they can be where new ideas take shape.

The solitude-creativity link

Offices are built for collaboration, where ideas get shaped through constant interaction. That misses one part of the creative process: the need for solitude. Deep thinking and new ideas often come during uninterrupted time, which a remote day makes easier to find.

The science behind it

Psychological research supports this. Solitude is linked to creativity because it makes room for reflection, daydreaming, and an uninterrupted flow of thought.

Away from a busy office, people can go deeper into their thinking and explore ideas that wouldn’t surface in a group.

Hybrid work gets both

Hybrid models make room for both kinds of work. Alternating between collaborative office days and focused remote sessions lets employees use the strengths of each.

The office gives people a space for collaboration and quick feedback. Remote days give them time to think and develop new ideas.

Most hybrid challenges come down to logistics, and the right software solves them. Technology is what makes the shift work day to day.

  • Book desks and meeting rooms before heading in

Name: 5 Inspiring Hybrid Work Model Examples From Big Companies [2024]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: The COVID-19 pandemic has made many employees worldwide realize that they don’t need to be in the office all day to stay productive.
Post body:
The COVID-19 pandemic has made many employees worldwide realize that they don’t need to be in the office all day to stay productive.

As a result, hybrid work is becoming popular. According to research by Microsoft, 52% of people are likely to consider switching to a fully remote or hybrid company in the next year.

Hybrid work comes in different shapes and forms, which leaves companies wondering which setup would best suit their needs and ensure employee engagement.

This article will explore the main different types of hybrid work model examples so you can pick the one that would best fit your workplace. Moreover, it will show how some of the top companies thrive in hybrid models.

Quick Summary: The five different types of hybrid work models are as follows:

  1. Mandatory office with a few flex days
  2. Office-first with optional remote work
  3. Hybrid (or 50/50 split)
  4. Remote-first with optional office visits
  5. Only from home with few onsite days

The right type of hybrid work model depends on the type of business you run and your employees’ needs.

Let’s dive into the five main hybrid work models.

Adopting the right hybrid work model for your organization can make or break your business. Take this short quiz to learn which model suits you best.

5 Hybrid Work Model Examples

Wondering what hybrid work model examples exist and which would best fit your business? Here are the five different hybrid work models, along with examples of companies that have adopted them:

Model #1: Mandatory Office With a Few Flex Days

For companies under this work model, working in the office remains a priority. However, this doesn’t mean that employees don’t work remotely from time to time.

Example:

At Goldman Sachs, working in the office remains a priority. According to its CEO, David Solomon, in an interview with Fortune magazine: “Remote work is not ideal for us, and it’s not normal. It’s an aberration that we’re going to correct as quickly as possible.”

The company believes that its best collaborative work comes when employees share ideas in the office. That said, individual managers can set up flexible work arrangements for employees who request it.

Model #2: Office-First With Optional Remote Work

Here, most employees work predominantly from the office, with the option or obligation to work from home once in a while.

Companies with an office-centric model usually have a baseline (e.g., three mandatory days per week onsite) and allow their employees to decide where to work for the rest of the time.

Example:

At JP Morgan, employees are under the obligation to work at the company office three days a week. However, employees also have the option to work from home during the last two work days of the week if that’s what they prefer. Only a small portion of their workforce works remotely full-time.

In fact, a few months ago, the company announced that it would cease hybrid working for its senior staff.

Model #3: Hybrid (or 50/50 Split)

A hybrid office environment offers employees the best of both worlds. Under the hybrid workplace model, companies opt to have their employees work in the office half the time and remotely the other half.

Example:

Microsoft understands that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution when it comes to how employees prefer working. Under its hybrid work policy, employees can choose how they’d prefer working, whether that’s at home or in the office.

Employees can also talk to their managers about the work hours that would best fit them, and, depending on their job, they may be able to choose which remote location(s) they’d like to work from.

Model #4: Remote-First With Optional Office Visits

With this model, remote is the default way of working, but the office is still open for everyone. Depending on the company and what its employees want, visits to the office may be optional or mandatory (once a week or every other week, for example).

In some cases, under this hybrid model, remote employees can choose the remote location they’d like to work from. This means they can be digital nomads, or employees who “hop” from location to location if they choose to.

Example:

Atlassian is a remote-first company that gives its remote workers full control over where and when they’d like to do their jobs.

As part of its guiding principles, Atlassian wants its employees “to explore the world or spend time with far-flung family and friends if that’s what keeps them energized and balanced.”

Employees can live in any of the 13 countries in which Atlassian has legal entities. As such, under this work model, Atlassian can hire employees from all over the world — giving them access to the best possible talent pool and adding diversity to its workforce.

Model #5: Only From Home With Few Onsite Days

In this model, aside from a few days of the year when the company’s employees must show up to the office, home is these employees’ main workplace.

Example:

At Salesforce, office workers have the option to work from home full-time if their job allows it. They only have to show up to the office for special company events.

“An immersive workspace is no longer limited to a desk in our Towers,” says Brent Hyder, Chief People Officer at Salesforce, in an article for Salesforce. “The 9-to-5 workday is dead, and the employee experience is about more than ping-pong tables and snacks.”

How to Create a Hybrid Work Model for Your Business

As you can see, there’s lots of variety when it comes to hybrid work models, and even the biggest companies in the world are still learning and experimenting. Here are a few common tips and ideas we found in many hybrid work strategies:

  • Talk to your team members. The last 2 years were unlike anything we’ve ever experienced. Things changed so much that your team members might be dealing with issues you hadn’t even thought of. That’s why you need to talk to them about what they’re struggling with, what’s working, what isn’t, what they’re missing, and so on. Also, asking what can be done to ensure they feel safe post-COVID is essential.
  • Create a workplace safety policy. Again, you need to ensure everyone is safe before returning to the office. Microsoft’s safety guidelines are a great example since they use local COVID-19 case data to encourage or discourage people from coming to the office. You don’t need to be so detailed, especially if you have just one office, but you still need to write a clear safety policy and distribute it to employees.
  • Define what a successful hybrid transition means for your business. Is it an increase in productivity, employee well-being, office space usage, better hiring options, stronger company culture, or a combination of many factors? You don’t know what you can’t measure, so defining success early and gathering feedback continuously are both essential for the integrity of your workplace.
  • Keep an open mind. For a while, we’re all in experimentation mode. The model you start with might not be the best for your goals, so don’t be afraid to switch things up. Like Brett Hautop (VP of Workplace at LinkedIn) says: “I think everybody realizes that we’re all figuring this out together…Only when people aren’t afraid to be around each other will we know the true amount of time they’re going to spend at home versus the office.”

Continue reading on how to build your own hybrid work policy.

Use Technology for a Smooth Transition to Hybrid Work

Hybrid work is here to stay, and modern offices must adapt. But it comes with a significant challenge: office space management.

But how do you ensure that your hybrid employees — who don’t have assigned desks — find available workstations on days when they want to work in the office? You don’t want your employees to have to scramble to find a space to do their work.

That’s where OfficeRnD Workplace comes in. Our hybrid workspace management solution gives you all the tools you need to better manage your workplace.

Here’s just some of what you can do with our software:

  • Create a visual floor plan of your office. A visual floor plan lets everyone in the company see which desks and rooms are available in real-time.
  • Allow your employees to easily book desks and meeting rooms with any device. Working without dedicated desks can easily get hectic, so it’s crucial for everyone to book a desk before coming to the office.
  • Show team members who else will be in the office. People who want to return to the office often yearn for in-person teamwork and collaboration, so knowing who will be there is vital for them.

What to Look for in a Tool That Integrates With MS Teams

When considering software that integrates with Microsoft Teams, evaluating several factors is essential to ensure a seamless and productive experience. Here are some key considerations to keep in mind:

  • Compatibility and integration: Make sure the software is fully compatible with the latest version of Microsoft Teams. Double-check whether the integration is surface-level or deep. Surface-level integration may only allow certain features, while deep-level integration provides full-feature access within Microsoft Teams.
  • Ease of installation: The integration process needs to be simple, with clear direction and support. Ideally, you’ll want to look for software that offers a “plug-and-play” experience.
  • Security: Ensure the software complies with industry-standard security protocols. Read reviews to determine whether previous customers have complained about the software’s security features.
  • User experience: Ensure the software isn’t too complicated and doesn’t require extensive staff training. It also shouldn’t disrupt the natural flow of your current processes. It’s best to look for software that has a similar UI to Microsoft Teams.
  • Performance: The software shouldn’t slow down current processes in Microsoft Teams. You can try a free trial of the software to test this. Or, if the tool doesn’t offer a free trial, check online reviews for any mention of its performance.
  • Support and updates: Make sure the software provider offers great customer support so you can get issues resolved quickly. The provider should also release frequent updates to maintain compatibility with Microsoft Teams.
  • Customizability: You may want the software to be customizable to your company’s specific needs. Look for customizability features or check online reviews.
  • Cost: Evaluate the software’s pricing models. Consider whether their monthly, yearly, or one-time payment option will give you the most bang for your buck. Also, ensure all the features you need are included in the plan you choose.

Name: 6 Proven Standing Desk Benefits [According To Experts]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Note: This article was fact-checked by Margaret Trashian MD .
Post body:
Note: This article was fact-checked by Margaret Trashian MD.

Sitting for extended periods can be a source of discomfort for workers, causing a slouched posture and strained neck that can lead to various aches and pains.

Using a standing desk may reduce the physical strain on your body, maintain an active working posture, and enhance productivity throughout the day.

This article will explore the many standing desk benefits and how it can improve your overall well-being.

Quick Summary

  • Research suggests that sedentary lifestyle choices and prolonged periods of time spent sitting can present multiple health risks, including neck strain, bad posture, and blood clots.
  • A standing desk or sit-stand desk can reduce the amount of time office workers spend sitting, and contribute to a more healthy lifestyle and a number of other health benefits.
  • In addition to the physical health benefits, standing desks can also boost productivity and improve employee satisfaction.

What Are the Physical Standing Desk Benefits?

A standing desk can have many physical benefits, including improved heart health, reduced sedentary behavior, enhanced productivity, and fewer musculoskeletal issues.

Improved Heart Health

The prolonged use of a sit-stand workstation has increased the time spent being active each day, resulting in positive changes in some heart health indicators.

Targeting sedentary work behaviors presents significant opportunities for effective intervention strategies to improve lifestyle habits.

Given the increased number of individuals working remotely from home due to the COVID-19 pandemic, reducing sedentary behavior is now more crucial than ever.

Research emphasizes the vascular health benefits achieved by simply substituting sitting with standing.

Check out this intuitive desk booking system in Office365.

Reduced Sedentary Behavior

Scientific studies have shown that not getting enough exercise and spending too much time sitting can negatively affect long-term health.

Sedentary behavior includes activities that don’t require much physical effort, like sitting, watching TV, reading, or driving. In the past 50 years, jobs that involve sitting have increased by 83% and now make up 80% of all jobs in the US.

This sedentary lifestyle has been linked to various health problems, including heart disease, cancer, and diabetes.[1]

Because so many people have sedentary jobs, finding ways to help employees be healthier is important. One solution that has gained popularity is using standing desks. To measure the impact of standing desks on health, researchers looked at how the blood vessels in the arms and legs functioned.

The health of these blood vessels is important because they can affect the risk of heart problems.

The researchers found that using a standing desk improved the function of the arm blood vessels, which suggests a reduced risk of cardiovascular events.[2]

Enhanced Work Performance

Sedentary behavior increases the risk of physical and mental health disorders and affects job performance, work engagement, and presenteeism (being present at work but not fully productive).

Improving workers’ health can lead to more energetic employees, a better work environment, and increased productivity.

Studies have shown that physical activity, such as exercise, can improve work engagement. Additionally, reducing the sitting time during the workday has been associated with increasing employee vitality and enthusiasm.

Employees with higher health risks also tend to experience more productivity loss due to poor physical health, including musculoskeletal issues like neck and back pain.[3]

Less Musculoskeletal Issues

Introducing sit-stand desks to reduce sitting time among desk workers and its impact on their health and work performance was measured:

Over three months, the intervention group showed a decrease in the amount of time spent sitting during work compared to both the pre-intervention and control groups.

The participants reported improved subjective health and experienced less neck and shoulder pain. Regarding work efficiency, the intervention group showed increased vitality and higher self-assessment of their performance.

These findings suggest that using sit-stand desks can reduce sitting time and positively affect health and workplace productivity.[4]

Some studies have shown that clerical work done while standing can lead to a higher energy expenditure (EE) compared to sitting. For example, one study suggested that full-time standing workers may burn an additional 384 calories per day compared to those who sit.[5]

While EE is an important focus, it’s worth considering other potential health benefits associated with standing compared to sitting.

Maintaining an upright posture while standing can lead to greater activation of muscles in the lower back and pelvic region compared to passive sitting postures.

This increased muscle activation is known to influence changes in metabolic rate. Similarly, standing posture has been found to activate thigh muscles more than sitting.[6]

Lastly, the subjective experience of comfort, fatigue, and preference during the standing posture should not be overlooked, as these factors can affect workers’ productivity.[7]

With the rise of the virtual office, many people have remote, hybrid, or flexible work arrangements whereby switching to a standing desk can be a simple yet effective way to promote a healthier and more comfortable work environment.

What Are the Cognitive Benefits of Using a Standing Desk?

The effectiveness of standing desks in reducing sedentary behavior in office settings is well-established, but what about their impact on cognitive productivity?

Improved Employee Satisfaction

An experimental study lasting 15 weeks was conducted with adults who used standing desks for their office tasks. The study showed that discomfort was reduced, which could positively impact task performance and overall job satisfaction. It is reasonable to assume that work efficiency and productivity could be promoted in office environments with stand-capable workstations.[8]

Increased Productivity

Employee productivity was assessed in a call-center environment for six months to compare the effects of stand-capable offices, which included standing desks.

The study used the company’s performance metric software to measure productivity. The results indicated that employees assigned to stand-capable desks exhibited higher productivity than those using traditional seated desks.[9]

During the six months, stand-capable employees had an average of 0.5 more successful calls per hour than their seated counterparts. This increase in successful calls resulted in significant additional revenue, as the company’s revenue was based on the completion of successful calls.[10]

Employees assigned to stand-capable workstations reported significantly lower body discomfort compared to seated controls and demonstrated the cognitive benefits of standing desks.[11]

Tips for using a standing desk

While there’s plenty of scientific evidence showing the potential health benefits of using ergonomic standing desks, there are a few things you can do to help yourself out.

Alternate Between Sitting and Standing Positions

Any cashier or server will tell you that standing on your feet all day can come with some serious discomfort. Make it a point to go sit in the break area, or catch up with a coworker.

If you’re working from home, go sit down outside and get some fresh air for a few minutes. You’ll feel refreshed and more energized once you go back to finish whatever you’re working on.

Stand On a Cushioned Mat

Working at a standing desk for extended periods of time is much more comfortable with a cushioned mat.

With more people opting for a standing setup, there are tons of extremely comfortable standing mats on the market to choose from.

Take a Break Every Few Hours

No matter how you work, every human body needs a break every now and then.

Office workers, remote employees, and hybrid teams can all benefit from stepping away from their workstations every two or three hours during the workday to stretch out or go for a short walk.

Position Height Adjustable Desks and Computer Screens Properly

Standing up while you work isn’t going to help you at all if you’re still having to strain to see what you’re working on. Follow the instructions and fitting setup guide to find the optimal height and placement for your desk.

(Image Source)

The Consensus on Stand-Up Desks

Using standing desks offers numerous benefits for physical and cognitive well-being in the workplace.

The negative effects of prolonged sitting have become increasingly evident, and standing desks provide a practical solution to combat these issues.

By incorporating standing into the work routine, individuals can reduce sedentary behavior and improve their overall health. From a physical standpoint, studies have shown that standing desks can improve cardiovascular health, vascular function, and cardiometabolic indicators.

Standing while working can reduce the risks associated with prolonged sitting, such as musculoskeletal problems and poor physical health.

Additionally, the introduction of standing desks has been linked to increased productivity, vitality, and employee engagement.

The ability to move and maintain an active posture while working can positively impact both physical comfort and mental focus. The cognitive benefits of using standing desks are also noteworthy. Employees who use standing desks report reduced discomfort and improved task performance, contributing to enhanced work efficiency and productivity.

Studies have shown that stand-capable workstations in office settings can significantly decrease body discomfort and a substantial increase in successful calls per hour compared to traditional seated desks.

These findings highlight the potential cognitive advantages of incorporating standing into the work environment.
