Name: Hot Desking Ergonomics: 7 Tips For A Healthy Workplace
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Hot desking and desk hoteling are essential in today’s hybrid work environment. But despite the renewed focus on employee well-being, Deloitte’s 2023 Well-being at Work survey found that most employees say their health stayed the same or worsened over the past year.
Post body:
Hot desking and desk hoteling are essential in today’s hybrid work environment. But despite the renewed focus on employee well-being, Deloitte’s 2023 Well-being at Work survey found that most employees say their health stayed the same or worsened over the past year.

Smart pre-planning and ergonomics are the keys to making hot desking work for your hybrid workplace.

This article will explore how hot desking ergonomics and thoughtful workplace design can provide a more comfortable and enjoyable environment for your hybrid employees.

Quick Summary

  • Key components of hot desking ergonomics include physical safety, comfort, productivity, and mental well-being.
  • Hot desking comes with various ergonomic challenges, such as desk space issues, poorly fitting workspaces, office clutter, and a lack of accessories to protect your hybrid office workers’ health and keep them comfortable.
  • Hybrid offices can improve their hot desking ergonomics by including illustrated seat adjustment guides in shared workspaces, implementing ergonomic accessories like document holders and keyboard trays, and having designated break areas and storage units.

The 4 Essentials of Workspace Ergonomics

Let’s start with the four essentials of workspace ergonomics:

1. Physical Health and Safety

According to The State of Employee Safety in 2023 report from Alert Media, 80% of employees believe that physical safety is important in the workplace. However, 75% also believe that efforts from employers to keep them safe haven’t been effective.

An ergonomic workspace prioritizes the physical safety of its hybrid employees so they can stay healthy while working.

2. Comfort

Working while sitting for hours at a time can be uncomfortable and strain your hybrid employees’ bodies. It can also hurt their posture, leading to back problems in the long run.

Ergonomic offices must optimize hybrid employees’ workstations for comfort. They allow these individuals to work for long hours without experiencing any strain on their bodies. Comfort is important to support people who have different working styles.

Are you using a desk booking system? Check this one that integrates with Microsoft Office 365.

3. Productivity

Nothing is less productive than a hybrid employee who’s unable to work — either at home or in-office — due to a sprained wrist or hip problems from sitting too long on uncomfortable furniture.

When it comes to workspace ergonomics, companies that rely on hybrid offices should consider how their design and furniture choices can both mitigate the harmful effects of bad ergonomics and, at the same time, choose implements that boost productivity.

This can be as simple as installing blue light blocker apps on computer workstations to reduce computer vision syndrome or using furniture like supports for the feet and desks stationed at the right height. This keeps the whole body, including the back, neck, and feet, in the ideal position to remain relaxed but alert.

4. Mental Well-being

Can you really support mental well-being with smart ergonomics? Yes — and it all comes down to safe working conditions.

Kevin Lombardo, President and CEO of wellness-based pain management company DORN, found that “companies that continued to invest in total worker wellness initiatives saw a corresponding reduction in ergonomic injuries.”

In other words, companies that prioritize mental health are more likely to have workers who experience fewer ergonomic-related injuries. Furthermore, Lombardo’s company found that the use of targeted ergonomic solutions in the workplace can reduce pain and stress and improve employee morale by 85%.

And that’s important because, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), companies lose 12 billion working days per year to employee depression and anxiety and $1 trillion per year in lost productivity.

For your hot desking strategy to work, you’ll need to create an ergonomic workspace where hybrid employees can balance work and relaxation in well-integrated spaces.

Common Ergonomics Challenges in Hybrid Workspaces

While flexible working provides employees with more control over their schedules, this work model comes with a set of challenges. These include the following:

  • Uncomfortable or poorly fitting desks: In a hot desking arrangement, an employee who decides to work in the office may find themself at a workstation that’s customized for someone who’s significantly larger or smaller than they are. This can lead to them scrambling to find a more comfortable space or wasting time trying to find a phone book to use as a booster seat.
  • Lack of ergonomic office equipment: Many workplaces lack the proper ergonomics accessories to keep employees healthy while eliminating back pain and bad posture. Footrests, keyboard trays, glare screens, headsets, and ergonomic mice can help avoid long-term damage to your team’s health. Check out some must-have hot desking accessories here.
  • Lack of break areas and storage space: Employees need areas to unwind, stretch, and catch up with their colleagues. Designated break rooms and lounge areas can help them recharge and be more productive when they go back to their desks. Since employees in a hot desking workplace don’t have their own desks, they often have nowhere to store their personal items. This can lead to clutter since they may have to place their belongings on the floor instead.

7 Best Practices for Improving Hot Desking Ergonomics

What are challenges if not opportunities to innovate?

With a solution like hot desking, there are several ways in which you can overcome ergonomics hurdles and create an environment in which your employees can do their best work:

1. Illustrated Seat Adjustment Guides

If 6-foot-something Alex used a workstation yesterday that barely-5-foot Mia reserved for today, some adjustments would likely be in order for Mia to be able to work comfortably.

Having illustrated guides in shared workspaces can help employees correctly adjust their chairs. Ergonomic chair adjustment guides should address the following:

  • Seat: how to adjust the height, depth, and angle of the seat
  • Backrest: how to adjust the height and angle of the backrest
  • Armrest: how to adjust the height and width/pivot of the armrests

2. Designated Break Areas

To help hybrid employees feel more at home when they enter the office, designate spaces where they can relax, socialize with other workers, and recharge.

Offering a quiet meditation area or including relaxing, reclining furniture in communal break rooms can help take the strain off their bodies when they go on a break.

These ideas promote positive mental health and give your employees the relaxing spaces they need during each workday.

3. Standing Desks

While they might not be for everyone, having a few standing workspaces in the office can be a great option for employees who are more comfortable working from a standing position.

However, rather than going all-in on standing desks, start with a few and see how popular they are among employees. If they aren’t being utilized, you can always transition back to traditional seated workspaces.

4. Implement Storage Units for Personal Items

A cluttered workspace makes it harder to focus and be productive. Hot-desking employees need places to store their personal belongings when they decide to work in the office.

Make sure to have locker rooms and storage units in your shared office spaces so your hybrid employees can drop off their belongings when they arrive at the office.

5. Keyboard Trays and Laptop Stands

Chairs aren’t the only part of a shared workstation that employees might need to adjust for a better fit. Keyboard trays allow employees to adjust the angle and height of their keyboard so they can type and use their mouse more comfortably.

Along those same lines, a laptop stand can help employees adjust their laptops to eye level and improve their posture.

6. Document Holders

Data entry can be a slow-going and uncomfortable process when an employee is constantly looking back and forth between their computer screen and the source document they’re working on.

Document holders make things a lot easier by holding documents closer to the monitor. Making documents easier to read and transpose can keep employees from spending their workday in uncomfortable or twisted working postures.

7. Keyboard Shortcuts

Keyboard shortcuts allow employees to use a few quick keyboard strokes instead of going back and forth between their keyboard and mouse to perform actions on their computer.

Mastering keyboard shortcuts in commonly used applications can help employees work more comfortably and be more productive. Here are the latest Windows 11 keyboard shortcuts that save a lot of work.

Consider offering training for employees so they can learn keyboard shortcuts that can make their job easier. For instance, you can offer specialized training for keyboard shortcuts for:

  • General keyboard shortcuts
  • Microsoft Excel shortcuts
  • Microsoft Word shortcuts
  • Internet browser shortcuts
  • Application or program-specific shortcuts.

Name: How Much Office Space Do I Need in 2026? [Full Answer]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: “How much office space do I need?” tends to come up at two moments: when a lease is up for renewal, or when your headcount changes.
Post body:
“How much office space do I need?” tends to come up at two moments: when a lease is up for renewal, or when your headcount changes.

Hybrid work is the default for most knowledge teams now, and that changes the math. The number that drives your office size is how many people come in on your busiest day, not your total headcount.

Below are the 2026 benchmarks, a clear method, and a worked example you can copy.

Quick answer:

Most hybrid offices plan for 150 to 250 square feet per employee at average density. The bigger lever in 2026 is your desk-to-attendance ratio. Size your desks to peak-day attendance, add space for meeting rooms, focus rooms, and break areas, then add 10 to 20% for growth.

Why office space still matters for hybrid teams

The office earns its cost when it does the things home can’t.

In-person time helps with problem-solving and teamwork, onboarding new people, and the quick back-and-forth that drives real collaboration.

Getting the amount right matters in both directions. Too much space and you pay rent on desks nobody uses. A half-empty floor can also leave people feeling isolated and less productive.

Too little space and people arrive to find no free desk on busy days, on top of the health and safety problems that come with a cramped floor.

The attendance shift you’re planning around

One thing has moved fast over the past year: office attendance has hardened.

JLL’s 2026 occupancy benchmark found the share of employees in the office three to four days a week jumped from 36% to 55% in a single year, while one-to-two-day attendance fell from 31% to 20%. Fixed in-office days are now required by 62% of organizations, up from 49% the year before.

If your plan still assumes light, unpredictable attendance, your busiest days will run short on desks. Plan for your peak day.

How do you calculate office space needs for hybrid workplaces?

The exact answer depends on several factors. Space planners still sort offices into three density bands:

  1. Low density (spacious): 250 to 500 square feet per employee. Common in law and architecture firms built around private offices.
  2. Average density: 150 to 250 square feet per employee. A mix of private offices, shared workstations, and meeting rooms. Most offices land here.
  3. High density: 80 to 150 square feet per employee. Mostly shared desks, with few private offices. Common in call centers and cost-focused teams.

The direction of travel is tighter space. Industry benchmarks show target density moving from about 165 toward 132 square feet per person as shared desks replace assigned ones.

Here’s a fuller guide on the amount of office space per hybrid employee. With the density bands in mind, here’s what to work through.

Your current situation

Different businesses need different amounts of office space, so start by assessing where you are.

How many employees do you have, and what types?

The count matters, and so does the role. Senior executives often need private offices, which means more space per head. Support and admin staff usually work in an open layout and need less.

How many work full-time vs part-time in the office? Do any work 100% remotely?

Some departments, like HR, may be in the office full-time. Others may rarely come in. In a hybrid setup, most people split their week between the office and home.

What hybrid work policies do you run?

Some companies set fixed in-office days and let people work remotely the rest of the week. With that model you need enough space for your busiest days, not so much that the floor sits empty on quiet ones.

Others rotate teams between on-site time and remote spaces on a set schedule. Here you size for your biggest department on-site.

Some managers let people choose their own days as long as they hit a minimum. As with fixed-day models, plan for the peak.

Desk-to-employee ratios are how you cut space without cutting seats people actually need. The common 2026 range is 3 to 7 desks per 10 employees, depending on how often people come in. With attendance rising, lean toward the higher end of that range.

Our data shows midweek (Tuesday to Thursday) now drives near-full occupancy, with Mondays and Fridays lighter. Size for those midweek peaks. Read more on occupancy planning and on hybrid work cost savings, where you’ll find a calculator.

Staff who are in every day may need dedicated desks. For people who come in occasionally, a desk-sharing system frees up room.

To see hybrid models in action, read “6 Hybrid Work Model Examples from Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and more.”

The office layout

How an office is laid out affects people more than they expect.

A poor layout isolates people, makes it hard to concentrate, deters collaboration, and raises the risk of spreading illness.

Some questions to help you find the right layout:

Who needs a private office, who needs a dedicated workstation, and who can use a shared desk?

Senior executives may need their own offices. Others only need a dedicated workstation. For everyone else, hot desking or desk hoteling saves space.

OfficeRnD Workplace lets people book desks and meeting rooms, so you can run a tighter footprint with confidence.

What communal areas do you need, and how many of each?

Communal areas might include:

  • conference rooms
  • quiet rooms
  • a break room
  • a reception area
  • a file room
  • hallways
  • bathrooms

The higher your density, the more communal space you’ll need to keep it comfortable.

Your company’s growth plans

How many people, and what types, do you plan to hire over the next few years?

It’s smart to assess where you are today, and just as smart to leave room for the hires you expect. You don’t want to sign a lease and outgrow it in a year.

Because moving offices is expensive, add 10 to 20% to your estimate for future growth.

Size from your attendance data

Headcount tells you how many people you employ. Attendance tells you how many need a desk at the same time. In a hybrid office, those are different numbers, and the second one sets your desk count.

Two figures do most of the work:

  • Average daily attendance sets your baseline.
  • Peak-day attendance, usually a midweek day, sets your ceiling, so nobody is left standing on the busiest day.

Pull both from your booking and check-in data. OfficeRnD Workplace reports desk and room utilization by day and floor, so you can see your real peak instead of guessing.

Quick method: take your peak-day attendance, add a 10 to 15% comfort margin, and that’s your desk target. A 200-person team that peaks at 120 on Wednesdays needs about 135 desks, well under the 200 a desk-per-person plan would buy.

You can check out our list of the best space management tools to learn more.

Don’t forget meeting and collaboration space

People increasingly come in to meet, so meeting space is where many plans go wrong. The pattern in 2026: most meetings are small, but most rooms are big.

Booking data across workplaces shows roughly 80% of meetings happen in rooms built for 6 or fewer people, while large boardrooms of 17 seats and up sit near 12% use. About 40% of booked rooms end as no-shows.

Plan more small rooms and focus booths, and fewer oversized boardrooms. Track room use the same way you track desks, then adjust. Conference rooms typically need 15 to 30 square feet per person who’ll use them.

How much office space do I need? An example

Say your hybrid company is in finance or tech and wants an average-density office.

You have 500 employees. Your policy is three days a week on-site, and most teams pick Tuesday to Thursday.

At average density, plan 150 to 250 square feet per person. Take 200. For a traditional office with a desk for everyone, that’s 100,000 square feet (200 x 500), and every employee gets their own desk.

But your people work remotely part of the week, so not everyone is in at once. With a three-day midweek policy, peak-day attendance often runs 60 to 70% of headcount. Say 65%, or about 325 people on a busy Wednesday. Add a 10% margin and you need roughly 360 desks.

That brings your floor area to about 72,000 square feet (360 x 200), before you trim further with shared desks for occasional visitors.

An older 1:2 rule would put you at 250 desks and 50,000 square feet. That worked when midweek attendance was lighter. At 2026 attendance levels it leaves Wednesdays short on seats. Run the math on your own peak-day number and you’ll land close to your real requirement.

Pros and cons of an office for hybrid work

If you’re unsure about taking an office at all, here’s the short version.

Pros of getting an office space

  • Looks professional
  • A place to meet clients and socialize
  • Supports company functions
  • Supports your company culture

Cons of getting an office space

  • It can be expensive
  • Some people prefer a fully remote setup

That’s why you need a digital transformation roadmap.

A digital transformation roadmap is the pathway from your goals to your results. It lays out the actions and tactics that will help create a successful business transformation.

This article will explain why these roadmaps matter and how to create one.

Then, we’ll go into how digital transformation roadmaps intersect with hybrid operations specifically and give you some real-world examples of these roadmaps put to use.

Quick Summary

  • A successful digital transformation roadmap helps a company’s transformation goals become a digital reality.
  • Hybrid work environments intensify the need for new technologies and digital processes to facilitate idea-sharing and a more collaborative environment.
  • Successful digital transformation, especially in hybrid models, relies heavily on leadership engagement, feedback-gathering tools, appropriate technology, and high-impact digital initiatives.

What Is a Digital Transformation Roadmap?

A digital transformation roadmap is a high-level plan that outlines the steps needed to connect your strategic vision to your digital transformation goals. A roadmap makes your digital transformation strategy clear, focused, and measurable.

Digital transformation involves incorporating new technologies into all aspects of a business, leading to dramatic shifts in:

  • Operations and strategy
  • Customer engagement
  • Internal processes

This profound change can be seen all around us. In fact, McKinsey & Company predicts the upcoming decade will see more technological advancements than the previous 100 years combined.

However, for your transformation strategies to work, you need direction. That’s where a digital transformation roadmap comes into play.

There’s no simple formula or one-size-fits-all solution.

To quote a 2022 research report in the Global Strategy Journal: “…digital transformation will likely look different and be different for different executives, even for those whose firms compete in the same industry or country.”

3 Key Aspects of a Digital Transformation Roadmap

Here are three key aspects of digital transformation that can help you map out your plan and its execution:

The Customer Experience

By using the right technology, businesses can enrich customer interactions and offer previously impossible levels of engagement. That promises long-term dividends.

PwC found in their 2023 Global Consumer Insights Pulse Survey that a majority of consumers have purchased products directly from a brand’s website. They expect that number will only grow.

This speaks to a broader trend: Consumers aren’t just interested in the cheapest price — they want to connect with and support their favorite companies.

Data and Analytics

In our increasingly digital world, data isn’t hard to come by. The real challenge is interpreting that data and successfully applying the insights you gain from it.

These analytics aren’t just about understanding the past but also helping to predict the future. Additionally, they drive a more personal experience for customers, increasing their satisfaction and loyalty.

And whether it’s at the strategy or tactics level, data analytics are a game-changer for decision-making.

Process Automation

Automating routine tasks isn’t about replacing humans. It’s about freeing up human capacity for more strategic roles.

Not only does automation help businesses achieve efficiency, but it can also allow for scalability and new growth opportunities.

Digital Transformation Strategy vs Roadmap

Digital transformation roadmaps are often confused with digital transformation strategies. But here’s the difference:

A digital transformation strategy provides an overarching vision. Think of it as the “why” or “what” — that is, why a business needs to transform or what its goals are.

Namely, this would include an organization’s:

  • Objectives
  • Purpose
  • Desired outcomes

A digital transformation roadmap is the practical application of that strategy. Think of it as the “how” — specifically, how a company tackles its goals and strategies.

That includes:

  • Specific steps or tasks
  • Timelines
  • Milestones

Why a Roadmap Matters

Trying to wade into the vast digital landscape without a clear, carefully thought-out plan is a recipe for disaster. Here’s what makes roadmaps so critical.

They Make Your Strategy and Goals Achievable

Digital transformation is an ambitious endeavor, but it’s more manageable when it’s broken down into digestible, actionable steps.

A structured approach helps ensure that every piece of the digital puzzle aligns with the overarching strategy.

A strategy without a concrete roadmap leads to:

  • Wasted resources
  • Misaligned effort
  • Unmet objectives

Check out the following digital transformation examples for more info.

They Give Your Transformation Clarity and Structure

Technologies are ever-shifting, and so are business paradigms.

A roadmap offers a clear trajectory without ambiguity. Defining milestones, timelines, and deliverables provides teams with a sense of direction and purpose.

That creates alignment and collaboration, and everyone understands their role as a result.

Consider a retail store transforming into an e-commerce platform. Without a roadmap, that shift can quickly become overwhelming.

But with a roadmap, the team can follow a step-by-step process — website creation, digital marketing, etc. — with each person having clearly defined roles to keep the transformation on track.

They Mitigate Risks and Challenges

Digital transformation is rife with possible pitfalls. A roadmap can help identify and plan for these challenges in advance by setting tangible milestones and providing checkpoints to evaluate progress and change course if necessary.

Regular assessments based on the roadmap can prevent costly missteps and ensure that resources are used efficiently and that goals are met.

How to Create a Digital Transformation Roadmap: Step-by-Step

This section offers a definitive guide to constructing your transformation roadmap and enabling your organization to realize its digital aspirations.

Step 1: Assess Your Current State

First, take a deep look at where you are through the following two components:

Technological

  • Catalog your existing platforms and tools. Examine why they’re relevant to your operation and how efficient they are.
  • Identify gaps or inefficiencies in your current digital capabilities. For example, maybe you’re still relying on paper-based processes or failing to capture and utilize customer data.

Organizational

  • Explore your organization’s ethos. Is there resistance to change, or is the team excited about digital prospects?
  • Conduct a skills audit to see how adept with technology your staff is and determine their training needs.
  • Review existing digital processes. Some might be streamlined with automation, while others may need a complete overhaul.

Step 2: Define Strategic Goals

First, clearly outline what you aim to achieve. What vision do you have for the future? And what methods can you use to accomplish that vision?

Maybe your objectives are a better experience for customers, improved efficiency, or both.

Align these targets with the business’s larger objectives to ensure cohesion with broader goals, such as expanding to new markets.

Then, set measurable key performance indicators (KPIs) for each goal. For example, a 20% increase in sales could be a measurable goal.

Step 3: Engage Stakeholders and Senior Management

Digital transformation affects every facet of a business. So, stakeholder buy-in is crucial. Articulate to your team the long-term value and immediate benefits of this transformation.

You can address concerns and describe the rewards in:

  • Workshops
  • Presentations
  • One-on-one meetings

Establish a clear decision-making hierarchy. While input is vital, having a structure helps streamline decisions and aligns the team’s digital transformation efforts with the roadmap.

Step 4: Choose the Right Digital Technologies and Tools

There’s no shortage of technologies available. Select the tools that align best with your needs.

For example, you may incorporate:

  • AI tools
  • Cloud solutions
  • Advanced analytics
  • Tools that integrate with MS Teams
  • Hybrid work management software

But always consider the future. These tools shouldn’t just address current challenges — they should also be scalable for upcoming demands.

Lastly, be wary of sales pitches, flashy solutions, or too many tools. Stay grounded in your goals and a broader awareness of your company’s long-term path.

Step 5: Allocate Resources

Determine the budget for each component of your roadmap. That includes the cost of the following:

  • New technology purchases
  • Potential hires
  • Training programs

Time is another resource to consider. Set clear timelines, understanding that while some tasks might be accomplished quickly, others, like a shift in culture, might take longer.

Step 6: Develop a Management Strategy

A well-thought-out management strategy will help with your digital transformation roadmap’s implementation. Identify the key players who will lead this transformation. Define a clear governance structure regarding who will do what.

Establish regular check-ins. Whether they’re weekly, monthly, or quarterly, schedule reviews to address challenges and make course corrections.

Then, adopt project management tools to ensure intentional collaboration and communication. Here’s a good list of collaboration tools.

An effective management strategy should also include:

  • Channels for feedback
  • Training and upskilling
  • Contingency plans

Step 7: Conduct a Pilot Test

Instead of implementing the roadmap company-wide, it’s wise to start with a segment. Maybe there’s a department that’s most in need or most adaptable to change.

Operate this pilot test in a controlled environment so you can easily gauge its success and any potential issues.

After the test is complete, analyze its outcomes meticulously.

Ask yourself:

  • What worked?
  • What didn’t work?
  • Did issues stem from the new process or tool itself or the team’s ability to use it?

Step 8: Roll the Roadmap Out in Phases

After you analyze the pilot test’s results, set a plan for the additional phases. Depending on the size and nature of the business, this could be department-wise or solution-wise.

Be prepared that each phase will have unique challenges. The sales department may transition easily, but logistics might run into problems.

Encourage an iterative approach.

After each phase:

  • Gather insights
  • Make the necessary tweaks
  • Move to the next phase

Step 9: Solicit Feedback

Constructive feedback is the foundation of continuous improvement.

Employ tools like surveys or feedback forms and create the following feedback loop:

  • Collect feedback
  • Analyze the feedback
  • Make improvements
  • Gather feedback again

You’ll need both employee and customer perspectives. Employee feedback is useful for optimizing internal processes, whereas customer feedback gives you insights into customer experience and preferences.

4 Tips for Ensuring Your Digital Transformation Is Successful

Navigating a digital transformation can be challenging, but these tips will help you do it right:

Tip 1: Start With a Good Leadership Team

Business leaders stand at the helm of any digital transformation journey. Their ability to guide, inspire, and anticipate changes sets the tone for the entire organization.

As stated in a 2021 report by MIT Sloan Management Review, “Efforts to lead digital transformation are unlikely to be effective without a leader’s own affective digital transformation — one that makes purpose, engagement, and fairness as important to workplace success as data-driven agility and productivity.”

Tip 2: Engage Your Employees

Digital transformation isn’t just about technology. It’s also about people.

Making sure your employees understand and embrace the change is crucial. Workshops, training sessions, and initiating feedback can bolster their engagement.

Neglecting this aspect can lead to resistance and hinder progress.

Tip 3: Help Your Team Through Change Management

As businesses evolve digitally, changes are inevitable.

Proper change management practices, such as clear communication, adequate training, and constant support, can help ease these transitions.

For example, General Electric helped their team through a successful transformation in the 2010s by training and upskilling current employees and encouraging a culture of digital innovation.

Tip 4: Leverage Data to Improve Decision-Making

Data is as good as gold. Harnessing data-driven insights can inform and optimize the digital transformation process.

Companies like Netflix have masterfully used data analytics. They use it to tailor their content, optimize user experience, and drive innovation.

Every data point that can be collected from your operating activities and customer interactions needs to be compiled and stored.

How Digital Technology Can Transform Your Hybrid Workplace

Hybrid work and digital transformation are two trends in business that go hand in hand. Here’s how hybrid work can support your transformation:

By Reshaping Operations

Cloud-based project management and collaboration platforms break down geographical constraints. This encourages business strategy to become more decentralized and agile.

And make sure any tools you use are well integrated. For example, OfficeRnD Workplace integrates with standard communication platforms like Microsoft Teams, Google Workspace, and Slack.

By Elevating the Customer Experience

Hybrid models take customer service to a new level.

Features like 24/7 virtual support and video consultations are helping companies exceed customer expectations in the digital era.

By Enhancing Adaptability

Hybrid work models keep businesses agile. This flexibility allows these companies to navigate unexpected challenges and quickly adapt.

For example, Slack transformed its approach during the pandemic to remote-first. Not only did that give them insights into their market, it better positioned the company to deploy new features quickly.

By Emphasizing Sustainability and Cost Efficiency

Thanks to video conferencing and asynchronous communication tools, many businesses’ need for physical office space, daily commutes, and in-person meetings has been greatly reduced. In addition to the cost savings, companies can tread a little lighter on the environment.

How to Make Your Roadmap Work for a Hybrid Environment

If your transformation goal is to become a hybrid company, follow these four tips specific to this type of workplace:

Start With Communication

Communication is even important when teams are dispersed.

Regular check-ins — either through video conferencing or scheduled in-person days — keep the team aligned.

Establish a feedback mechanism through a tool like SurveyMonkey or Typeform and create the right hybrid work questions. That can capture employee insights and allow them a channel for communication.

Prioritize Seamless Integration

In a hybrid world, frictionless integration is a cornerstone of operational efficiency.

Adopting all-in-one platforms that combine diverse functions, like chat, task allocation, and document collaboration, bridges the gap between remote and onsite workers.

For example, check out how OfficeRnD Workplace integrates with the most common work tools:

Further, you can prioritize cloud solutions, ensuring essential tools and documents are both easily accessible and securely stored.

Build in Flexibility

Formulate a digital transformation process that is future-proof.

Design it to flex with your hybrid workforce’s evolving demands. This flexibility will prepare you for the long haul.

Ensure Data Is Secure

With spread-out teams, safeguarding data is critical.

Advocate for using VPNs and ensure data encryption is standard practice. Periodic security audits are also crucial for identifying potential vulnerabilities and rectifying them promptly.

Examples of Digital Transformation Roadmaps

Learn from these companies who’ve already enacted their digital transformation strategies with an effective roadmap:

Adobe

Strategy: Adobe planned to become a cloud-based service provider instead of selling boxed software.

Roadmap: They achieved this transformation by launching the Adobe Creative Cloud. That included apps that allowed for seamless updates, collaboration, and a subscription-based pricing model.

DBS Bank

Strategy: Recognizing the dominance of digital banking trends, DBS aimed to become the “world’s best digital bank.”

Roadmap: DBS introduced a series of digital transformation initiatives to realize its goal.

First, they set up a mobile-only banking approach in certain markets. They also employed data analytics for real-time insights and partnered with fintech startups to integrate innovative solutions.

Lastly, they created a “digibank” offering in India, which operates without a single physical branch.

Philips

Strategy: Philips wanted to transition from being an electronics company to a health technology leader.

Roadmap: The company moved investments from its legacy businesses to health tech.

Their roadmap included the launch of connected care solutions, partnerships with hospitals for advanced medical equipment, and the establishment of digital health platforms. It emphasized predictive analytics and patient-centered care.

Name: What Is Workplace Experience And How To Improve It [2024]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Hiring and retaining the right people has never been easy.
Post body:
Hiring and retaining the right people has never been easy.

The pandemic brought down physical barriers, and people can now choose from workplaces all over the world. New work horizons, alongside factors like job dissatisfaction and wage stagnation, led to the Great Resignation — a massive wave of employee resignations starting in 2021.

Historically, companies and business leaders have focused excessively on customer experience (as they should). However, a great customer experience doesn’t happen out of the blue — motivated, engaged, and properly trained employees make it possible.

This, alongside the Great Resignation, is forcing businesses to take a closer look at the other side of the coin: workplace experience.

In this guide, we’ll answer the question, “What is workplace experience?” and explore its importance, benefits, and best practices.

Quick Summary

  • Workplace experience describes the way employees experience and interact with the physical surroundings, the digital work environment, and the workplace culture.
  • Positive workplace experiences can boost employee engagement, increase employee engagement, and improve talent retention, ultimately leading to better business outcomes and strengthening company culture.
  • Understanding how employees feel, hiring a workplace experience manager, and implementing the right workplace technology can help employees perform more meaningful work and contribute to a company’s overall success.

Let’s get started.

What Is Workplace Experience?

Workplace experience is the sum of all touchpoints employees have with the workplace environment. This environment includes three components — the physical office, the digital workplace, and the workforce — as well as the relationship between them.

Some companies also use the term employee experience instead of workplace experience to describe the same thing. However, workplace experience puts more emphasis on the additional aspects of getting quality work done, like flexibility, physical space, and digital tooling.

Why Is Workplace Experience Important?

To truly understand workplace experience and why it’s important, we need to take a holistic approach when looking at these three components and consider how they overlap. This is especially important in hybrid work environments, where people work partly in the office and partly remotely.

As Brent Hyder, President and Chief People Officer at Salesforce, said:

An immersive workspace is no longer limited to a desk in our Towers; the 9-to-5 workday is dead; and the employee experience is about more than ping-pong tables and snacks.

Considering that many employees can now work from wherever they want, it’s more important than ever to deliver a positive workplace experience if you still want them to work in the office. And, as you’ll see below, a positive workplace experience involves much more than table games and free food.

A Positive vs Negative Employee Experience

Do you ever read reviews on websites such as Indeed and Glassdoor? You know, the ones that lambast poor company culture, a toxic work environment, and a lack of meaningful work?

Well, all those reviews are the result of employee experiences.

When employees have positive experiences working at a company, they’ll typically rate that company highly. On the other hand, when their experiences are negative, they’ll leave bad reviews.

Obviously, you want to prevent negative reviews from happening, as they’ll sour your reputation for potential job candidates.

You don’t want the best talent going somewhere else, after all. Therefore, it’s imperative to create a workplace experience that guarantees employee satisfaction and supports all work styles.

What Affects the Workplace Experience?

As we’ve already mentioned, workplace experience encompasses the interactions employees have with their work environment, which is made up of the physical workspace, the digital workplace, and the workforce.

But how do these components work together to create a great workplace experience instead of a merely tolerable one — or, worse, a terrible one?

As an example, let’s take one of the most important employee experience perks — flexibility. The pandemic resulted in flexibility becoming one of the most important perks for job candidates.

However, offering options for flexible working (like fully remote or hybrid work) has implications for all three components:

1. The Physical Workplace

The physical workplace becomes more unpredictable, as not everyone works there, 9 to 5, all week.

As a result, the need to reserve a desk and see who else will be in the office arises naturally, especially with unassigned seating (i.e., hot desking or desk hoteling).

And that’s not to mention all the other things that make the office environment appealing for employees, such as comfortable lighting and ergonomic chairs.

Therefore, it’s essential for the facilities management department to collaborate with workplace leaders to design the optimal environment for employee engagement.

2. The Digital Workplace

The digital workplace has become just as important as the physical office. Employees need to have easy access to all the necessary tools to do their best work on any device from any location.

These may include using video conferencing software and a way to book meeting spaces easily. To make this transition as frictionless as possible, the IT team must be involved.

Even something as little as properly naming your meetings can make a great workplace and employee experience.

3. The Workforce

The workforce is also affected as teams become more dispersed. This means you’ll need a strong company culture and evaluation systems focused on results and performance so that employees are guaranteed equal opportunities, regardless of where they choose to work. That will result in an improved work ethic.

It also means putting guardrails in place to prevent employees from burning out, mastering a collaborative conflict style, and whatever else it takes (within reason) to keep employees engaged.

As you can see, workplace experience can get quite complex in today’s environment. Companies are scrambling to get the hang of it while rethinking their entire hiring, onboarding, and employee retention strategies.

It’s also telling that among LinkedIn’s 25 jobs on the rise in the US, four are directly responsible for providing a great workplace experience — Human Resources Analytics Manager (number 2), Diversity and Inclusion Manager (number 3), Employee Experience Manager (number 5), and Chief People Officer (number 15).

3 Benefits of Providing a Great Workplace Experience

While a great workplace experience can offer tons of different benefits, the following three are vital for pretty much every organization out there.

1. More (and Easier) Hiring Opportunities

Clearly, everyone wants to work for a company that cares about the workplace experience.

That’s why companies are including more and more components of workplace experience as part of their employee value proposition.

Again, going back to flexibility, LinkedIn data suggests that employees are 2.1 times more likely to recommend working for a company that satisfies their need for time and location flexibility.

Besides workplace experience, this also affects hiring strategies and budgets since recommendations and referrals are a much easier and cheaper way to fill positions.

The result of this trend is a 343% increase in mentions of flexibility in company posts since 2019, according to LinkedIn’s research.

2. Higher Employee Engagement and Retention

Low employee productivity, engagement, and retention are natural consequences of a poor workplace experience.

You likely won’t be too motivated to work at a company that doesn’t offer a comfortable place to get your work done (physical component), easy access to the tools you need (digital component), or has a poor culture (workforce component).

In contrast, excelling in workplace experience is a great way to ensure people are more engaged at work and reduce turnover and absenteeism.

This also benefits your clients, as employee experiences directly affect client experiences.

As this Harvard Business Review article correctly notes:

As more customers look to align their purchase decisions with their values, they have become increasingly interested in how companies engage with employees and tend to prioritize doing business with those who value their employees, treat them fairly, and prioritize their well-being. And employees are interacting with more customers more directly – and because of that the nature of employee engagement has more impact on customers.

3. More Efficient Space Usage and Lower Real Estate Costs

Human-centered workplace design is a pillar of successful workplaces.

As we said, people expect flexibility, which entails offering remote work options while also creating workspaces that suit their needs for collaboration and teamwork, as well as seclusion.

For most companies, this means implementing unassigned seating via desk hoteling, for example. Desk hoteling allows businesses to allocate office space efficiently.

This translates to improved occupancy, a greater variety of spaces dedicated to different purposes (office neighborhoods), as well as reduced desk vacancy. Another good option is designing your office with feng shui in mind.

In general, with more efficient space usage come opportunities for reducing real estate costs.

5 Best Practices for Improving Your Workplace Experience

Before we dive into the specifics, please note that there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to workplace experience.

What we’re describing here isn’t a linear process that you should blindly follow step by step. Instead, these five best practices should be treated as a starting point upon which you can customize the process based on your needs and company culture.

If you’d like to know more about what hybrid workplace trends are coming up in 2024, sign up for our upcoming webinar on Evolving Workplaces: Top Hybrid Work Trends in 2024.

1. Listen to Your Employees

The first step to most workplace initiatives is to gather feedback from your employees.

You can do this via surveys, 1-on-1 interviews, or even all-hands meetings. Your goal here is to figure out what employees are struggling with and identify areas for improvement.

Some questions you should try to answer at this stage:

  • Does the office satisfy everyone’s work needs?
  • Are work schedules flexible enough to accommodate people’s personal and professional needs?
  • Do people have access to the right tools and physical spaces to get their work done?
  • Do team members feel like they’re collaborating enough with their colleagues and managers?
  • What else can the company do to ensure a more positive experience for employees?

This is by no means an exhaustive list. Companies with different work models should also add other relevant questions.

For example, if you recently transitioned to a hybrid work model, you should add questions regarding the transition and the way you’ve organized desk sharing.

2. Make Someone (or an Entire Team) Responsible for Workplace Experience

Traditionally, HR departments have helmed employee engagement and experience programs.

But as companies start realizing the importance of workplace experience in a competitive job market, they’re also seeing the need to separate the workplace experience function.

Some companies hire Workplace Experience Managers, Employee Experience Managers, or even Chief Employee Experience Officers.

The idea is to have someone (or a group of people) responsible for overseeing, improving, and reporting on the workplace experience process.

Also, remember that workplace experience starts during the hiring process, so reassess your recruitment practices if needed.

3. Invest in a Workplace Experience Platform

As we said, workplace experience is all about three components — the physical office, the digital workplace, and the workforce — and the connections between them.

On that note, technology can help you bridge all three components, ensure a seamless experience, and boost employee engagement.

For example, here’s how a workplace experience platform can help bring people together in vibrant, collaborative, and flexible workplaces:

  • First, you can let employees book desks, meeting rooms, conference rooms, and other types of space via web and mobile apps — or even directly in Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Slack, or Google Calendar.
  • You can easily communicate company benefits, events, and policies to everyone.
  • You can also streamline facility requests and ticket management, making it much easier for your employees to report issues and track their resolution.

OfficeRnD Workplace also offers lots of other capabilities, which you can learn more about here.

4. Ensure Cross-Team Collaboration Between HR, IT Operations, Security, and Facility Teams

This process will look different depending on your organization’s size. But in any case, improving workplace experience will likely require cross-team collaboration.

HR teams are typically responsible for building and maintaining company policies, collecting employee feedback, and making sure new hires are settled into the organization.

Obviously, this has massive implications for workplace experience. That’s why the HR department is usually the first one to start considering workplace experience strategies.

IT Operations and Security teams also have to be deeply involved in the process, especially when implementing flexible work arrangements.

Your digital tools and services have to be useful and easy to access but also secure, regardless of where employees decide to work from. For example, you might want to ensure having tools that integrate with Microsoft Teams to facilitate communication even more.

Lastly, facility teams are another vital piece of the puzzle, as they take care of everything related to the company’s physical spaces.

5. Measure Workplace Experience and Adjust Accordingly

The biggest reason we started this list with the suggestion to talk to your employees is so you can have a baseline.

That way, you can know whether your workplace experience initiatives are moving in the right direction. However, you should also go further and set specific workplace experience goals, KPIs, and metrics.

For example, the Employee Net Promoter Score (eNPS) is a common way to evaluate the employee experience. eNPS measures how likely employees are to recommend your company as a good place to work.

It’s easy to calculate since employees only have to answer one question — “On a scale of 0–10, how likely are you to recommend our company as a place to work? It’s also a decent gauge of workplace experience — if the eNPS is increasing, you’re likely doing something right regarding the employee experience.

Another crucial factor to measure is workplace utilization. For that, OfficeRnD Workplace’s Advanced Workspace Analytics allows you to track space usage and understand how teams are using your office.

This data becomes the foundation for future iterations. For example, you might see that some areas of the office are barely used, while others are constantly crowded.

In these cases, re-designing the underutilized spaces to fit specific work needs (which you can uncover by talking to employees) can be a good strategy.

Implementing a hybrid work model in your company could me the key to a more productive and collaborative workforce. Take this hybrid work quiz to find out which model is the right one for you.

Elevate Your Workplace Experience With OfficeRnD Workplace

You should now know the answer to the question, “What is workplace experience?”

As you can see, there’s a lot to think about when it comes to workplace experience. And while there’s no one-size-fits-all approach, workplace technology should be at the core of creating and consistently delivering an exceptional experience.

Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Have you ever wondered how you’d describe an intelligent workplace to anyone asking?
Post body:
Have you ever wondered how you’d describe an intelligent workplace to anyone asking?

An intelligent workplace is a work environment that uses digital tools, automation, and data to help people work more efficiently and to run office operations with less friction.

The modern workplace keeps changing. With more hybrid work and steady advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI), technology plays a bigger role in how work gets done day to day.

Employees now use digital tools to automate many of their most repetitive tasks. They have tools to limit distractions, work more efficiently, and spend more time on their job’s core responsibilities.

This guide covers what an intelligent workplace is and what you can do to build one for your team.

Quick Summary

  • An intelligent workplace improves business performance by using digital technology to streamline workflows and boost productivity.
  • Key features of an intelligent workplace include automation, virtual training, employee tracking, and asynchronous communication.
  • The benefits of building an intelligent workplace include better work flexibility, improved communication, and improved business performance.

What is an intelligent workplace?

An intelligent workplace is a work environment that uses digital tools and technology to maximize employee productivity and streamline operations.

The goal is a setting where employees work more efficiently and effectively.

It involves streamlining workflows and making sure employees can reach the information and digital tools they need.

“As more companies shift to a smart hybrid working model, the demand for a smart workplace keeps growing,” says Jeremy Nunn, founder of Workmetrics, in a Forbes article.

After all, digital dexterity is at the heart of the workplace of tomorrow, where seamless integration of work through physical and virtual space, people, and technology yields better and faster output.

Intelligent workplace vs hybrid workplace: what’s the difference?

A hybrid work environment combines remote work and traditional in-office work.

These digital workplaces use cloud-based apps and asynchronous communication tools to keep team members connected, even in different time zones. They also have a strategic digital transformation roadmap.

Hybrid workplaces often use:

  • remote collaboration tools
  • instant messaging and chat tools
  • virtual meetings
  • mobile apps and office badge tools
  • web-based knowledge management

Intelligent workplaces go a few steps further. They use current technology to compile and analyze company data and employee preferences, then use that to create the conditions for people to do their best work.

Intelligent workplaces often use:

  • virtual assistants
  • digital signage
  • AI-driven search
  • advanced data analytics tools
  • smart spaces

The evolution of intelligent workplaces

The modern workplace has come a long way to become what it is today. Here’s what it has looked like, and how it’s changed, over the years:

Company intranets

Companies began using their internal networks to communicate internally and store digital files and data.

They then moved on to social intranets, which added features such as search functionality to make it easier for employees to find what they were looking for.

Virtual tools

In the 2000s, different types of virtual tools appeared that encouraged asynchronous communication and removed the requirement to be in the office to be productive.

These include workplace communication tools like video conferencing, project management platforms, and HR software. Don’t miss our guide on the most successful communication best practices.

Intelligent workplaces

Using tools like machine learning, AI, and other digital tech, companies are changing the modern workplace and how employees work.

An intelligent workplace is the result of a successful digital transformation strategy.

The benefits of building an intelligent workplace

Here’s how an intelligent workplace pays off for you and your employees:

Higher productivity

By automating repetitive, time-consuming work, employees in an intelligent workplace get more done in less time.

Automating manual tasks that are prone to human error can also improve data accuracy.

More flexibility

Employees expect flexibility, and most who work in remote-capable roles want to keep it. Gallup reports that six in 10 employees with remote-capable jobs want a hybrid work arrangement, with about a third preferring fully remote and fewer than 10% preferring on-site. Roughly half of full-time U.S. employees have remote-capable jobs.

Intelligent workplace technology gives employees more control over how and when they work.

Some become digital nomads, using technology to travel and work at the same time.

Improved communication

Intelligent workplace technology keeps essential information in one place for employees to reach anytime.

It also makes asynchronous communication possible, removing the pressure on hybrid employees to respond immediately and improving communication across time zones.

Remember, good communication is a sign of a strong work ethic.

Key features of an intelligent workplace

The digital tools used in intelligent workplaces can boost employee productivity and improve your overall business performance.

There’s a lot of technology you can use to make a workplace smarter. Here are some of the more common examples.

Automation and AI-powered tools

An intelligent workplace uses AI-powered software to automate manual processes and repetitive tasks, saving employees time.

For example, some intelligent workplaces give employees AI-powered digital assistants that work like a private secretary. These assistants handle basic tasks like formatting large data files, sending meeting reminders, booking travel, and flagging overdue tasks.

Wayfinding tools

If you’re managing a large or spread-out operation, new hires and visitors can struggle to find their way around.

Wayfinding technology helps employees and visitors navigate the building. It usually comes with mobile integration and navigation features that make it easy to reach the right destination.

Smart searches

Smart search technology is another common ingredient. It customizes search results so employees can find what they need faster.

Smart search might factor in whether the user works in engineering or HR to predict intent and return the most relevant results.

Internet of Things sensors with predictive maintenance

Power outages, network crashes, and other tech problems happen. They tend to hit when you least expect it, and they can bring work to a standstill.

Internet of Things (IoT) sensors can spot potential system issues and overdue maintenance and flag them to your IT department right away.

That lets companies fix problems before they escalate.

Virtual training

Invest in your employees so they can advance in their careers. An intelligent workplace encourages people to learn new skills and sharpen existing ones through virtual training.

Virtual training platforms worth considering include:

  • Udemy: a virtual learning platform with courses across subjects including sales, marketing, and project management.
  • Coursera: an online learning platform that offers professional certificates. Some courses come from reputable institutions and companies, including Stanford, Google, and IBM.
  • LinkedIn Learning: lessons that help employees pick up new skills, with a free first month for companies getting started.

Employee tracking

Many organizations have employees across different locations. That can make it hard for managers to see the work being done and the progress on tasks.

Hybrid work tools can help companies track individual performance.

Companies can then use that data to see how much time employees spend on different parts of their work and identify who is falling behind.

How to make your hybrid workplace more intelligent

“Traditional models for the delivery of corporate resources to employees create friction, impede productivity, degrade experience, and do not adequately support hybrid ways of working,” says Holly Muscolino, Research Vice President at IDC, in a ClearPeople article.

The intelligent digital workspace is a fundamental change in the way that we deliver those resources to workers, which puts workers at its core.

To build a more intelligent workplace, you need the right tools. And a more intelligent workplace is often a more hospitable workplace too, which lifts employee morale.

Many types of digital tools can help hybrid teams improve their processes and build a smarter workplace.

Desk booking software

If you’re managing a hybrid office team, people will need to work at the office some days. But there isn’t always a desk for everyone, and employees need to know they’ll have a spot.

With the right desk-booking software, hybrid employees can see which desks are free and reserve one before they come in. No scrambling for a seat.

Virtual conference software

Virtual conference software, including Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, lets employees set up online meetings at times that fit their respective time zones.

They just check coworkers’ calendars for availability and send invites.

Project management software

Keep track of your team’s progress. Project management software makes it easier to see which tasks you’re delegating, who’s completing what, and where everything sits in the pipeline.

Knowledge base

A knowledge base or wiki stores the critical information about your company’s processes.

This is essential for onboarding new employees who aren’t yet familiar with how things work.

For HR, facilities, and IT teams building a smarter office, it covers the practical parts: an interactive floor plan for booking desks and rooms, presence tracking with check-ins, and utilization data to inform space decisions. It integrates natively with Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Microsoft Teams, Slack, and Okta, so people book from the tools they already use.

Help your hybrid team work smarter (not harder)

Work keeps changing, and companies need the right skills and tools to keep up.

An intelligent workplace improves performance by identifying what employees need and giving them the information and tools to succeed.

Name: 9 Game-Changing Digital Transformation Trends For 2024
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: In the current fast-paced digital era, staying ahead of the curve is crucial. And as things continue to evolve, yesterday’s cutting-edge technology may not deliver the same extraordinary results tomorrow.
Post body:
In the current fast-paced digital era, staying ahead of the curve is crucial. And as things continue to evolve, yesterday’s cutting-edge technology may not deliver the same extraordinary results tomorrow.

That’s why understanding the latest digital transformation trends is vital for your organization’s success.

In this article, we’ll explore the top digital transformation trends shaping the landscape in 2023-2024. From artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to customer data platforms (CDPs) and the Internet of Things (IoT), we’ll delve into actionable strategies and practical techniques that can revolutionize your approach.

Quick Summary:

The nine most important digital transformation trends in 2023-2024 include the following:

  1. AI and ML
  2. Automation
  3. Cloud-based solutions
  4. Cybersecurity
  5. CDPs
  6. Hybrid work and workforce transformation
  7. Everything as a service (XaaS)
  8. Edge computing
  9. The IoT

Let’s dive right in!

What Is Digital Transformation?

Digital transformation is the process of using digital technology to completely transform business operations, satisfy customer expectations, and keep up with the ever-changing digital world.

It involves using digital tools, data, and ways of working to:

  • Increase productivity
  • Save time and resources
  • Make better-informed strategic decisions
  • Personalize your products or services to meet customer needs
  • Strengthen relationships with customers
  • Boost agility and innovation

With over half (53%) of global executives now fast-tracking their digital transformation, it’s time to get ahead and stay competitive in the digital age.

9 Digital Transformation Trends for 2023

Before beginning your digital transformation, you should know more about the different tools and technology businesses are using to completely rewire their operations.

Here are the nine latest digital transformation trends to look out for:

1. AI and ML

AI has been the talk of the town ever since ChatGPT exploded in the market. In fact, 35% of organizations have embraced AI in their operations, with an additional 42% considering adopting it in the future.

And it’s easy to see why. AI is driving automation, helping organizations improve customer experiences, enable data-driven decision-making, and support hybrid and remote workers.

For instance, humans are horrible at multitasking; it strains our brains. AI isn’t limited by such constraints — plus, it’s available 24/7.

So while you and I are sleeping, AI-powered work assistants are sifting through mountains of data, analyzing it, and generating valuable insights.

Businesses are using AI and ML for everything from sales forecasting and sentiment analysis to creative endeavors and customer service chatbots.

As these technologies continue to advance, their potential cost savings and applications within organizations will only become more impactful.

2. Automation

Again, AI and ML are two of the biggest forces driving automation. Automation can benefit organizations by:

  • streamlining business processes
  • reducing human error
  • increasing operational efficiency

There are two types of automation:

Robotic process automation (RPA): Software robots that automate repetitive, low-value tasks so your team can focus on more meaningful work.

Low-code no-code (LCNC) automation: LCNC platforms simplify app creation for non-technical users through visual interfaces, pre-built components, and drag-and-drop features.

For example, using an Excel spreadsheet to manually keep track of work schedules, reserve desks, and block off conference rooms is tedious and time-consuming.

Tools such as OfficeRnD Workplace simplify and streamline desk scheduling and hot desking processes.

All you have to do is integrate it with the apps you’re already using and reserve desks through your chosen platform.

Easy peasy!

3. Cloud-Based Solutions

As more companies move to hybrid work, they’re also migrating more of their workloads to the cloud. In fact, most organizations plan to spend $8 out of every $10 of their IT budget on the cloud by 2024.

There are many good reasons for this, including:

  • Cloud migration lets businesses scale resources as needed without investing in extra hardware or infrastructure.
  • Businesses save money by not needing to maintain and operate their own physical servers and hardware.
  • Cloud-based solutions liberate employees from location restrictions. They grant access to data and apps from anywhere with an Internet connection.
  • Cloud platforms offer powerful tools for working together, making it easy to communicate instantly, share files, and work on documents simultaneously. For example, check out the tools that offer integration with MS Teams.

Of course, cloud-based solutions also have potential risks. Data security is a big concern, and relying on a third-party provider means giving them control over part of your IT infrastructure.

There’s also the risk of vendor lock-in, which makes switching providers and migrating data difficult.

4. CDPs

A CDP is a customer data platform that helps to consolidate and centralize your customer data, making it more secure and accessible.

CDPs help businesses make smarter, more informed decisions that enhance customer experiences.

In addition to providing businesses with a complete understanding of their customers, CDPs offer several important benefits. For instance:

  • They gather customer data from various sources, like websites, mobile apps, social media, and stores, and then put all this data together in one central place.
  • They collect data about what customers buy, what they like, and how they interact with the company.

This helps businesses create a detailed profile of each customer so they can learn more about customers’ preferences, behaviors, and needs.

They can then use this knowledge to provide products and services that better match customers expectations.

And since customers prefer personalized customer service, a CDP can empower your customer service agents to do just that.

5. Cybersecurity

Digital transformation brings about several cybersecurity challenges and potential risks that organizations need to be aware of.

And with hybrid work on the rise, it’s easier than ever for company data to be compromised. Cybersecurity risks include the following:

  • Data breaches
  • Ransomware attacks
  • Disruption of services
  • Intellectual property theft

For example, two Australian companies — Optus and Medibank — experienced a data breach in 2022, exposing thousands of customers’ sensitive data to potential cybercriminals.

You don’t want that happening to your company, so here are some tips for enhancing your cybersecurity measures and safeguarding your sensitive data:

  • Implement strong access controls, such as good passwords, multi-factor authentication (MFA), and role-based access control (RBAC).
  • Keep your systems and software up to date.
  • Train your employees on cybersecurity awareness.
  • Encrypt your sensitive data.
  • Regularly back up your data.
  • Implement a strong firewall.

The first four tips are especially important for hybrid workers, who may handle sensitive data off-premises.

6. Hybrid Work and Workforce Transformation

We talk about hybrid work a lot on this blog, and that’s because that’s the direction the winds are blowing.

In fact, 68% of global employees prefer hybrid working, while a whopping 95% of UK executives see hybrid work as the key to making their businesses future-proof.

But to make hybrid work, well, work, you need flexible collaboration tools, remote work capabilities, and employee engagement strategies.

Fortunately, this is an area that hybrid work management platforms such as OfficeRnD Workplace specialize in. With it, you can:

  • Streamline work scheduling, desk scheduling, and meeting room booking with just a few clicks.
  • Make sure everyone is on the same page by sharing your hybrid work policies, events, and benefits straight from the software.
  • Adapt your office space for hybrid work with office maps and enable activity-based working via neighborhoods.
  • Make more informed business decisions thanks to advanced workplace analytics.
  • Facilitate in-person collaboration with advanced collaborative scheduling.

When managed properly, hybrid work can give employees the autonomy and flexibility to perform at their best. And using the right tools for that is crucial.

7. XaaS

XaaS is a business model that offers a wide range of products, solutions, and services to customers in a subscription-based or on-demand format. Think Uber, Netflix, and, yes, even our own OfficeRnD Workplace.

There are a couple of benefits of offering XaaS.

First, it helps businesses focus on what they’re good at while relying on service providers for specialized solutions. Powerful tools like OfficeRnD Workplace’s desk scheduling system can save both time and money.

Second, businesses can offer their own products and services at scale, giving them greater flexibility.

So instead of offering one movie on a DVD, they can now offer millions of movies on demand via a streaming service, like Netflix.

Just watch out for challenges related to data security, vendor selection, and integration with existing systems.

8. Edge Computing

We’ve discussed moving workloads to the cloud, but what about faster data processing?

That’s where edge computing comes in. It brings computing power and data processing closer to where the data is generated using small and powerful computers called edge devices or servers.

Edge computing offers several advantages, including:

  • It allows for faster processing by reducing data travel time.
  • It enables real-time capabilities, which are vital for time-sensitive applications like the IoT, manufacturing systems, and remote monitoring.
  • Edge devices remain reliable even with an unstable network connection, providing continuous operation.
  • It optimizes network usage and reduces latency, as only relevant data is sent to the cloud.

Edge computing and cloud computing go hand-in-hand with remote and hybrid work — allowing for faster decision-making, real-time responses, and a more agile work environment.

9. IoT

Imagine a world in which everyday objects, like your refrigerator, car, and toothbrush, can talk to each other through the Internet.

That’s the IoT, a powerful digital transformation trend that has the potential to transform businesses and industries.

The IoT can play a crucial role in supporting and enhancing hybrid work environments by:

  • Deploying sensors to optimize energy, lighting, and air quality, as well as check occupancy limits.
  • Boosting collaboration with IoT-integrated tools, like smart displays and whiteboards, that capture and share notes in real time.
  • Keeping track of assets in real-time, whether they’re remote or on-site.
  • Granting secure access with IoT-enabled control systems based on credentials or biometrics.
  • Enhancing security via surveillance cameras, motion sensors, and smart locks.

IoT can make it easier for businesses to thrive in their chosen hybrid work model while empowering facilities management. But remember to consider cybersecurity risks when implementing IoT in the workplace.

Navigating Digital Transformation Challenges and Overcoming Resistance

Preparing your company for digital transformation initiatives is a huge undertaking and requires a well-planned strategy, so it’s not surprising that there’s some resistance within the ranks. After all, the following challenges need to be addressed first:

Resistance to change: Some employees may be worried about job security, changes in roles and responsibilities, or a lack of understanding about the benefits of digital transformation.

Data management and privacy: A lot of data is generated with digital transformation, and it can be challenging to manage it and keep it private.

Legacy systems and infrastructure: Companies often have old systems that don’t work well with new tech. Integrating and updating them can be a tough and lengthy process.

Scalability and complexity: As digital transformation progresses throughout your company, you may find it difficult to scale it in a consistent, efficient, and unified manner.

Fortunately, you can address these challenges by:

  • Communicating transparently about the expected changes, benefits, and potential challenges of digital transformation.
  • Providing your employees with training to adapt to advanced technologies and processes.
  • Starting with small-scale pilot projects that deliver quick wins. People are more likely to overcome resistance when they see tangible results.
  • Implementing a change management process and involving your employees in it.
  • Continually evaluating your progress and adjusting your technique as needed.

Remember, change doesn’t come easy. But communicating effectively, keeping everyone in the loop, and tracking your progress encourages your team to adapt to the changes successful digital transformation brings. You’ll definitely need a well-planned digital transformation roadmap to succeed.

And if you want some inspiration from successful companies, check out these digital transformation examples.

Embrace the Future Today and Unlock Your Path to Success With the Right Tools

Digital transformation isn’t just a buzzword — it’s a powerful catalyst for growth and success in today’s dynamic business landscape.

Understanding and capitalizing on the latest digital transformation trends helps you revolutionize your business and stay ahead of the competition.
