Name: Hot Desking vs. Hoteling vs. Desk Sharing [Full 2026 Guide]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Adopting a hybrid work model often lands companies in a predicament: more employees than available desks.
Post body:
Adopting a hybrid work model often lands companies in a predicament: more employees than available desks.

This calls for a fresh approach to office space organization, one where desks are mainly shared, with limited or no individual assignments.

Your workplace has two options for implementing this arrangement — hot desking and desk hoteling, terms that are often used interchangeably.

When it comes to hot desking vs hoteling, the differences between these two office organization systems are vital. In this blog post, we’ll discuss these differences in-depth, so you can decide which approach to take.

We’ll also consider the benefits and drawbacks of each approach and the role technology plays in the process.

Quick Summary: In hot desking, workstations are neither assigned nor pre-booked, meaning employees don’t know where they’ll be sitting before each workday. In hoteling, employees use desk booking systems to reserve workstations prior to coming to work.

Hot Desking vs Hoteling vs Desk Sharing

Again, you may have heard terms like hot desking, desk hoteling, and desk sharing used interchangeably, so it’s easy to get the impression that they’re the same thing.

That’s not the case (which is why people often compare desk sharing vs hot desking vs hoteling), so here are the main differences between them:

  • Desk sharing is an umbrella term that denotes a work arrangement without assigned desks. Instead, desks are shared based on some principle. Hot desking and desk hoteling are two different implementations of desk sharing.
  • Hot desking is an office setup where workstations (shared desks) aren’t assigned or pre-booked, so employees don’t know where they’ll be sitting on any given day. Employees choose seats daily, either on a “first come, first serve” basis or on a rotational or shift-based principle. A hot desking arrangement offers more freedom but less control over desk availability and is often used by companies that don’t enforce office attendance. Check out our complete hot desking guide for more info.
  • Hoteling (sometimes called office hoteling or desk hoteling) lets employees reserve workstations through desk booking systems before coming to the office. Hoteling enhances employee control and removes the risk of arriving at work only to find no available workstations. It’s common in companies with mature hybrid work models, especially those with mandated weekly office days.

So, now that you know the differences, let’s talk about the pros and cons of hot desking and office hoteling.

Check out the most useful desk booking tool in Office365.

What Are the Pros and Cons of Hot Desking?

Hot desking is often employed in more flexible work environments that don’t require employees to come in regularly. At such companies, employees often switch locations weekly and drop by the office for meetings or other events.

Unfortunately, hot desking has garnered a bad reputation. It’s sometimes described as a jungle due to a lack of stability and organization, especially for employees who are used to working at the same desk every day.

However, issues with hot desking usually stem from companies trying to implement it while also enforcing office returns without providing enough workstations.

Plus, problems multiply when managers use obsolete Excel templates instead of proper software.

That said, here are the pros and cons of hot desking.

Hot Desking Pros

1. Desk availability on short notice

With hot desking, employees can show up at any time and just get to work. This arrangement can also be useful for people in the company who travel and need to stop by and do a bit of work or those who mostly work from home but want to change the scenery from time to time.

2. Greater employee freedom

Hot desking (vs desk sharing in general) takes employee autonomy to the next level. It may not seem like much for separate individuals, but for teams, it signifies trust. This setup greatly favors self-directed teams accustomed to independence.

3. Freshness, inspiration, and collaboration

Hot desking’s dynamic nature revitalizes creativity. It breaks routines and heightens alertness. As a result, it can disrupt repetitive patterns and help people approach problems differently. It also nurtures spontaneous collaboration through interactions with fresh faces.

4. Reduced costs and fast implementation

Removing dedicated desks enables increased workstation sharing, which can reduce your office space needs and minimize rental costs.

Plus, if you do decide to implement hot desking, you don’t need a lot of preparation or a complicated setup.

Hot Desking Cons

1. Limited or no seating options

The absence of assigned desks can leave employees without a place to work. Even if desks are open, they might not suit a worker’s specific needs.

Similarly, meeting rooms are also used on a first-come, first-served basis. Along with the constant movement of people coming and going, all of this may lead to drops in productivity and reduced focus.

Here’s a useful guide on the ideal office seating arrangement.

2. Communication breakdown

Communication may falter in hot desking when colleagues lack designated desks or their own private offices.

Clear communication guidelines are essential to mitigating this, as even if someone doesn’t show up at the office, they can reliably be tracked down with little effort.

3. Hierarchy disruption

Hot desking can disrupt a company’s hierarchy, which may be appealing to some businesses. However, traditional companies with a clear hierarchical structure may struggle to erase employee distinctions, possibly impacting motivation and accountability.

4. Health and safety hazards

The COVID-19 pandemic’s impact is visible across desk-sharing arrangements but is usually most pronounced with hot desking.

Numerous employees coming and going amps up the risk of diseases spreading throughout the office. Greater personal responsibility and clear safety protocols need to be put in place to minimize health risks.

As a related resource, don’t miss our article about the main differences between activity-based working and hot desking.

Lastly, you’ll have to invest in some must-have hot desking accessories to maximize its potential.

What Are the Pros and Cons of Desk Hoteling?

Before we dive in, it’s important to consider desk hoteling in the context of a hybrid workplace, where some employees work remotely on a regular basis while others split their time between working on-site and remotely.

Given this scenario, companies often hesitate to overinvest in new workstations (since they may remain unused), so they end up with more employees than desk space. That’s why it’s essential to have a proper desk reservation system in place.

Desk Hoteling Pros

1. Improved space utilization

By implementing the right office hoteling policy, desk hoteling optimizes the allocation of available office space. This translates into improved occupancy, diverse designated spaces (like office neighborhoods), and reduced desk vacancy.

By the way, feel free to use our free office space calculator to optimize your space.

2. Reduced costs

Similar to hot desking, desk hoteling leads to improved desk space utilization, which reduces real estate costs (usually one of the highest overhead costs).

3. Greater control and no uncertainty for employees

Reserving spaces in advance empowers employees to tailor their work environment according to their needs and preferences.

This proves vital in setups with designated spaces for different purposes, giving employees a choice between a conference room, silent areas, or multiple adjacent desks for collaborative endeavors.

Technology is pivotal here, and companies that opt for office hoteling vs hot desking typically use hybrid workplace management platforms to steer this process.

These systems take the burden off managers and administrators and make the workspace allocation process largely self-managed.

4. Increased employee satisfaction and collaboration

Unlike the potential chaos and alienation of hot desking, desk hoteling promotes a sense of community and connection at work — two factors that improve employee satisfaction.

This largely stems from the balance offered by working under a hybrid model while at the same time being able to control when and how to use the office.

5. Improved cleanliness and organization

In the battle between hoteling vs hot desking, the former is more effective at maintaining office cleanliness and hygiene. This is simply due to the increased accountability that comes with booking and looking after a desk for a specific duration.

Check out this article to see what the best desk booking software is for 2026.

Desk Hoteling Cons

1. The required setup

Unlike hot desking, organizations need to set up desk hoteling in advance. At a minimum, this means creating a virtual floor plan and providing a way for employees to book desks. this is usually done via a hybrid work management solution such as OfficeRnD Workplace:

Although a robust hybrid workspace management platform simplifies this process, it’s still more demanding than simply turning all desks into hot desks.

2. Organizational flaws

Due to its reliance on scheduling, employees can sometimes encounter double bookings and check-in issues when trying to reserve desks, conference rooms, cubicles, or a private office on short notice.

Moreover, if not carefully implemented, the limited workspace can create problems during unexpected office surges for an urgent project or emergency meeting. Again, you can avoid all of these issues with a good hybrid workspace solution.

3. Disruptive for teams

Both hot desking and desk hoteling share a common downside: teams who want to work closely in one spot may find it difficult to do so.

However, you can resolve this by establishing office neighborhoods, where desks are reserved only by team members working on a specific project.

Make the Most of Your Organization’s Office Space

We’ve said before that we believe desk hoteling is the better alternative, especially for companies that are setting a baseline for employees to be at the office, e.g., three days per week.

However, there’s no one-size-fits-all when it comes to hybrid work and workspace arrangement. Some companies prefer hot desking.

Others go for desk hoteling, and some even combine both methods across different teams. Consider your organization’s goals, culture, and employee satisfaction before anything else.

If you decide to adopt hybrid work, a tech solution is vital for handling its challenges effectively. Name: What Is A Hybrid Work Schedule? [A Complete Guide]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: What is a hybrid work schedule?
Post body:
What is a hybrid work schedule?

A natural byproduct of mixing traditional office and remote work is the need to create a hybrid work schedule that determines when employees or entire teams work in the office and when they work remotely.

There are many variables to consider when selecting a hybrid work schedule. Familiarizing yourself with the different types and understanding their pros and cons can help you choose the best hybrid work schedule for your team.

Quick Summary

A hybrid work schedule blends traditional office-based work with remote work. Employees split their time between the workplace and a location of their choice, based on company policies.

Let’s get started.

What Is a Hybrid Work Schedule?

A hybrid work schedule is an official company arrangement where employees split their time between working remotely and onsite. The proportion of remote and onsite workdays varies depending on company policies and individual preferences.

Hybrid work schedules support and streamline hybrid work models.

We’ll explore four different approaches to hybrid work schedules below. But first, let’s take a quick look at the benefits of a hybrid work schedule for employers and employees.

What Are the Benefits of a Hybrid Work Schedule for Employers?

When structured and implemented correctly, hybrid work schedules can improve productivity, collaboration, employee retention, and overall business performance.

Let’s talk about how.

Increased Productivity

By design, hybrid schedules are more flexible than traditional 9 to 5, full-time office schedules. This flexibility can empower employees to choose their office time and days, depending on the tasks they need to get done, resulting in enhanced productivity.

This is especially true if you organize your office space in areas that accommodate different work needs, i.e., office neighborhoods. Office neighborhoods give people the chance to work in various spaces, depending on the type of task they need to get done.

For some employees, a quiet space built for job duties that require intense concentration might be a great choice on Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday.

However, they might have meetings or brainstorming sessions on Wednesdays and Fridays, meaning a more collaborative space will likely be a better fit.

Again, a flexible hybrid work schedule combined with the proper office neighborhoods lets employees make that choice, depending on their needs.

Productivity is also a crucial key performance indicator for hybrid work.

Improved Work Relationships and Collaboration

Much of the talk surrounding remote and hybrid work has been focused on the detrimental effects of having too many virtual meetings (e.g., Zoom fatigue or burnout) and less time for physical interactions.

However, a well-designed hybrid workplace and schedule can actually benefit company culture and collaboration.

One way to achieve this is to implement a good desk booking solution, so employees can reserve a desk and see who else will be in the office.

Using hybrid-specific tools helps promote collaboration and teamwork, as team members can connect more easily.

In-person collaboration is actually a huge factor when it comes to choosing where to work. For example, this Gallup study found that “38% of fully remote workers would prefer hybrid work environments.

In other words, although fully remote employees enjoy their flexibility, four in 10 would give up some of that time at home to have in-person office experiences.

Failed collaboration is a hybrid work mistake you want to avoid.

Talent Attraction and Retention

Many job seekers now prioritize flexible work arrangements when evaluating job opportunities. So, a company that offers hybrid work options becomes more attractive to a broader talent pool.

Accommodating employees’ preferences for remote work can increase employee satisfaction and reduce turnover.

Cost Savings

Lastly, companies can reduce operating costs by switching to hybrid work schedules.

Allowing employees to work remotely for part of the week can lower the cost of rent, utilities, office supplies, and many other overhead expenses.

Hybrid work models also strengthen a company’s ability to manage work disruptions due to inclement weather, natural disasters, or other unforeseen events.

With a distributed workforce, operations can continue even if physical offices are temporarily inaccessible.

How Do Employees Benefit from a Hybrid Work Schedule?

Hybrid work schedules offer numerous benefits to employees, including a sense of empowerment, increased employee satisfaction and well-being, and a more innovative and creative office environment.

Feel free to check out this hybrid work schedule template in Excel.

A Sense of Empowerment

Giving employees the autonomy to choose when and where they work demonstrates companies’ trust in their workforce.

Hybrid work schedules empower employees to customize their work environments based on their preferences and needs. This empowerment can lead to higher levels of engagement and commitment.

Increased Employee Satisfaction and Well-being

Giving employees the autonomy to choose where, how, and when they work can increase their satisfaction and well-being.

In most cases, there still have to be some boundaries, but the more flexible and personalized your schedule, the more chances you have to achieve a great work-life balance.

And obviously, employees appreciate it when they feel trusted to perform their tasks without a supervisor timing their every move.

On that note, LinkedIn’s research suggests that employees are twice as likely to recommend working for a company that offers flexible working options.

Innovation and Creativity

A hybrid work environment can contribute to different modes of thinking and problem-solving.

Employees may find new inspiration in different settings and experience more creativity and innovation — benefiting both the employee and the company they work for.

In short, when managed right, hybrid work schedules can be a win-win!

4 Different Types of Hybrid Work Schedules

Creating and managing a hybrid schedule that fits your organization can be tricky. That’s why it’s best to first decide on a type of schedule and then move on to the specifics.

Here are four common types of hybrid schedules, starting with two of the least flexible models: cohort and staggered hybrid schedules.

Cohort Schedules

A cohort is a group of people who share a common characteristic for a certain period of time. Think of a cluster of people working in the same department, a sales team focused on the same geographic area, or a special task force for a temporary project, like launching a new product.

In the same vein, a cohort schedule organizes employees into functional groups that each have specific onsite and remote workdays.

A cohort schedule is a highly structured hybrid work schedule. It’s a favorite for office environments where in-person collaboration is vital. Employees have a clear understanding of when they are expected to be at the office and can plan their collaborations accordingly.

You can create a cohort schedule by assigning specific employees to work in the office on certain days of the week.

Alternatively, you can schedule teams or groups of employees to work onsite during a set period (e.g., the first two weeks of each month).

For example, the Finance department can be scheduled to be in the office on Mondays and Wednesdays or the first and third week of the month, while the Marketing department takes Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays or the second and last week of the month.

Pros of cohort schedules:

  • High predictability as everyone knows who will be onsite and when.
  • Low time investment because the same team works the same workdays or workweeks, which requires minimal time management.
  • Equal flexibility for all team members.

Cons of cohort schedules:

  • Low flexibility overall since the office days may not align with individual needs.
  • Potential issues with cross-team collaboration if teams come in on different days or weeks.

Overall, cohort schedules are best for teams or departments that need in-person work or collaboration.

They are also ideal for companies that require team members to be in the office at a given time without the need for them to engage with other departments.

Staggered Hybrid Schedules

These schedules are almost similar to cohort schedules but are a little more rigid. With a staggered schedule, employees must always come into and leave the office at a set time to prevent congestion and ensure that only a certain number of people are onsite at a time.

Usually, the relevant departments define the schedule for their employees. These types of schedules are suitable for shift-driven work, such as in warehouses or medical facilities.

For example, the facility management department may be set to arrive on Monday and Thursday at 8 a.m. and depart at 3 p.m., while the warehouse department arrives on Wednesday and Friday at 9 a.m. and leaves at 5 p.m.

Pros of staggered hybrid schedules:

  • Easy to predict how many individuals will be in the office at a given time (provided you have good hybrid work software in place).
  • Similar flexibility for all team members.

Cons of staggered hybrid schedules:

  • Low flexibility for employees whose schedules don’t match their needs.
  • Low collaboration chances as there might be a limited window for interaction during shifts.
  • More time and effort to manage than cohort schedules since you must plan down to the hour instead of just assigning days or weeks to specific teams.

Schedules Set by Managers

These schedules are typically created by direct managers and their direct reports coming up with a solution that works for everyone.

For example, managers can talk to their hybrid team and decide which days everyone should be in the office for team meetings (check out some really cool meeting names here) or other office work. Alternatively, managers can work with each team member to create an individual schedule for them.

This model can be accompanied by a larger, company-wide policy that sets a baseline for being in the office.

For instance, the company policy might say that everyone should be in the office at least two days a week. From there, employees and their managers can decide which days to choose.

Pros of manager-set hybrid schedules:

  • Opportunities to promote in-person collaboration.
  • Equal flexibility for everyone, provided the same rules go for all team members.
  • More chances for aligning individual work schedules with the team’s needs.

Cons of manager-set hybrid schedules:

  • Potentially low predictability if employees have to wait for approval every time they want to work away from the office.
  • Harder for managers to organize since they have to balance company and employee requirements.

DIY Employee Schedules

DIY employee schedules, or self-determined schedules, trust employees to choose where and when they work.

This is the true definition of a flexible work arrangement since there’s no set requirement to come to the office on any particular day.

Employees can decide when to be in the office and choose remote days based on their needs.

These flexible schedules can also enable employees to come to and leave the office earlier or later than they typically could, so they can avoid rush hour traffic or drive their kids to school, for example.

DIY employee schedules pros:

  • High flexibility and personalization since employees have complete control over their time.
  • Great opportunities for individuals to predict and organize their work.
  • Requires little to no managerial oversight or administrative effort.

DIY employee schedules cons:

  • High competition for access to the workplace due to unpredictable employee schedules. For instance, some days may be much more crowded than others.
  • Unpredictably can make it difficult for team members to coordinate their schedules.

How to Choose the Best Hybrid Work Schedule for Your Company

Given all these hybrid schedule options, how do you choose the best one for your company?

Hybrid scheduling decisions are best made case-by-case, depending on the employee’s role, rather than a one-size-fits-all hybrid work schedule that every employee must follow. There are many factors you’ll want to consider, including:

  • company needs and goals
  • team dynamics
  • nature of the work
  • employee roles and preferences
  • technology and infrastructure
  • company culture and values

Here’s a handy checklist to help you sift through the options. The answers can guide you in making decisions for specific teams or the company as a whole.

Start With a Trial Period

Once you’ve decided on the best hybrid schedule and made it to the implementation stage, consider an initial trial period. This adjustment phase allows employees to experiment with and fine-tune their new schedules.

As you solicit employee feedback during this trial period, here are a few questions to consider:

  • How are team members doing with their hybrid work schedules?
  • How is the new office schedule affecting relationships with customers and vendors?
  • What do the results tell you?

Knowing how your policy is affecting your employees is essential to make the most of hybrid scheduling.

Name: 5 Powerful Ways Collaboration Tools Help Your Business [2026]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Collaboration tools help teams stay productive and connected whether they work hybrid or fully remote, and they let people support clients faster. The right tools can clear bottlenecks, or stop them forming in the first place.
Post body:
Collaboration tools help teams stay productive and connected whether they work hybrid or fully remote, and they let people support clients faster. The right tools can clear bottlenecks, or stop them forming in the first place.

Below are five ways online collaboration tools improve your business, plus five ways they help your clients. You’ll also find answers to questions like “How can collaboration tools improve team communication?” and “How do collaboration tools improve productivity?”

Quick Summary

  • A collaboration tool is software that lets people communicate, share work, and coordinate tasks in one place, whether they sit in the same room or on different continents.
  • There are several types of collaboration tools, including those for communication, cloud documentation, task management, and meetings.
  • Collaboration tools change how a business runs, touching productivity, problem-solving, teamwork, and data security.
  • The benefits reach your end customers too, through shorter wait times, better service, and faster human-to-human communication.

Types of Collaboration Tools

Collaborative tools and technology can be anything from video to chatbots to instant messaging to organizational options and cloud documents. Nearly 80% of workers now use collaboration tools in their work, and adoption keeps climbing as more teams split time between home and the office.

Communication Tools

Communication tools can include instant messaging or collaborative video platforms. These usually do the following:

  • They allow for visual explanations of technical or detailed processes, which are perfect for particularly technical topics.
  • They let the customer “follow along” and help themselves, giving them a sense of agency.
  • They speed up onboarding. Recordings can be saved for each client to refer to later, which cuts the number of support requests.

Some of the most useful communication tools:

  • Slack
  • MS Teams (check out the applications that have MS Teams integration here).
  • Zoom
  • Trello
  • Asana

Cloud Documentation

Google Workspace, Google Drive, and Google Docs all run in the cloud. The main advantages:

  1. Everything stays in one place.
  2. Anyone with access can edit without keeping a copy on their own system.
  3. If local copies get deleted, a backup remains in the cloud.
  4. Members can see specific feedback easily.
  5. The interface looks similar to Word and other word processors.
  6. File sharing is built in.
  7. The feature set keeps growing.

Task Management

Task management tools give team members one place to see their tasks for the day or the week. They let people “tag” each other, which improves communication.

They also keep a text record of everything discussed, which supports better organization and a sharper focus on customer needs.

In short, they make collaboration faster and easier.

This matters most in hybrid work, where it helps everyone stay on the same page for the length of a project.

Some popular task management tools:

  • ClickUp
  • Todoist
  • Proofhub
  • Hubspot Task Management

Tools like these belong in your digital transformation strategy and roadmap.

Meeting Tools

Meetings get a bad reputation, and often for good reason. A single meeting doesn’t have to turn into a three-hour session where nothing gets decided.

Structured well, with clear goals and objectives, meetings are a strong source of problem-solving, ideation, and collaboration.

With OfficeRnD Workplace’s room booking system, managers stop chasing people down to lock in a time.

You can find and book any available space, set it as private, one-time, or recurring, and the software sends notifications and reminders. That beats tracking down the one person who always vanishes right before a meeting, asynchronous or synchronous.

You can book from inside apps like Microsoft Teams, Slack, or Google Calendar.

You can also see the floor plan, which helps you check what’s already taken and plan the amenities you’ll need ahead of time.

For hybrid meetings, you also need the right equipment.

5 Ways Collaboration Tools Can Help Your Business

The best way to avoid paying for tools that add no value is to check how they can help your business. Here are five ways collaboration tools do this.

#1 They Can Boost Productivity

Digital workplaces and online collaboration software can lift productivity by up to 30%, and employees feel the difference: about 45% say digital communication makes them feel more connected to their team.

Founders see it too. In one survey, 76% said productivity stayed the same or increased with employees working remotely.

With the right tools, upper management and CEOs can do what they do best while letting their teams do the same.

#2 They Can Help Improve Communication

Morale and efficiency drop when teams can’t communicate well. You get longer learning curves for new hires, slower responses to customer issues, and miscommunication between teams.

With collaboration tools handling communication, documentation, task management, and scheduling, people communicate more easily, with much of the effect of being face-to-face.

Research by Gallup shows communication influences performance. Better communication helps people feel more engaged and more invested in the company culture, while avoiding the distractions that come with a busy office.

Whether you’re an administrator who wants to support the team without overwhelming them, an office manager making the most of your resources, a manager focused on productivity and cohesion, or a team member who wants to get more done, OfficeRnD Workplace covers the following collaboration features:

  • A weekly planner
  • Desk bookings shown on an interactive floor plan
  • Onsite meeting details, including time, duration, date, and attendees
  • Up to 15 “favorite” colleagues you can send custom invites to for the moments that matter

Team member or employer, you’ll always know where your favorite colleagues are, what’s on the schedule, meeting details, and what the week ahead looks like. That keeps you and your team organized and moving through the week faster.

#3 They Can Help Teams Solve Problems Faster

When someone hits a problem they can’t solve alone, and has no easy way to reach a teammate, you get frustration and low morale.

Tools like Microsoft Teams help everyone here, raising productivity and cutting the hours spent stuck. The cost of getting this wrong is real: about 64% of workers say poor collaboration loses them three or more hours of productivity a week.

#4 They Help Improve Teamwork

Many workplaces already run flexible and hybrid models. Building teamwork and camaraderie is hard when people rely on phone, fax, or email alone.

Zoom lets teams see and hear each other rather than lean on text and email. Tone and intent come through.

Video conferencing tools can record online meetings, and those recordings can be referenced later.

Zoom’s AI Companion now summarizes meetings, drafts agendas, and catches you up if you join late.

Read more about current digital transformation trends here.

#5 They Help Keep Data Secure

Customers and employees care more than ever about keeping personal data safe from criminals, hackers, and other companies.

IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach Report puts the global average cost of a breach at $4.99 million, a 12% jump and a record high. In the United States the average runs far higher, which makes strong controls a business necessity rather than a nice-to-have.

With ClickUp, Asana, and similar project management software, security options like 2-factor authentication and 256-bit encryption protect proprietary company and client data.

That’s safer than physical file folders in a cabinet, and it makes data easier to organize and search.

When judging security, check whether the software has a clean SOC 2 Type 2 report.

5 Ways Collaboration Tools Help Your Clients

#1 They Offer Faster Solutions

As customers, we’ve all felt the pain of sending a ticket and waiting. With instant messaging, a customer speaks to a team member right away and gets the problem solved.

Communication tools also support real-time collaboration, so the customer knows they’re dealing with a human.

A chatbot adds something on top: it can guide the customer to an answer, point to the exact instructions they need, and, if needed, take a message.

#2 They Improve Customer Satisfaction

The more ways customers have to reach you, the faster they get on with their day.

Chat with a customer or guide their onboarding over a tool like Zoom, and they feel supported and free up mental space for everything else. Repeat business follows.

Customers aren’t tied to a laptop or desktop either. Mobile apps keep the conversation going on the move.

#3 Wait Times Are Shorter

Before chatbots, customers sent a ticket or email and waited, which raised stress and the sense that no one was moving quickly enough.

Chatbots changed that. Live chat backs it up: it earns roughly a 73% satisfaction score, ahead of email at 61% and phone at 44%.

The time a customer used to lose on hold is gone.

Whether the issue hits at 1 p.m. or 12 a.m., the chatbot is always on. It doesn’t need sleep, sick days, or anything else a human needs.

#4 They Help Reduce Stress

When a customer has an issue with a product or service, the thought of going through support can be stressful on its own.

They have to give up time and hope someone solves the problem quickly.

If they can’t, they may be frustrated enough to switch to a competitor or drop the product entirely.

Tools like Zoom or instant chat ease that, because unlike phone support there are usually no menus to navigate and no long hold times.

#5 They Lead to Greater Transparency

If a customer feels a company isn’t being straight with them, they can switch to a competitor fast.

With instant chat and ticketing systems, a customer can check the status of a request and add information when needed.

That gives them a sense of agency and the assurance that they’re part of solving the problem. They feel less like a number, and less like a nuisance.

Why Does Helping Clients via Collaboration Tools Matter?

It Provides a Better Customer Experience

Instant messaging and chatbots connect customers with a team member right away, so issues get resolved almost immediately.

Consider two facts:

  1. 41% of customers prefer live chat over other customer service channels.
  2. Live chat cuts wait times and raises satisfaction.

Tools like Zoom and Loom help onboarding by letting team members set customers up and walk them through everything, then hand over video recordings for later reference.

It Boosts Team Morale

Few things wear people down like feeling that every problem at work is theirs alone to solve. It’s worse when you work remotely. Burnout, fatigue, and the loss of a good team member can follow.

Tools like ClickUp and Zoom mean you can always reach the right person to help.

That builds morale and togetherness whether the team is spread across the country or the world. Video tools also cut confusion about intent.

It Helps Build a More Efficient Company

Without tools that help employees do their jobs and keep the routine parts (like billing) organized, competing gets hard.

Collaboration tools are now a baseline. Even so, in-person time still counts: over 80% of business professionals say face-to-face meetings build client relationships and trust.

Want a more collaborative office?

Its collaborative scheduling features raise face-to-face collaboration, which lifts productivity and engagement, so you connect with colleagues without playing tag.

Take the guesswork out of teamwork and support clearer collaboration and communication.

Name: 10 Successful Digital Transformation Examples [2023 Guide]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: For many business owners, digital transformation is an intimidating and unnecessary venture.
Post body:
For many business owners, digital transformation is an intimidating and unnecessary venture.

It’s a buzzword — a passing trend. Why would I pour time, effort, and resources into a concept I don’t see the need for?

Because without it, your competitors will leave you in the dust. We live in a digital age that demands that companies either keep up or get left behind.

Fortunately, digital transformation is attainable for businesses of every size in every industry. With the right digital tools, companies can optimize their operations, boost employee satisfaction, and gain a competitive advantage.

This article will explain what digital transformation is, what it means for your business, explore 10 real world examples of digital transformation, and discuss how hybrid work systems drive digital transformation.

What Is Digital Transformation?

Digital transformation is the process of replacing outdated systems and manual processes with digital technologies and tools to maximize employee productivity and improve overall business performance.

Digital transformation allows companies to:

  • simplify and optimize processes
  • facilitate internal collaboration and communication
  • reduce the time spent on manual tasks
  • make more informed, data-driven decisions
  • increase business agility
  • improve customer experiences

Embracing digital transformation is important, as it can help streamline your business’s workflow and boost productivity company-wide — giving you an edge over the competition.

Because of its enormous potential, global investment in digital transformation is expected to reach $3.4 trillion by 2026. For more info on that, check our article on the 9 game-changing digital transformation trends for 2023.

Most businesses are already shifting toward digitization. In KPMG’s 2022 U.S. Technology Survey Report, 80% of respondents said their organizations have successfully transitioned to cloud-based infrastructure, and 66% have been very or extremely successful in using digital transformation to advance business strategy.

10 Successful Digital Transformation Examples

Digital transformation looks different for every business and every industry. A three-person start-up will have different needs and challenges than an established business with multiple operating segments.

Below are 10 successful digital transformation examples across several industries. You can use these examples as inspiration and guidance as your company begins its transformation journey.

Banking

It’s notoriously difficult to evolve within the banking industry. Only 30% of banks that pursue digital transformation initiatives manage to successfully implement their digital strategy.

In this industry, the primary goal of digital transformation efforts is to create customer-centric processes and products.

Banks can improve the customer experience by optimizing their mobile and online banking platforms and working to reduce or eliminate manual and paper-based processes by offering features like mobile check deposit.

The following two digital transformation examples illustrate successful digital growth within the banking and finance industry:

Intergiro

Intergiro is a tech company that builds financial infrastructure to facilitate smooth business banking. They saw the need for digitization within the financial sector and developed a solution to fill that gap.

Intergiro built embedded banking, a digital business banking system that gives customers a new way to manage their finances.Embedded banking automates financial processes within businesses and integrates with check-outs, wallets, and holding cards.

Now, other businesses can use Intergiro’s services on their own digital transformation journeys.

HSBC

HSBC is one of the world’s leading banking and financial services firms. Their response to the increased need for digitization included migrating certain databases to a third-party, cloud-based platform.

By transitioning to cloud computing, HSBC was able to replace its outdated, legacy applications and scale services based on customer demands.

Also, like many businesses, HSBC shifted to a hybrid work model following the COVID-19 pandemic and shrunk its headquarters by 25% to reduce expenses and energy costs.

If you’re looking to implement a similar hybrid approach to working, using an office space management system can streamline the process.

Tools such as OfficeRnD Hybrid offer support for workplaces that inevitably feel the need to go hybrid.

Retail

In the retail industry, the goals of the digital transformation strategy are to increase convenience and improve the in-store and online customer experience.

Retailers can achieve this goal by adopting a buy-online-pick-up-in-store (BOPIS) model and connecting the online shopping experience to the in-store experience.

Ikea, which we discuss below, is one of the best examples of digital transformation in retail.

Ikea

Ikea is a well-known and well-loved furniture store that operates worldwide. To compete with the increasing popularity of online shopping, they transformed their in-store shopping experience.

To do this, they turned stores into fulfillment centers — allowing shoppers to blend their online shopping with in-store experiences.

Using Ikea’s website, you can design custom cabinetry for your home, save your design in their system, and visit any Ikea store to choose finishes in person.

Ikea also uses algorithms for supply chain management and inventory management, reducing the wait time for customers when they order out-of-stock pieces and boosting the customer experience as a result.

Ikea’s digital transformation strategy shows how integrating new technology with established systems can build customer loyalty for a brand.

Hospitality

The goals of digital transformation initiatives within the hospitality industry are to improve customers’ booking experiences and increase staff safety.

Adopting contactless solutions can help organizations improve customer experiences. Digital platforms can be used to more effectively manage booking, messaging, payments, room service, mobile room keys, and the check-in and check-out processes.

Going contactless is a priority for most hotels, motels, bed-and-breakfasts, and resorts. In fact, just over 39% of hospitality executives say that implementing contactless technologies at the front desk is a priority for them until at least 2025.

Contactless systems reduce cleaning staff’s risk of exposure to germs. They can also help track linen inventory so you can keep storerooms well-stocked.

Four Sisters Inns implemented a fully contactless system and have reaped the rewards ever since.

Four Sisters Inns

Four Sisters Inns operates 17 beautiful boutique inns across some of California’s most popular destinations.

They pride themselves on providing a curated luxury vacation experience — made all the more luxurious with the use of fully contactless communications.

Four Sisters saw the increase in interest in a contactless approach and immediately implemented a messaging platform for guests to communicate with the staff at their inns. Guests can enjoy contactless check-in, room service, turn-down service, and more.

Logistics

In the logistics industry, digital transformation efforts focus on optimization. You want to minimize any fallout from human error, speed up delivery, and improve parcel tracking for customers to improve their experience. And you can achieve these goals through automation.

Let’s use UPS as an example of how automation improves real-time parcel tracking for customers.

UPS

As the popularity of online shopping grew, UPS knew they needed to find new ways to stay competitive and create a competitive roadmap for digital transformation.

Over the past several years, they have completely changed their methods of storing, sorting, and delivering through digital systems and digital technology.

UPS drivers now use a system called On-Road Integrated Optimization and Navigation (ORION), which helps them navigate using the optimal route. ORION reduces wait times for customers and fuel costs for the business.

Workers use Bluetooth devices that alert them if they’ve loaded a parcel into the incorrect truck, reducing the chances of shipping delays caused by human error.

In 2016, UPS implemented new data collection practices. They’ve used data they collected to optimize every step of their packaging and delivery process.

This has changed how workers sort packages to send to different locations, how workers load packages into delivery vehicles, and how the company recruits and trains temporary employees during busier holiday seasons.

Healthcare

Digital advances in the healthcare industry focus on optimization and streamlined patient management.

The goal is to reduce wait times for patients, optimize physicians’ time, and lessen the amount of manual paperwork for patients and physicians.

Most hospitals are moving toward a cloud-based digital data management system, using e-portals for simplified patient data collection and storage.

A 48,000-physician shortage is projected by 2024. As such, many hospitals are turning to remote patient-monitoring methods to manage patients with chronic health conditions.

Physicians can use digital tools, such as wristbands or skin patches with software components, to monitor patients’ vitals — all while those patients remain at home.

Other hospitals offer virtual appointments and consultations to reduce wait and travel times for patients.

The following two digital transformation examples demonstrate how healthcare providers can use new technologies to meet customer needs.

NHS

The National Health Service (NHS) is the UK’s publicly funded healthcare system. Their goal is to provide healthcare based on needs, not patients’ ability to pay.

The NHS has set the industry standard for chronic condition remote monitoring. Between November 2020 and January 2023, the NHS supported over 487,000 patients at home using digital home care and remote monitoring technologies.

Transitioning to a remote patient monitoring system allowed the NHS to streamline the patient treatment process.

BetterHelp

BetterHelp is the world’s largest online therapy platform. Its users can access over 23,000 licensed therapists via text, phone calls, or video calls.

BetterHelp makes therapy more accessible by removing the barriers that often limit a patient’s access to traditional therapy.

These barriers include costs, travel times, and scheduling difficulties. BetterHelp is also less expensive than traditional in-person therapy, can be used from anywhere in the world, and allows for greater flexibility for users to interact with their therapists.

BetterHelp all digital setup is beneficial for therapists, too. Therapists who were limited to in-person visits in the past can use the BetterHelp platform to connect with patients all over the world.

Manufacturing

In the manufacturing industry, digital transformation goals revolve around increasing production efficiency and improving inventory and supply chain management.

Manufacturing companies can use predictive analytics to increase their supply chain cost savings, track their maintenance needs, and reduce their energy consumption.

One of the most useful digital transformation upgrades within the manufacturing industry was implementing Internet of Things (IoT) sensors.

Industrial IoT sensors

Industrial IoT sensors collect performance data on industrial processes. They’re used in manufacturing plants and other locations to monitor equipment performance and track occupancy.

IoT sensors can include gas sensors to measure oxygen levels, temperature sensors to measure the temperature of machines and their surroundings, or pressure sensors to measure changes in air pressure around a machine.

The data that these devices collect helps manufacturing companies monitor their plant operations, industrial equipment, energy consumption, inventory, maintenance needs, and environmental conditions that could impact production.

Supermarkets

Digitization in supermarkets is aimed at increasing customer convenience and reducing the amount of time spent finding groceries in-store, bagging, and checking out.

Many supermarkets have adopted the BOPIS or buy-online-pick-up-at-curbside (BOPAC) model to reduce wait and travel times, respectively.

In fact, online grocery shopping is projected to account for 20% of all grocery sales in the US by 2026.

Smaller retailers can use a multi-vendor marketplace rather than setting up their own online shopping platform.

A multi-vendor marketplace is an online hub for stores that don’t have an online store. These platforms reduce costs for small businesses and provide consumers with a one-stop-shopping experience.

The two digital transformation examples below demonstrate the value of optimizing business processes and knowing your customers so you can gain a competitive edge over your rivals.

Thrive Market

Thrive Market is a membership-based online store that claims to “cut out the middleman” to provide organic brands at wholesale prices.

It’s convenient and cost-effective, and it also uses artificial intelligence to recommend items and brands that users may enjoy. Members order their groceries online and enjoy curbside delivery within a few days.

Walmart

Another way to digitize grocery shopping is through the use of reward or incentive programs. These programs can use machine learning algorithms to offer personalized deals and savings.

Walmart is a multinational retail and supermarket chain based in the US. As the world moved into the digital age, Walmart stayed relevant by implementing a digital transformation strategy that complemented their existing business model and made shopping more convenient for customers.

By joining the Walmart+ reward system, members can use the Walmart app to purchase eligible items to gain a coupon-like reward and save on future purchases.

Walmart+ members can even use the app to scan items while shopping in-store, then checkout within the app and completely avoid checkout lines.

It makes shopping more convenient for the customer and helps to prevent long lines at checkout for cashiers.

How Can Hybrid Work Drive Digital Transformation?

Companies that adopt a hybrid work model have no choice but to embrace digital transformation.

Since hybrid employees aren’t in the same place all the time, paper-based forms and processes must be digitized so they’re accessible from anywhere.

It’s important to prioritize the personalization of digitalization when working toward a thorough digital transformation.

Your company’s digital transformation process will look different depending on your starting point, needs, and growth priorities.

To accelerate the digital transformation process, powerful hybrid work tools like OfficeRnD Workplace can help companies:

  • Easily create hybrid work schedules
  • communicate clearly and collaborate more effectively
  • simplify desk booking and meeting room booking
  • increase employee engagement

With the right tools, hybrid organizations can rise to meet the challenges of adopting a hybrid setup.

A well-managed hybrid workplace offers flexibility for employees to manage their time however they choose, improving employee satisfaction and reducing stress.

Trusting employees with higher levels of autonomy in the workplace encourages them to take initiative and increase their productivity.

Successful transformation to a hybrid system makes it easy to transition between office and work-from-home spaces by ensuring that employee expectations are clear and internal communication channels are open.

Running a successful hybrid setup drives digital transformation in the following ways:

Name: The Importance Of A Sustainable Workplace [2024 Guide]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Sustainability has become crucial in today’s world — and for good reason. Waste generation is estimated to reach 3.88 billion tons in 2050. And unsustainable business practices, like mandating in-office work for employees in remote-capable roles, are a big part of the problem.
Post body:
Sustainability has become crucial in today’s world — and for good reason. Waste generation is estimated to reach 3.88 billion tons in 2050. And unsustainable business practices, like mandating in-office work for employees in remote-capable roles, are a big part of the problem.

Not only do unsustainable business practices worsen the environmental challenges facing our planet, like climate change and resource depletion, but they have significant economic and social consequences as well.

Fortunately, more and more businesses are realizing that sustainable practices are good for more than just the environment — they can also help companies improve their bottom line and outperform their competitors.

This article will take you through everything you need to know about the benefits of sustainable business practices, why they’re important for your business’s operations, and how to go about creating a more sustainable workplace.

Ready to jump in?

Quick Summary

  • A sustainable workplace encourages socially, environmentally, and economically responsible behavior.
  • In addition to reducing your carbon footprint, introducing sustainability practices in the workplace can help companies save money, attract new customers, and improve employee morale.
  • Understanding the seven key areas of sustainability and embracing hybrid work are essential for today’s businesses.

What is Workplace Sustainability?

Workplace sustainability refers to business practices and policies that promote resource conservation and encourage more socially, environmentally, and economically responsible behavior. Whether you employ a hybrid organizational structure or a standard one doesn’t matter. The concept could be applied anywhere.

It’s important to understand the different components of workplace sustainability and how they can help businesses operate in a more responsible and thoughtful way.

The seven key areas of sustainability in the workplace are as follows:

  1. Social responsibility
  2. Resource conservation
  3. Employee involvement
  4. Transparency and reporting
  5. Hybrid and remote work models
  6. Collaboration and partnerships
  7. Leadership commitment

We all know that sustainability is essential for the environment, but why is it important in the workplace?

3 Types of Sustainability

Many people make the mistake of believing that corporate sustainability only refers to the environment.

However, the concept of sustainability is based on three interconnected pillars. A comprehensive sustainability program considers how a company’s processes and actions impact the environment, society, and the economy.

We’ll discuss each of them below.

Environment

Environmental issues can have a direct impact on a business’s everyday functions. Environmental sustainability involves addressing aspects of your workplace that negatively affect the planet and finding “greener” alternatives.

Environmental sustainability can include the following:

  • Reducing water consumption
  • Reducing carbon footprint
  • Cutting down on paper and plastic use
  • Introducing a recycling system

Environmental sustainability can also involve converting your workplace from a traditional practice, like in-office work, to a hybrid model, thus making it a more intelligent workplace.

Society

Social sustainability involves identifying and managing essential aspects of your business to enhance employee experience and ensure that your company is having a positive impact on the world.

Social sustainability can include the following:

  • Ensuring employees along supply chains are treated fairly
  • Providing healthcare and workplace safety
  • Performing vendor and supplier background checks
  • Promoting diversity and inclusion

The data continues to show that consumers want to support ethical companies that are committed to sustainability.

Social sustainability is based on the understanding that people are the foundation of any successful business and, therefore, should be prioritized for long-term success.

Economy

Economic sustainability is the final pillar in creating a sustainable workplace. It’s crucial to ensure that your business practices are helping to promote economic conditions that will make life livable for more people.

People all around the globe are still picking up the pieces left behind by the COVID-19 pandemic.

A recent study found that only 5% of the world’s population lives in a country where GDP has caught up to pre-pandemic levels.

Initiatives that prioritize economic sustainability help achieve long-term financial stability and growth while also promoting social and environmental responsibility.

For example:

  • Ensuring employees are paid fair wages
  • Not working with suppliers or vendors that violate labor laws
  • Opting for low-impact economic development
  • Upholding basic working rights and safety standards for all workers

What Is the Impact of a Sustainable Workplace?

As mentioned, making sustainability initiatives part of your company culture and daily business operations can have far-reaching effects.

Some business impacts include the following:

  • Reduce waste: Conscious practices like recycling, using digital devices, and printing on double-sided paper can lead to a healthy environment and cost savings.
  • Preserve brand reputation: Employees and customers are becoming increasingly environmentally conscious. They expect companies to prioritize sustainable workplace practices, too. Choosing not to implement sustainable workplace practices can seriously impact your reputation among employees and customers.
  • Increase productivity: Using energy-efficient lighting and temperature control systems in your physical office space creates a more comfortable work setting that can naturally improve employee productivity.
  • Boost employee morale: Showing your commitment to eco-friendly practices can create a stronger sense of community among your team, boosting employee morale and job satisfaction rates. In return, employees feel more engaged, which leads to more integrity in the workplace.
  • Improved financial performance: Companies that show their commitment to sustainability by adopting environmentally, economically, and socially responsible business practices can increase shareholder value.

How to Make Your Workplace Sustainable

With growing concerns about economic instability, climate change, and resource depletion, there’s never been a better time to reassess your approach to resource management and create a new workplace strategy centered around sustainability.

Here are 12 simple ways you can make your workplace more sustainable:

  1. Reduce paper usage by going 100% digital
  2. Cut out single-use plastics
  3. Switch to energy-efficient light bulbs
  4. Embrace hot desking, virtual offices, and other flexible workspaces
  5. Use sustainable cleaning products
  6. Offer meatless food options
  7. Incorporate renewable energy
  8. Introduce a recycling system
  9. Limit unnecessary business travel
  10. Opt for video conferences over in-person meetings whenever possible
  11. Use eco-friendly transportation
  12. Create a sustainable supply chain

What Is a Real-World Example of Workplace Sustainability?

At LEGO®, sustainability initiatives are on a whole other level. Many elements in their products are made with renewable, durable plastic that’s derived from Brazilian sugarcane.

LEGO® Stores around the world started phasing out single-use shopping bags in 2020. As part of the company’s commitment to using more sustainable materials, their products are packaged with cardboard that’s made from 75% recycled materials.

Google is another company that prioritizes sustainable work practices. Operating under a hybrid work model, Google believes people don’t need to be in the office every day to be productive.

Adopting sustainability practices into your business like Google and Lego can help you promote a healthier workplace and cut down on the costs of operations.

How Can You Maintain a Healthy and Sustainable Workplace?

Setting up sustainable workplace practices is only half the battle — now you have to make it work in the long term.

Here are some tips for maintaining a healthy and sustainable workplace long term:

  1. Regularly assess and evaluate the sustainability of workplace policies and practices.
  2. Conduct supplier and vendor site audits to ensure you’re part of a sustainable supply chain.
  3. Encourage employee feedback and suggestions.
  4. Create sustainability workshops for employees.
  5. Continuously seek out fun and innovative ways to be sustainable.
  6. Partner with other sustainable organizations.
  7. Keep a high level of workplace compliance.

How Hybrid Work Leads to a More Sustainable Workplace

If you haven’t already, letting go of the traditional 9–5 in-office work day in favor of hybrid work arrangements is a great way to transition to a more sustainable workplace.

In a recent survey that asked more than 3,000 C-suite and senior executives spread throughout North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific, 70% of respondents said remote work technologies were most effective in their sustainability efforts.

The right hybrid work software can help you enable and manage a thriving workplace that’s not only productive and collaborative but also more sustainable.

Think of how much money you spent on transportation costs this week alone. Now multiply that by the number of employees in your office.

Introducing the hybrid work model in your office can help you:

  • Lower your utilities and facilities costs
  • Reduce your environmental impact by cutting down employee commutes.
  • Improve your employees’ work-life balance

Here’s a full guide on developing a working organizational sustainability strategy.

Common Mistakes Workplaces Make When It Comes to Sustainability (and How to Avoid Them)

Knowing the right way to go about implementing sustainable workplace strategies can be difficult.

That’s why, although some companies are trying to achieve a greener workplace, they’re running into a whole range of issues.

Determining the best sustainability plan for your office is a matter of trial and error. However, we’ve made a list of the most common mistakes companies make when rolling out a sustainability plan so you can avoid them.

These include the following:

Failing to measure or track their progress

Without clear metrics and reporting mechanisms, it’s difficult to track the impact of sustainability initiatives.

This can lead to companies spending time and money implementing sustainability practices that don’t match the needs of their office, which can result in poor work ethic.

Utilizing space usage analytics and other powerful tools can help hybrid teams make the most of their office space, identify areas for improvement, and succeed in their sustainability efforts.

Neglecting their social and economic impact

While environmental sustainability is important, it’s only one piece of the puzzle. Due to the association sustainability has with the environment, companies tend to confine their efforts to environmental changes — ultimately neglecting economic and social sustainability.

To avoid this, consider sustainability from a holistic viewpoint at the very beginning stages of planning.

Not making sustainability a part of company culture

For sustainability initiatives to stand the test of time, they need to be ingrained into the company’s culture and business model, not as standalone initiatives. Companies that fail to make sustainability a fundamental part of their day-to-day business operations are unlikely to see any lasting impact.

To avoid this, spend time considering the social, environmental, and economic impact of different aspects of your business.

Ensuring that your business model, company culture, and strategic vision reflect your organization’s commitment to sustainable business practices will make them more likely to succeed.

Rejecting remote and hybrid work arrangements

With the recent rise in gas and electricity rates, working in the office every day can be incredibly costly.

Forcing employees to work this way can increase energy consumption and carbon emissions, as well as reduce employee satisfaction and production.

With the right collaboration and communication tools, a hybrid work model can help businesses operate in a more effective and environmentally conscious way.

Ready to Make Your Workplace Sustainable?

Committing to a more sustainable workplace can improve your company’s bottom line and impact future generations.

If you’re looking for a quick and simple sustainability solution, a hybrid work model is a great place to start.

Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: The agile manifesto changed software development in the early 2000s and has been gaining steam ever since.
Post body:
The agile manifesto changed software development in the early 2000s and has been gaining steam ever since.

Industries worldwide now use agile techniques to encourage innovation, promote change, and improve productivity.

In its broadest sense, an agile work environment is both a way of working and a guiding philosophy. Agile methods are rooted in flexibility, adaptability, and iterative progress.

In agile organizations, the project managers and teams work within a highly collaborative structure where they can react quickly to changing conditions and face challenges head-on rather than sticking to a prescribed plan.

But successfully putting agile processes and tools in place is harder than it sounds.

Quick Summary

  • In the workplace, an agile environment is a highly flexible and adaptable approach to how people work and manage teams.
  • Agile work environments prioritize flexibility, adaptability, iterative approaches, and working collaboratively.
  • The right digital processes and tools can help teams overcome the challenges of applying the agile approach in remote and hybrid environments.

Here’s what you need to know about agile environments: the advantages of agile practices, common misconceptions about agile tools and frameworks, and how project teams can succeed in remote and hybrid settings.

What is an agile environment?

An agile environment is a collaborative, adaptive approach to project management and product development that breaks work into short cycles and adjusts to feedback as it goes.

It came out of the software industry in the early 2000s with the Agile Manifesto, and it puts flexibility, customer feedback, and iterative progress first.

Agile methodologies, such as Scrum and Kanban, are the frameworks teams most often use to run it.

These methods rely on short, focused work cycles called sprints, and continuous improvement based on stakeholder feedback.

Key components of an agile environment

“To truly become a high-performing agile organization,” says Tom Godden, enterprise strategist at Amazon Web Services, “you must look at your organization structure differently and be willing to change your mindset and behavior.”

An agile environment lets teams evolve, experiment, and innovate when they hit unforeseen challenges or changing project requirements.

Here are the key components.

Small empowered teams

An agile team needs to be small to respond quickly to customer needs and act on opportunities as they arise. The larger the team, the harder it is to get everyone on the same page.

But even when project teams are well-staffed and the right size, they only work well when they have the authority and ability to take action when needed.

According to Amazon’s “Two-Pizza Teams” mantra, a project team that takes more than two pizzas to feed is too big.

Continuous improvement and feedback

Agile practices use an iterative approach to drive productivity and find process improvements. They build in constant growth, continuous learning, and refinement at both the individual and the team levels.

Traditional project management follows a linear, step-by-step process, which is fine when things are stable and predictable.

Agile project management breaks work into a series of sprints, each one ending in a deliverable. That opens the door to customer collaboration, stakeholder feedback, and continuous improvement.

Effective, self-aware leaders help drive value and let teams thrive by helping members assess what worked well, what challenges they encountered, and which areas need improvement.

This process repeats continuously, so teams can work customer feedback into project objectives.

Fast-paced environment

An agile environment runs on momentum. Rather than putting out a single, complete deliverable at the end, the agile mindset prioritizes gradual delivery, incremental value, and continuous improvement.

Instead of waiting months on a finished product, software development teams can experience and test individual components and features as they’re completed. This approach improves later iterations and keeps customers happier.

The customer benefits from this constant delivery model too, since they don’t have to wait for the final product to see progress. In an agile environment, customers stay involved and updated throughout.

Agile methodology myths

Here are some common myths about agile environments, and why they don’t hold up.

Myth #1: Agile workplaces only value speed

Many people believe agile teams favor speed above all else.

Agile environments do tend to allow for quicker turnarounds, but they also make sure the job is done right. That sometimes means pressing pause and checking in with the customer.

Or consider a global team that uses agile methodologies in a “follow-the-sun” format. Work is passed between time zones to keep the project moving 24/7.

Even though work continues around the clock, teams still commit to regular feedback, daily stand-ups, and iterative sessions to maintain quality.

Myth #2: Agile approaches don’t require planning

Agile frameworks involve a great deal of planning. It just happens in a different way.

Traditional business practices involve detailed planning at the start of a project. In an agile environment, planning is an ongoing activity that continues throughout a project’s life cycle.

With each iteration, an agile team can adjust its approach based on feedback. That flexibility lets teams respond to shifting requirements and changing conditions.

Myth #3: Agile environments and remote teams don’t mix

The pandemic showed that despite the physical distance between team members, project teams can still thrive in remote and hybrid settings.

With the right online collaboration tools to maintain communication, hybrid and remote project teams can still work in an agile way.

A hybrid customer service team, for example, could use video conferencing to hold daily scrum meetings.

Virtual meetings to evaluate each sprint and realign processes can be recorded and made available for playback in case any team members can’t attend.

How to make agile work for hybrid teams

Building on that last myth, here are three practical ways hybrid teams can do agile well.

Company leadership strongly influences whether agile teams succeed or fail.

In hybrid and remote environments, the leader shifts from supervisor to facilitator. The culture runs on trust, empowerment, and shared responsibility rather than control.

Here are three essential agile practices.

Sensing and seizing opportunities

Success in an agile environment takes some intentionality. Managers and teams should be encouraged to:

  • Observe proactively
  • Identify potential improvements
  • Take calculated risks

According to McKinsey, being intentional and capturing opportunities is a common theme in successful agile organizations.

When Amazon decided to invest in Amazon Web Services (AWS), it was a risky diversion from its core retail business.

Today, AWS is the largest cloud infrastructure provider in the world, holding roughly 30% of the global market. It brings in a big share of Amazon’s operating income and new growth. But it didn’t happen without calculated risk-taking.

Allocating resources effectively

The nature of agile work (short cycles, cross-functional teams, and customer involvement) means resources have to be ready and redeployed as needed.

A team member might need to join another team unexpectedly. Or a sudden technology shift might call for a budget increase.

This adaptability keeps resources matched to evolving project needs and drives results.

Using the right digital tools

The right tools make or break agile work.

Asynchronous communication and other digital tools can ease the friction for team members working across separate time zones.

Tools like Slack, Microsoft Teams, and Zoom keep interaction and collaboration between team members flowing.

Project management tools like Jira, Trello, or Asana work well for tracking tasks, monitoring progress, and keeping everyone on the same page.

Finally, workplace analytics within these tools help teams find improvements and adjust their work plans accordingly.

Start your agile transformation

Now that you know what an agile environment is, you and your team can put this into practice and adopt an agile mindset. It’s not an all-or-nothing approach.

For teams adopting agile project management processes, how far you get depends on the tools you use.
