Note, however, that while virtual games are fun, you don’t want to distract your employees while they’re still in the middle of work. So the ideal time to host these activities with your remote employees is after they’ve finished their work for the day.

2. Remote Workshops

Remote workshops help remote employees learn new skills — and even discover new passions — virtually. Examples of a remote workshop include a cooking workshop or a yoga session.

3. Virtual Team Bonding Activities

Bonding activities aim to help remote employees get to know each other on a more personal level. They create a more casual environment where employees can talk about whatever they want and meet their fellow coworkers, just as they would in a traditional work environment.

4. Show-and-Tell Sessions

Show-and-tell sessions allow remote employees to show their unique skills, interests, and talents to their team members. They help create a work environment in which employees can be themselves and share aspects of their lives with their coworkers.

5. Special Company Events

You can organize a special company event to announce essential updates in your company, recognize remote team employees, or celebrate special occasions. An example of a special company event could be celebrating an upcoming holiday, such as the Fourth of July, with your team.

6. Picture-Sharing Virtual Events

This activity requires each employee to share a picture with your team via video conference or the workplace communication tool your company uses. Typically, these pictures are personal to your employees and are a way for them to share little bits of their lives with their coworkers.

37 Best Virtual Team-Building Activities

Here is a list of 37 virtual team-building activities you can try out to make your remote team feel more connected and help them build better relationships:

1. Two Truths, One Lie

This activity aims to get remote employees to know each other better through fun facts.

This is a great bonding activity, as employees can share funny or interesting stories about their personal lives.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding activity.
  • Time: 2–5 minutes per person.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Each employee must make three statements about themselves. As the name of the game suggests, two of them have to be true and one of them false.

The rest of the team then has to guess which statement is the false one. Here are a couple of two truths, one lie examples you can use for inspiration:

“I’ve lived in three countries (true), I have one cat (true), and I’ve done bungee jumping before (false).”

“I’ve skydived before (true), I’ve talked to Keanu Reeves (true), and my favorite color is blue (false).”

“I know how to headspin (true), I went on a one-year gap year in India (true), and I speak four languages (false).”

2. Pictionary

A simple way to engage your remote team is to have them all play a game of virtual Pictionary. Just like playing this game in real life, a remote employee picks out a card with a word and then draws it out for the others to guess.

  • Type of activity: Virtual game.
  • Time: 10–20 min.
  • Tools required: Pictionary tools, such as Drawful by Jackbox Games, Pictionary Generator, and Virtual Pictionary.

Instructions

First, share access to your Pictionary tool of choice with your team. During the virtual activity, the tool will generate random words that the employees will have to draw in front of the others.

The employees will take turns drawing out the random word on a piece of paper and screen-sharing their drawing for everyone else to see. The rest of the team will then have to guess what the drawings represent.

The remote employee with the most correct guesses wins.

Watch the video below, which explains how to play Pictionary further.

3. “Name That Song” Challenge

Music is an excellent way to help your remote team members bond. As its name suggests, the “Name That Song” challenge involves playing a song in the background that the employees will then have to guess the title of.

  • Type of activity: Virtual game.
  • Time: 20 minutes.
  • Tools required: Music guessing tools, such as SongTrivia or Songlio.

Instructions

Prepare a list of songs with the music-guessing tool of your choice. Next, divide your team into different groups.

Then, play a song. Each team will then have 15 seconds to guess the song’s name.

The team with the most correct guesses wins.

4. “Who’s the Baby?”

This virtual activity is a fun way for remote employees to share childhood memories through baby pictures. It will surely bring out some laughs from your employees and brighten their mood.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: 2–3 minutes for each person.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Each person on your video call must provide a baby picture. The leader of the activity then shares the photos individually, and the employees match each photo to the correct person.

5. Virtual Lunch

Virtual lunch sessions allow employees to eat together during their lunch break, just like they would in a traditional work setting. This gives employees an opportunity to relax, eat their food, and get to know their remote coworkers better.

As a bonus, you could offer gift cards to your remote employees on platforms such as Uber Eats and Doordash to encourage them to have more virtual lunches.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: 30 minutes–1 hour.
  • Tools: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Find a time that fits each team member’s schedule to have a lunch meeting. Next, schedule the virtual lunch with your fellow team members so you can eat together and chat.

6. “Whose Office Is It?” Challenge

During this challenge, a leader displays a picture of each employee’s home office, and the remote employees guess to whom the office belongs.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: 30 minutes.
  • Tools: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Ask each of your remote employees to share a picture of their home office with you. Then, during your next meeting call, display each picture one by one. Everyone on the call must make a guess as to whom the workstation belongs.

7. Virtual Escape Room

In this fun virtual game, employees work together, completing puzzles to escape from a “room” such as a cabin or prison. This type of activity allows employees to collaborate, work on a common challenge, and have fun at the same time.

  • Type of activity: Virtual game.
  • Time: 60–90 minutes.
  • Tools required: Games such as Modern Genius Escape Game or Lost In The Arctic Escape.

Instructions

Run a survey to ask your remote employees which type of virtual escape room game they’re most interested in. You can easily create surveys with a hybrid work management solution such as OfficeRnD Workplace.

Next, find a time to organize your virtual escape via a web conference.

Before you start the virtual escape room session, split the employees into different teams. Then, following the instructions, each team must beat the escape room challenge as quickly as possible. The team that “escapes” first wins the game.

8. Virtual Movie Night

A virtual movie night is similar to a movie night with friends, except everything is done remotely. It’s a fun way to spend time outside of work and make sure everyone on your team has a good time in front of some entertainment.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: 1.5–2 hours (depending on the movie length).
  • Tools required: A live streaming platform such as Teleparty or Scener.

Instructions

Run a poll with your team to determine which type of movie they’d like to see and pick a date for the screening. Next, find a time when you can host the movie screening via a web conference for everyone to watch together.

9. Guess the TV Show or Movie

In a traditional work environment, employees may talk about their favorite TV shows or movies. This activity allows employees to take a break from work and talk about pop culture in a more casual environment.

  • Type of activity: Picture-sharing.
  • Time: 30 minutes.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Before your call, get everyone on your remote team to share pictures of characters from their favorite TV shows or movies.

Create a slideshow displaying all the pictures you received. Then, via a video call, the remote employees can guess from which show or movie each character is from.

The employee with the most correct guesses wins.

10. “Things That Make Me Happy” Channel

For a nice, positive break for your remote employees during their workday, consider creating a “things that make me happy” channel on Slack or whichever communication tool you use.

On this channel, employees can share anything that puts a smile on their faces, such as memes, funny things they notice in their day-to-day lives, or entertaining Youtube videos.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: One minute per employee who participates.
  • Tools required: A workplace communication tool such as Slack.

Instructions

Create a designated channel in which employees can share things that put them in a good mood or warm their hearts. Employees will be able to check the channel out whenever they need some good laughs and positive energy throughout their workday.

11. Virtual Debate Club

In this activity, employees can debate a subject of their choice in a safe environment. This is a perfect virtual activity if you have people on your team who are passionate about certain topics and hold strong opinions.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding/show-and-tell session.
  • Time: One hour.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Run a poll to see which of your remote employees would be interested in participating in a virtual debate club. Next, find a time to schedule your virtual debate that fits the schedules of everyone who agreed to participate.

Make sure to have a moderator during your virtual debate club sessions. Also, try to avoid anything too controversial that could create tension between employees and divide your team instead of helping them bond.

12. Virtual Karaoke Session

Virtual karaoke is a fun way for your employees to express themselves through music. Remote employees don’t even need a perfect singing voice to enjoy this virtual team-building activity.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: 30 minutes.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom and a virtual karaoke app such as Singa, Smule, or StarMaker.

Instructions

Agree on a time with your team to set up the virtual karaoke session. Next, choose the karaoke app you want to use for the virtual activity meeting, along with the playlist you want to choose from.

13. Virtual Personality Test

Personality tests help employees get to know their strengths and weaknesses. They’re a way for your team to get to know each other better and determine how personalities differ across your team.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: 2–4 minutes per remote employee.
  • Tools required: A personality test tool such as the DiSC assessment, the Who Am I? Quiz, or the VIA CharacterStrengths Survey.

Instructions

Ask each employee to complete a personality test with the tool of your choice. Then, at your next meeting, let them each share their test results with their coworkers.

14. Virtual Friday Happy Hour

To help your remote team members celebrate the upcoming weekend, you can host a Friday virtual happy hour where the team gets together to relax and enjoy some drinks.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding and a special company event.
  • Time: 30–60 minutes.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Agree on a time when your team can meet each Friday. Then, schedule weekly Zoom calls during which everyone can get together and chat over some drinks.

15. Virtual Talent Show

A virtual talent show allows employees to express themselves to other team members by showcasing their special skills. For example, they might be able to do some cool dance moves or play an instrument.

  • Type of activity: Special company event.
  • Time: One hour.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

First, give your employees time to prepare for the virtual talent show. Make sure that you make the announcement at least one month in advance so the employees can decide on what they want to present.

Ask the remote employees to record a video of themselves showcasing their talent, and set a date and time for the virtual talent show. During your video conference of the event, share the videos your employees submitted one by one.

16. Virtual Dance Party

A nice way to have fun with an energetic, extroverted team is to host a 30-minute party where you put on some music and let everyone dance to it. You can host this event once a month with your company as a special event.

It’s worth noting, though, that this might not be the best virtual team-building activity for more introverted employees. So make sure you don’t force anyone to participate if they don’t want to!

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding/special company event.
  • Time: 30 minutes.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom, and Twitch for finding a livestream DJ.

Instructions

First, find a time for the virtual dance party that fits your remote team’s schedule. Next, find a live stream DJ on Twitch with music that each participant can play in their home so everyone can dance to the same music.

17. Open Mic

Virtual open mic sessions help employees to have some fun by allowing them to express themselves in front of their coworkers however they’d like. They can use this activity as an opportunity to do some stand-up comedy, recite poetry, or do anything else they’d like.

  • Type of activity: Show-and-tell session.
  • Time: 30 minutes–1 hour.
  • Tools: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Run a poll with your team to identify which of your remote employees would be interested in your virtual open mic sessions. Then, book a time for the session that would fit everyone’s schedule.

You can decide whether you want to adopt a theme for your open mic session (such as poetry or comedy) or let employees present whatever they want.

18. 50 States Challenge

This virtual team-building activity allows you to test your remote team’s US geography skills in the form of a game.

  • Type of activity: Virtual game.
  • Time: 30 minutes.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Before your virtual meeting, prepare photos of different state maps in the US. Next, create a slideshow that you can present to showcase these maps in your next meeting.

Your employees will then have to guess the US state from each map shown on the screen. The person with the most correct guesses wins the game.

19. Virtual Cooking Classes

Virtual cooking classes can make the remote work experience more fun by allowing employees to learn some new recipes at home.

  • Type of activity: Remote workshop.
  • Time: One hour.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Run a pool with your remote team to decide on which recipe they’d like to learn. Then, organize a time that fits your team’s schedule for hosting your virtual cooking class together.

20. Virtual Book Club Session

Do any of your remote team members have a passion for reading?

If so, consider hosting a virtual book club session. During this session, remote employees can share reviews of books they read recently with their coworkers.

  • Type of activity: Show-and-tell session.
  • Time: 30 minutes.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

These virtual book club sessions should be 100% voluntary for remote employees. Ask your team to see if anyone would be interested in meeting up once a month to discuss a book they recently read.

Next, host monthly meetings for remote team members who want to participate in this book club.

21. Virtual Murder Mystery

In this virtual game, remote employees have to work together to solve a murder. This game will test your employees’ analysis and collaboration skills in the face of challenges and is a fun way to spend time outside of work.

  • Type of activity: Virtual game.
  • Time: 1–1.5 hours.
  • Tools required: Murder mystery games such as The Murder Mystery by Dr. Ness, Virtual Murder Mystery by Let’s Roam, or Black Noir Virtual Murder Mystery.

Instructions

Run a poll with your team to see which murder mystery they want to play. Next, open the game during a video conference and solve the mystery together before time runs out.

22. Rose, Thorn, and Bud Icebreaker

A rose, thorn, and bud icebreaker session allows remote employees to share their accomplishments with others and any challenges they’re experiencing.

This session is a way of letting your employees be vulnerable around others in a non-judgmental environment. It’ll also help your employees improve their sense of empathy toward others.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: 2 minutes per employee.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Each employee shares a rose (a win), a thorn (any negative news or challenges they’re experiencing), and a bud (something new they’d like to work on). Give each employee around two minutes to talk.

You can also choose the types of challenges you’d like your team members to share. They can be either company-related or personal.

23. “Day in the Life” Pictures

Encourage employees to share little bits of their lives through pictures. They can be pictures of their hobbies, their pets, or the TV shows they’re watching, for example.

This adds a human side to your workplace communication and makes the remote experience feel more personal.

  • Type of activity: Show-and-tell session.
  • Time: 2–4 minutes per person.
  • Tools required: A workplace communication tool such as Slack.

Instructions

Create a designated Slack channel where employees can share pictures of things going on in their lives. Encourage your team members to drop comments on the pictures to increase engagement.

24. Online Workout Sessions

Sitting down too much and not getting enough physical activity can lead to health problems such as obesity and diabetes.

Online workout sessions can help remote team members stay active throughout their workday. In addition to helping keep them healthy, workout sessions can improve their productivity, as healthy employees are less likely to call in sick from work.

  • Type of activity: Remote workshop.
  • Time: 30 minutes–1 hour.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom and an online workout platform such as Obé Fitness, Alo Moves, or Aaptiv.

Instructions

Schedule a time for your workout session with your team. Then, pick an online fitness class with the online workout platform of your choice and host the class via video conference.

25. Virtual Travel Tour

Virtual travel tours allow you to explore a new destination with your team from the comfort of your own home.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: 30 minutes–1 hour.
  • Tools required: Online virtual tour tools such as the Yosemite National Park tour or the Louvre Collection tour.

Instructions

Run a poll to help your team decide which country, city, or place they’d like to explore. Next, organize a time that works for everyone and host the virtual tour together via a video conference call.

26. Knowledge-Sharing Sessions

During knowledge-sharing sessions, employees discuss a topic that’s close to them with other team members. This could be any hobby or topic they’re passionate about, such as environmental activism.

  • Type of activity: Show-and-tell session.
  • Time: 5–10 minutes per person.
  • Tools Required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Let your team members know about your upcoming knowledge-sharing session one week ahead so they have time to prepare. Then, during a video conference, allow each employee to share their knowledge on their topic of choice.

27. Charades

Virtual charades are a great way to give your employees some good laughs while they work together as a team. During the game, a remote team member acts out a word or phrase that the others must guess.

  • Type of activity: Virtual game.
  • Time: 30 minutes.
  • Tools required: A word generator tool such as Random Word Generator or GetCharadesIdeas.

Instructions

During your charade game split your remote team into two groups. Next, choose one of the word generator tools to generate a word.

During the video call, delegate someone to act out the charade while the rest of the team guesses what the word or phrase is. Set a timer for 40 seconds per word to give your team members enough time to guess. The team with the most correct guesses wins.

28. Virtual Meditation Sessions

Mental health can be difficult to maintain when you’re at home working all the time. A virtual meditation session can help remote employees destress, ultimately creating a company culture that promotes mental health.

Many companies, such as Twello, offer professional meditation sessions for corporate companies you can host from home.

  • Type of activity: Remote workshop.
  • Time: 30 minutes.
  • Tools required: You can book a time with a virtual meditation session company like Twello. Or host the session yourself with a video conferencing platform such as Zoom.

Instructions

Run a poll to determine whether any of your remote team members would be interested in a virtual meditation session. Next, find a time that fits your team’s schedule. Lastly, host the meditation session.

29. Employee Recognition Meetings

According to the 2022 Engagement and Retention Report from Achievers Workforce, 72% of employees say that feeling appreciated improves their mood during their work.

Employee recognition meetings show remote employees how grateful you are that they’re on your team. They provide them with encouragement, which motivates them to work even harder on future projects.

  • Type of activity: Special company event.
  • Time: 30 minutes–1 hour.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Agree on a time that works for everyone to host an employee recognition meeting once a month. Before the meeting, ask your remote employees to find five positive adjectives to describe their team members.

During the web conference, read aloud what each team member had to say about their coworkers.

30. Virtual Bingo

During a Bingo game, employees must try to match numbers in different arrangements on a card. There are many online tools you can use to host a Bingo game virtually.

  • Type of activity: Virtual game.
  • Time: 30 minutes.
  • Tools required: Virtual Bingo tools such as Bingomaker, My Free Bingo Cards, or Let’s Play Bingo!

Instructions

Set up the virtual Bingo tool you’ll be using for your conference meeting. Distribute the virtual cards to your team members, and divide your employees into different breakout rooms. The first team that completes a row wins.

31. Icebreaker Questions

Icebreaker questions are random questions that employees answer to get to know each other better. They are a simple and engaging way to better understand your remote employees’ personalities.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: 2–4 minutes per person.
  • Tools required: Icebreaker question tools such as Range or EasyRetro.

Instructions

Schedule a video conference with your team members. During the meeting, use the icebreaker question tool of your choice to generate questions that team members can answer.

32. Picture-Sharing

They say that a picture is worth a thousand words. In this virtual activity, remote employees take a picture of something that means a lot to them and share a story about it with their coworkers.

  • Type of activity: Picture-sharing virtual event.
  • Time: 10–15 minutes.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom and a slideshow presentation tool like Pitch.

Instructions

Ask each of your remote employees to share a picture of something that’s important to them with you. Then, with your slideshow presentation tool, go through each photo in a video conference and ask each remote employee to share their story about their photo.

33. Virtual Themed and Festive Holiday Events

In a traditional work environment, you can customize your office with holiday-themed decor to get people in a festive spirit.

While this isn’t possible in a remote work setting, you can still celebrate special holiday events with your team through themed virtual calls. This is a great way of getting everyone in the holiday spirit.

  • Type of activity: Special company event.
  • Time: 30–60 minutes.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Schedule a video conference meeting for special events throughout the year, such as Halloween and Christmas. Encourage your remote employees to decorate their homes according to whatever holiday they’re celebrating.

34. Donut Calls

Workplace platform Slack has a 100% free feature called the Donut Bot, which allows team members to set up video calls and have non-work-related discussions with each other.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: 30 min.
  • Tools required: A workplace management tool like Slack.

Instructions

Install Donut as part of Slack. Before the call, it’d be helpful if each participant prepared a list of questions that they could ask the others.

35. Virtual Scavenger Hunt

During a virtual scavenger hunt, remote employees must solve a puzzle or find items before time runs out. This activity is a good way to incorporate some fun competition into your remote work environment.

  • Type of activity: Virtual game.
  • Time: 1–2 hours.
  • Tools required: A virtual scavenger hunt tool such as Scavify or TurfHunt.

Instructions

Decide on a virtual scavenger game you want to play with your team. On a video conference call, create split sessions for different teams, and set a timer for the game. The team that collects the most items before time runs out wins.

36. Virtual Coworking

Getting to work with other people, even if it’s virtual, helps motivate remote employees to stay on top of their tasks. Virtual coworking allows employees to work together remotely and stay productive.

  • Type of activity: Employee bonding.
  • Time: 3–5 hours.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom and a workplace management tool such as Slack.

Instructions

Create a channel on Slack called #coworking with a link to a virtual coworking video session that employees can join at any time.

37. Coffee Hour With the CEO

An excellent virtual team-building activity to make your remote team members feel more connected to your company is to host a weekly or monthly coffee hour with the CEO.

During this time, remote team members that have time to join the call can ask any questions they want about what’s happening within the company. This is also an opportunity for the CEO to meet and welcome remote employees who recently joined the company.

  • Type of activity: Special company event.
  • Time: 30 minutes.
  • Tools required: A video conferencing tool such as Zoom.

Instructions

Make sure to touch base with your CEO to find a time in their likely busy schedule when they can host the coffee hour. Once you agree on a time, schedule a weekly meeting with a link that employees can click on to join the call.

Why Is Virtual Team Building Important?

Virtual team building comes with a multitude of benefits for remote and hybrid employees — and this extends to your company’s overall growth.

Let’s take a detailed look at some of these advantages.

Stronger Relationships Between Remote Teams

It’s hard to build relationships with coworkers who live thousands of miles away from you — but it’s essential to a cohesive team.

In a study of 1,000 full-time employees, 96% believe that team bonding improves their relationships with their coworkers, and 68% of remote employees think that social connections are essential during their workday.

Virtual team-building helps recreate the camaraderie found in a traditional work environment, where employees spend every work day in the office.

With virtual team-building activities, remote and hybrid employees (no matter their generation) can improve their collaboration skills and may even become more comfortable expressing themselves.

These activities allow employees to get to know their coworkers better (and outside of a work context) so they’re more than just people on a screen.

As a result, that boosts collaboration and productivity.

Improved Team Morale and Health

Loneliness can negatively impact remote employees’ health and morale. According to the National Institutes of Health, lonely people are more likely to feel pessimistic and less likely to be happy.

And older adult employees are at greater risk: the data shows that loneliness increases the risk of heart disease by 29%, the risk of stroke by 35%, and the risk of dementia by 50%.

Virtual team-building activities help remote employees feel less alone during their workdays, reducing stress as a result and ultimately helping to improve the team’s mental and physical health as a whole.

A Strong Company Culture

Having a strong company culture is important for companies looking to hire new talent. According to a survey by Indeed, 46% of job seekers consider a company’s culture before deciding whether to apply.

Virtual team-building improves remote company culture by building a sense of community. It keeps everyone on your team engaged and aligned, even with the often large distances that separate them.

Improved Company Diversity

Research from The Manifest shows that 70% of job seekers want to work for a company that makes an effort towards diversity. And if your company is hybrid or remote, it’s likely you’ll have employees who live in countries and time zones other than your own.

Virtual team-building activities provide an opportunity for employees to connect with coworkers across different time zones and perhaps even discover new cultures — ultimately helping create a more diverse corporate environment.

How to Organize a Great Virtual Team-Building Activity in 4 Steps

Here are some tips you can follow to ensure that your virtual team-building activity is a success:

1. Ensure That You Have the Proper Tools and Equipment

Before you start organizing a great virtual team-building activity, be sure to have the proper technology setup to host that activity effectively.

For example, you’ll need a joint calendar tool so that you know at which times your employees are available for the virtual team-building activity.

Other important tools include a web conferencing platform to host your virtual event and workplace communication software for better communication with colleagues.

Don’t forget to follow proper calendar invite etiquette when sending invites to all participants.

2. Run a Poll to Determine Preferred Activities

Next, reach out to your employees to see which activities they’d prefer to do. You can uncover this information by sending them a poll or survey on the types of activities they like doing the best.

3. Choose an Activity

Based on the results of your poll or survey, pick a list of activities to host, focusing on the ones that had the most votes. You could also divide your remote employees into different groups based on the activities they prefer.

4. Choose an Appropriate Time

The last step is to pick a time that fits everyone’s schedule for your virtual team-building activity. Make sure that you’re considerate of different time zones, especially if you have remote employees who live overseas.

Help Employees Feel More Connected With Virtual Team-Building Activities

It’s common for remote employees to feel lonely. However, it doesn’t have to be that way. You can work to keep them engaged with virtual team-building activities.

Virtual team-building activities help remote employees build strong relationships with each other. This will help them feel less lonely and more connected — and will likely improve your overall company culture as a result.

To get started with virtual team-building activities, start with simple and free ones, such as donut calls.

Post body:
The age-old debate of whether remote work increases productivity has taken on a new level of significance in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. While some swear by the perks of working from home, others fear it’s a productivity killer.

So, what’s the truth? Can working from home really boost your output, or will it leave you feeling like a couch potato?

Recent studies have attempted to answer the questions about remote work productivity, and the results have been mixed. Owl Labs’ report found that remote workers in the US were 22% more likely to feel productive in their jobs than on-site workers. However, these remote workers worked an additional 1.4 days per month compared to on-site workers, increasing their risk of burnout.

The question of whether working from home increases productivity is complex, and the answer varies depending on the individual and the job. This article explores the impact of working from home on productivity, delving into the many advantages and disadvantages.

Quick Summary

  • There are a variety of flex working models, including work-from-home, remote work, hybrid work, office decentralization, and flexible work.
  • Employees overwhelmingly favor flexible work — and they want more of it. Survey after survey proves that employees feel more productive and focused when they’re given the option of hybrid work.
  • Organizations are reporting 5 key trends arising from remote work, including an increase in coworking, flex, and hybrid spaces, rethinking office space function and design to support workers, the expansion of recruitment and talent to a global scale, a significant cost reduction for companies eschewing traditional offices, and an overall increase in manager-employee trust.
  • There are several ways to support remote work productivity, including innovative workspaces, better time management, a culture of flexibility, and the use of the right software and tools.

Working From Home vs Remote Work

Working from home, remote work, flexible working — what do all these terms really mean? Do they all refer to the same thing?

Although these terms are all related to the concept of flexible work arrangements, there are some key differences. We’ll explain each model and its trends below.

Working From Home

This work model involves employees working from their own homes instead of commuting to a physical workplace. This could be a full-time or part-time arrangement.

The US Census Bureau notes a considerable uptick in people working from home between 2019 and 2021. During this period, the number of people primarily working from home tripled from 5.7% (roughly 9 million people) to 17.9% (27.6 million people).

Remote Work

Remote work means working from any location outside a conventional office. This can include working from home, but it can also include coworking spaces, coffee shops, or even outdoor areas like beaches. So although working from home is a type of remote work, not all remote work is done from home.

Upwork research highlights the growing trend of remote work, with approximately 36 million Americans expected to embrace this work style by 2025.

Hybrid Work

In a hybrid work model, employees split their time between working from home and working from their employer’s physical workplace. Hybrid work merges on-site and remote work, giving employees the flexibility to divide their time between the office and remote environments.

Hybrid work has become increasingly popular, and the trend shows no sign of slowing down. An AT&T study projects that this blended model will skyrocket from 42% in 2021 to 81% by 2024.

Here’s an interesting article on keeping hybrid workers engaged.

Flexible Working

Flexible working gives employees the freedom to decide when, where, and how they work. This can include working from home, but it can also include flexible hours or job sharing.

CNBC data reveals that 67% of workers say they feel more empowered to take advantage of flexible working arrangements at their companies — a significant increase from 26% pre-pandemic.

Office Decentralization

Office decentralization involves moving away from having a centralized physical office. Instead, companies disperse their office spaces across multiple locations.

This could mean multiple smaller “satellite” offices or coworking spaces in different places. CBRE findings show that 39% of companies plan to expand their office portfolios within the next three years.

How Does Working Offsite Increase Remote Work Productivity?

With remote work exploding over the past few years, the debate about whether it increases productivity has intensified.

Some managers hold “productivity paranoia” and fear that their remote workers are not as productive as they would be in the office. In fact, half of all business leaders believe that when employees are working “out of sight,” they don’t work as hard.

But as the debate between management and employees continues, one thing is clear: employees overwhelmingly value flexibility. A McKinsey study shows that between in-office or remote working, 87% of employees prefer working remotely.

Despite some managers’ concerns, a closer look at the evidence suggests that remote work does, in fact, boost productivity. And there are facts to prove it.

  • According to an Owl Labs study, 62% of remote workers feel more productive when working from home.
  • Stanford University’s research shows that remote workers are 13% more productive than their in-office colleagues.
  • FlexJobs found that employees with flexible schedules are 29% more productive and 53% more focused than those with traditional working arrangements.

5 Trends Emerging From the Rise in Remote Work

As remote work becomes the new normal, it’s not just employees’ professional and personal lives that are affected. The working world is shifting, and companies need to adapt to ensure their remote workers remain engaged and productive.

Here are five key trends shaping the new world of work and what they mean for remote workers’ productivity:

Rise in Coworking Spaces

The remote work boom has resulted in a remarkable expansion of available coworking spaces. Research and Markets anticipates the global coworking spaces market to grow by $14,124.67 million between 2022 and 2027, and the rising number of freelancers, startups, and remote employees looking for professional workspaces will propel this growth.

Unsurprisingly, companies searching for flexible office space solutions are also getting in on the coworking trend. Not only are coworking spaces beneficial for remote work productivity, but they also provide a sense of community and collaboration among remote workers.

Reinvention of the Office

As remote work becomes more prevalent, companies are rethinking the purpose and design of their physical offices to ensure remote work productivity.

A Harvard Business Review article highlights the transformation of offices into collaborative social spaces that foster employee well-being and productivity. Companies are also investing in technology and digital tools to facilitate communication and collaboration among remote teams.

Global Talent Acquisition

Remote work has made it easier for companies to access talent from anywhere in the world. This can lead to increased innovation, creativity, and improved employee performance.

Many companies are taking advantage of this by hiring remote workers from other countries. This trend has both created new opportunities for workers in countries with lower costs of living and allowed companies to tap into a more diverse and global talent pool.

HR Brew reports that 54% of organizations operate in at least two countries, tapping into a diverse range of skills and expertise.

Cost Reduction for Companies

Remote work can lead to considerable cost savings for companies. By allowing employees to work from home or other remote locations, companies can save money on office space and related expenses, such as rent, utilities, and office supplies. According to a Lemon.io blog post, startups can save up to $10,601,000 annually on remote workers.

These savings can then be invested in remote work productivity tools like collaboration software, project management tools, and communication platforms.

Read more on that topic here.

Nurturing Trust

Fostering trust between managers and remote workers is crucial for maintaining morale and productivity within an organization. Without trust, managers may dictate what remote workers should or should not do. This hinders creativity and innovation, which can lead to a less productive team.

Many at-home employees feel that their managers lack trust in them — often due to close monitoring during work hours. An Owl Labs study reveals that 44% of employees are concerned about potential micromanagement.

The Advantages of Remote Work

Working remotely has multiple potential advantages, many of which can increase employee productivity. Let’s look at a few of them.

Less Travel Time

Commuting can be a source of stress for some employees and take up a lot of their day. Before the pandemic, US workers spent an average of 54 minutes commuting each day.

For those working from home, travel time to and from work is reduced to zero (barring those few minutes of walking from the bedroom to the at-home office).

Fewer Interruptions

Working remotely can provide a more focused and productive work environment for some. Employees aren’t subject to the same interruptions and distractions as those in a traditional office setting.

According to a study by FlexJobs, distractions at the office take up 78 minutes of the work day compared to just 43 minutes of the day when working from home. With fewer interruptions, employees can better concentrate on their work and complete their tasks more efficiently.

Better Work-Life Balance

Without the necessary time and stress of commuting, remote workers have more time for healthy activities, like exercising, hobbies, and cooking at home. This contributes to better physical and mental health and, therefore, improved employee well-being and productivity.

According to a study by Owl Labs, 33% of fully remote employees say they have a better work-life balance, compared to 25% of hybrid working employees and 17% of fully in-person employees.

The Challenges of Remote Work

Just as there are perks to working remotely, there are downsides.

Let’s take a look at a few of these consequences.

Isolation and Loneliness

Remote employees may feel detached from their colleagues and company culture, potentially leading to loneliness and reduced remote work productivity.

A study involving over 1,000 remote workers across 55 countries revealed that 21% of participants experienced recurring loneliness.

In addition, that impacts employee collaboration and engagement.

Limited Access to Resources

Remote workers may not have access to the same resources and equipment as those in a traditional office setting.

One common problem is technological difficulties, such as unreliable connectivity. In a study by Slack, almost 1 in 4 employees (24%) recognized unstable remote connectivity as a challenge.

Overworking and Burnout

Without clear boundaries between their work and personal lives, remote workers may find it difficult to disconnect from work, leading to overworking and burnout. A recent study found that 51% of workers were concerned about experiencing burnout due to consecutive calls when working from home. This can have a negative impact on their mental health and job performance.

5 Tips to Increase Remote Work Productivity

Increasing remote work productivity comes down to helping employees feel organized and in-control of their work and workday.

Let’s look at some best practices for employees working remotely to prevent challenges like loneliness and burnout.

Create a Schedule

Creating a consistent schedule for work and personal activities can help you maintain a healthy work-life balance and stay on task. This could include setting specific work hours, scheduling breaks and meals, and allocating time for personal activities.

Mix It Up

Prevent the monotony of working and living in the same space by using coworking spaces. Or if your company is using a hybrid work model, visit the office on certain days. This change in your environment can be refreshing, helping to foster social connections and camaraderie with your colleagues.

Time Box Tasks

Designate timeframes for tasks to stay focused and motivated. Try using the Pomodoro Technique, which includes working for a set duration (typically 25 minutes) followed by a brief break.

Set Boundaries

Establish boundaries between your work and personal life to maintain a healthy work-life balance.

Set limits on your work hours, avoid checking work-related messages outside of work hours, and create a physical separation between your work and personal spaces.

Create a Designated Workspace

​​Establishing a dedicated workspace can help minimize distractions and encourage a healthy work-life balance. Allocate a section of your home for work purposes to mentally separate your professional life from your personal one.

5 Tips for Managers to Support Remote Workers’ Productivity

It’s important for managers to support their employees who are working from home. Here are six tips for managers to support WFH employees and boost their remote work productivity.

Encourage a Work-Life Balance

Encouraging a solid work-life balance can help remote workers stay motivated and focused. This can involve setting clear expectations around work hours and communication, as well as promoting healthy habits like exercise and mindfulness.

Don’t Micromanage

Trust forms the foundation of a successful remote work environment. Giving employees autonomy and trust can foster a more positive work culture and increase productivity. Managers should prioritize the quality of the work produced over the quantity.

Build Trust With Your Employees

Trust between managers and remote employees can boost morale and productivity. Regular check-ins, transparent communication, and professional development opportunities are essential to fostering it.

Embrace Flexibility

Accommodating diverse work arrangements shows employees that they are valued and respected. This can involve offering flexible work hours, allowing employees to work from different locations, and encouraging creative problem-solving.

Name: What Executives Are Saying About the Future of Hybrid Work
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: There used to be a time when going to work meant driving to the office from Monday to Friday. Then the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020.
Post body:
There used to be a time when going to work meant driving to the office from Monday to Friday. Then the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020.

Suddenly, in-office employees began working from home — and many loved it.

Years later, the debate over where work happens hasn’t gone away. Some large employers have pushed for a full return to the office, but most companies have settled somewhere in between with hybrid work.

Whether they like it or not, most executives now treat hybrid as a permanent part of how their companies operate. According to findings from Stanford and the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta’s Survey of Business Uncertainty, many companies are standing firm on their hybrid or fully remote work policies, and they don’t intend to change their stance for the next 12 months.

Here’s what executives are saying about the future of hybrid work, and what the latest data shows.

Quick Summary

  • Hybrid work has stabilized as the dominant model for remote-capable jobs, and executives expect it to stay
  • Leaders see flexibility as a retention lever: removing it pushes people toward the door
  • Companies keep redesigning their spaces, policies, and management practices around hybrid work, and are investing in the tools to run it

What is hybrid work?

Hybrid work is a model where employees split their time between a workplace and a remote location, usually their home, instead of being in the office five days a week.

It’s now the default for people who can work remotely. Among US employees in remote-capable jobs, 52% work hybrid, 26% work fully remote, and 22% work on-site, according to Gallup.

That pattern has held for a while. The share of paid working days performed from home is stable at about 20 percent of paid workdays, and other sources also show stability in WFH rates since early 2023.

What are executives saying about the future of hybrid work?

Executives who run hybrid or remote teams mostly plan to keep them. When Stanford and the Atlanta Fed surveyed more than a thousand business leaders, the answer was clear. Just 12 percent of the executives that currently have hybrid or remote workers report plans for an RTO mandate in the year ahead. And even those aren’t usually full recalls. More than a quarter of the planned RTOs will require onsite work only 1 to 4 days a week.

Executives cite concrete reasons for holding the line. Many employers like remote work because it reduces floorspace needs, raises productivity, and lowers quits. The Stanford researchers put it plainly: “Whatever happens in the U.S. economy over the next year, we think working from home is here to stay.”

Leaders aren’t uniform on this, though. There’s a generational split in how executives view the office. Forty-eight percent of Gen Z employers believe remote work is most productive, while only 28% of Boomer employers agree. As younger leaders move into more senior roles, that gap will shape company policy.

Here’s what Google CEO Sundar Pichai said when Google set its hybrid approach:

Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google

“We’ll move to a hybrid work week where most Googlers spend approximately three days in the office and two days wherever they work best. Since in-office time will be focused on collaboration, your product areas and functions will help decide which days teams will come together in the office. There will also be roles that may need to be on-site more than three days a week due to the nature of the work.”

Why do executives believe flexibility helps retain talent?

Employees want flexibility, and executives who ignore that risk losing people.

The retention evidence is strong. A Stanford study published in Nature ran a randomized trial with more than 1,600 employees and found that resignations dropped 33% when staff moved from full-time office work to two remote days a week, with women, non-managers, and people with long commutes the least likely to quit.

The threat of quitting isn’t hypothetical either. 46% of people with home-capable jobs say they would be unlikely to stay if they could no longer work from home, according to Pew Research Center. Among high performers, the number is higher still. In Cisco’s survey, 78% of high performers would consider leaving a company if the work policies were not flexible enough.

At the same time, most leaders and employees still see real value in office time. Nine out of 10 employees rank collaboration and community as very important aspects of office culture, the highest of any attribute, and developing a sense of belonging and collaborating with team members are the top drivers for wanting to spend more time in the office. That’s the balance executives keep trying to strike: flexibility for focus and life, office time for the work that’s better done together.

Here’s what Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has said about the future of work:

Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft

“Employee expectations are changing, and we will need to define productivity much more broadly — inclusive of collaboration, learning, and wellbeing to drive career advancement for every worker, including frontline and knowledge workers, as well as for new graduates and those who are in the workforce today. All this needs to be done with flexibility in when, where, and how people work.”

How are companies reinventing their work processes?

As companies settle into hybrid work, executives keep redesigning their practices to fit it. That covers real estate, hiring, and how managers run teams.

Office space is one place the change shows up. Many leaders have trimmed footprints and rebuilt what’s left around collaboration. By lessening the call for everyday office presence, leaders can counter the need for larger office spaces and their high rents and use smart-workplace tech to make better use of the space they have.

Hiring practices have shifted too, since flexible roles now draw a wider candidate pool. Robert Half’s benefits and perks survey of over 500 HR managers in the United States found that 88% of employers provide some hybrid work options, although this varies by seniority level and individual circumstances.

Here’s what Chief Learning Officer of Udemy, Melissa Daimler, has said about the culture side of this shift:

Melissa Daimler, Chief Learning Officer of Udemy

“It’s important to clarify how to work together. We are codifying our values through a “re-culturing” process — identifying specific behaviors we expect and want to see for each value and then embedding those into our processes of hiring, onboarding, and talent managing. Doing so provides a clear playbook for everyone, making it easier and psychologically safer for everyone to do their job well. We can no longer hide behind free food and ping-pong tables when defining culture.”

How are executives adapting to hybrid work?

The clearest signal of where executives stand is what they do, not what they say. Most are building policies and spaces that assume hybrid is permanent.

They’re doing it even against economic pressure. Eighty-five percent of the executives say WFH policies at their firms won’t change if unemployment doubles. That’s a strong sign leaders view flexibility as a business decision, not a perk they’ll drop at the first downturn.

Technology carries a lot of the weight in a hybrid workplace. Facilitating communication between teams, running meetings with on-site and off-site people, and creating room for collaboration are still central to workplace productivity. Yet many companies underinvest here. A full 90% of employees see value in collaboration tools, but only 32% of employers are investing in the high-grade collaboration technology that supports flexible, hybrid work models.

Here’s what the cofounder and CEO of The Escape Game, Mark Flint, says about staying adaptable:

Mark Flint, Cofounder and CEO of The Escape Game

“With the job market as tight and volatile as it has been, there is very little margin for error, and being adaptable and creative is essential. The ‘rules of the game’ are different and still changing; if our team is going to win, we know we have to change as well. For our WFH policies, we tried many different versions for various periods of time. We were intentional and transparent in our communication with our teams and honest about the fact that we would experiment with different models.”

How are executives leading differently in the hybrid workplace?

Managing people you don’t see every day takes different habits than managing a room. Leaders who invest in that skill get better results.

The productivity case now runs in hybrid’s favor. 69% of managers believe that working hybrid or remotely has made their team more productive. That undercuts the old assumption that presence equals output.

As hybrid work stays the norm, companies that design and develop spaces to keep people connected will likely see stronger results in productivity, customer satisfaction, employee engagement, and diversity and inclusion.

Here’s what CEO of Qualcomm, Cristiano Amon, has said about balancing culture and flexibility:

Cristiano Amon, CEO of Qualcomm

“I’m a firm believer in the importance of in-person collaboration. Yes, we have the ability to work remotely, but we also want to preserve our culture. The reality is, if you don’t create as a community, it’s very difficult to maintain a strong culture. It’s all about striking the right balance between flexibility and providing people with an environment to work together effectively. We had a phased approach in bringing our employees back to the office, and we’re now embracing a hybrid schedule. We allow flexibility but are leaning into opportunities for people to spend time together and continue to build our incredible culture.”

What tools are executives investing in for hybrid work?

Running hybrid well means giving teams a shared system for where people sit, when they’re in, and how they book space. AI is now part of that conversation. 80% of employees say they’re using AI in the workplace, up from 72% in 2024. Cisco found leaders are behind on it, with only 44% of employers investing in AI.

Name: A Complete Hot Desking Guide [Updated For 2026]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Walk any office floor on a Friday and count the empty desks. In 2026 that count is the whole story. Companies stopped buying one desk per person, and the data is blunt about it: in CBRE’s 2026 workplace benchmark, not a single organization still targets a one-to-one desk ratio, and 69% now have more than 40% of their people sharing desks.
Post body:
Walk any office floor on a Friday and count the empty desks. In 2026 that count is the whole story. Companies stopped buying one desk per person, and the data is blunt about it: in CBRE’s 2026 workplace benchmark, not a single organization still targets a one-to-one desk ratio, and 69% now have more than 40% of their people sharing desks.

That is the world hot desking was built for. What started in the 1990s as a fix for shift workers and expensive real estate is now the default seating model for hybrid offices. Some people once argued it would hurt your company. The argument lost. Attendance is uneven, most desks sit empty for a third of the week, and paying rent on seats nobody uses is a hard cost to defend.

Hot desking fixes that. It lets a smaller pool of desks serve a larger team, cuts overhead, and gives people the flexibility they now expect. Done badly, it turns into a daily scramble for a seat. Done well, it is invisible: people book in seconds, sit near their team, and get to work.

This hot desking guide covers:

  • What hot desking is, and how it differs from desk sharing and hoteling
  • The seating models to choose from, and which fits your team
  • The real advantages and the honest tradeoffs
  • How to run it well, and how to measure whether it’s working
  • The etiquette and policy that keep it fair

What is hot desking?

Hot desking is a flexible work arrangement where employees use any available desk instead of a permanently assigned one. They pick a spot that fits the day, plug in, and leave it for the next person.

It suits modern workplaces where schedules vary, and people split time between home and the office. Without a system like this, a company ends up paying for a large office full of empty desks while half the team works remotely.

Some offices run hot desks first-come, first-served. That works until a busy Tuesday, when people arrive and find nothing open. Booking software solves it. OfficeRnD Workplace pairs an easy desk booking system with shared-desk scheduling so people can see what’s free and claim it before they leave home. It also runs a Google Workspace desk booking system for teams already in that ecosystem.

Why is it called “hot desking”?

The name comes from “hot racking,” a naval practice where sailors on different shifts shared the same bunk, or rack, to save space on a ship. The bunk was still warm when the next sailor took it.

The office version is the same idea. Different people use the same desk at different times of the day, so each desk earns its keep instead of sitting cold.

Hot desking vs desk sharing vs hoteling

People use these three terms as if they mean the same thing. They don’t, and the difference matters when you set policy.

Hot desking

  • Hot desking is a workplace strategy where multiple employees use the same workspace at different times.
  • Nobody has an assigned desk.
  • People take whatever is free when they arrive, or book a spot through hot desking software.
  • It’s a cost-effective way to run a workspace and mix teams up.

For a shortlist of tools, see our guide to the best hot desk booking software for 2026.

Desk sharing

  • Desk sharing means two or more employees share the same workspace, often across different shifts or times of day.
  • A single workstation might be used by several people over a week.
  • It’s common where space is tight or in high demand.

Here’s a practical guide to sharing a desk in a hybrid office.

Desk hoteling

  • Desk hoteling means employees reserve a workspace or meeting room for a set period, usually as needed.
  • It runs on an online reservation system, so people book a specific spot in advance.
  • It’s useful for remote workers and visiting staff who need a guaranteed seat.

The short version: hot desking is same-day and spontaneous, hoteling is booked ahead. For a full breakdown, see hot desking vs desk hoteling.

The seating models: which hot desking setup fits your team

“Hot desking” is an umbrella term. Underneath it sit several models, and picking the wrong one is how good intentions turn into a scramble for seats. Here are the five that matter, with the teams they suit.

First-come, first-served

Anyone walks in and takes any open desk. It’s the simplest model and it stops people reserving seats they never use. The catch: on peak days, latecomers can arrive to nothing. It works best for small teams or offices where attendance rarely spikes.

Reserved desks

People book a specific seat in advance, so they know where they’ll sit and who’s nearby. No-shows are the main risk, which is why booking software that flags unused reservations matters. This is the default for most hybrid teams.

Neighborhoods

You group desks into zones tied to a team or function. People still book freely inside their zone, but they land near the colleagues they work with. Neighborhoods scale well for large offices, where a single zone can hold 60 desks or more.

Activity-based workspaces

Here the office offers different settings for different work: quiet zones for focus, open areas for collaboration, booths for calls. People move to the space that fits the task. It suits teams whose days swing between heads-down work and group sessions.

Check out our guide on activity-based working for more info.

Free addressing

Free addressing looks like first-come, first-served, but sensors track which desks are occupied in real time. People check an app to see what’s actually open instead of walking the floor. It’s the most hands-off model, and it needs sensor hardware to work.

Most companies blend these. A common pattern: neighborhoods for teams, a few activity-based zones for focus and collaboration, and same-day booking on top. Match the model to how your people actually use the office, not to how you wish they would.

Hot desking advantages

Companies adopt hot desking for concrete reasons. Here’s what you gain, and what an executive should expect from it.

More use out of the space you already pay for

In CBRE’s 2026 benchmark, the global office utilization rate hit 53%, up from 35% in 2023, and 48% of organizations now target a desk-sharing ratio between 1.01 and 1.49 people per seat. In plain terms, most companies are fitting more people into the same footprint on a rotating basis.

Hot desking is how they do it. Instead of rows of empty desks while half the team is remote, the desks that exist get used. You can optimize your floor plan and, in many cases, check how much office space you actually need. This space calculator helps you size it.

Less space means lower rent, cheaper cleaning, and fewer overheads. That frees money for work that matters and makes it easier to run a more sustainable workspace. Higher-education teams see the same savings.

It makes hybrid work actually work

Two-thirds of office workers are now hybrid, in the building one to four days a week. A one-desk-per-person policy can’t survive that math. Hot desking is the seating model that fits the flexibility hybrid work depends on, where the office is one place work happens, not the only one.

It also takes the pressure off. With fewer desks than headcount, nobody feels they have to be in every day to justify a seat.

Better cross-team communication

Shared desks flatten the office. When seating isn’t fixed, people from different teams end up next to each other, and that mixing tends to produce ideas that siloed seating never would. Teams working on the same project can cluster for a sprint, then break up and regroup with different people next time.

In our recent hybrid work playbook for 2026, we share that one of the reasons why many employees come to the office is the social element – including in-person collaboration.

A break from the routine

Changing spots in the office keeps things fresh. New desk neighbors can be a small daily lift. And if two people don’t click, they’re only next to each other for the day.

Hot desking disadvantages

Plenty of companies love hot desking, including us at OfficeRnD. However, it still has limits, and it’s better to plan for them than to discover them.

No personal desk

The clearest tradeoff for culture is the loss of a spot that’s yours. Some people miss the photos, the plants, the drawer of snacks. You can soften it: privacy screens, shared personalization boards, or a small set of dedicated desks for people who need one.

Research bears this out. A 2024 Leesman study found that in offices with no extra spaces like quiet rooms, only 41% of people said they could work productively, but in offices with a mix of focus and team zones, that jumped to 85%.

Hardware setups

Some roles need a fixed technical setup that can’t move every day. Dragging monitors and docks around a shared floor isn’t practical. For these cases, keep a few permanent or project-based desks inside the shared space.

It can get chaotic without a system

Tracking who sits where, and when, gets overwhelming fast on paper. The fix is planning plus software. Set clear rules for desk and room booking, give people an easy way to reserve, and watch the trends so you can adjust.

Security of personal items

People can’t leave laptops and belongings on a desk overnight, which raises the question of where things go. Lockers answer most of it. With good desk booking software you also keep a record of who sat where, which helps if a security issue comes up.

More cleaning

Different people use the same desk on consecutive days, and each of them deserves a clean one. That means stricter hygiene rules: people clear their desks at the end of the day, and surfaces get wiped before the next person arrives.

How to make hot desking work for your team

With some preparation you can skip the common pitfalls and give people a setup they actually like.

Figure out your desk needs

Start with the numbers.

Map your attendance over a few weeks: how many people come in on a peak day versus a quiet one. Size fixed seating to the average and cover busy days with shared, bookable desks. That way the office works on Tuesday without paying for an empty Friday.

Consider how teams collaborate

Your team’s dynamics should drive the layout. Think through:

  • Which people need to work together, and how often
  • Whether you need zones or neighborhoods for specific teams
  • Who’s in most days versus who’s remote-first

At OfficeRnD, our collaborative scheduling tool is built for exactly this. It helps people in a hybrid team coordinate their in-office days:

  • Shared calendar: people see each other’s schedules and plan in-person days, so nobody drives in to find their team at home.
  • Desk reservations: people book a specific desk ahead of time and can sit near their project team.
  • Meeting room booking: people grab a room for in-person sessions without the back-and-forth.

In-person collaboration is where hybrid teams build trust and solve problems faster than another video call ever would. The tool’s job is to make those moments easy to plan.

Provide storage and keep it secure

People still bring things to the office. Give them somewhere to put them.

Lockers are the usual answer, and they double as one of the more useful hot desking investments you can make. When people trust that their things are safe, they warm to the shared setup. You can also offer standing desks for people who want them.

Set up private spaces

Different people do their best work in different settings, and everyone needs a quiet spot sometimes: a sensitive call, focused work, a hard conversation. Alongside the shared desks, offer conference rooms, phone booths, or lounges, and make them bookable the same way.

How to measure hot desking success

Hot desking isn’t a set-it-and-forget-it project. The seat counts and zones that work in month one drift as attendance shifts. These are the metrics that tell you whether the model still fits, and where to adjust.

  • Occupancy rate. The share of seats filled at peak. CBRE puts the global occupancy rate at 111% in 2026, meaning companies now assign more people to a building than it has seats. A healthy target for most offices lands between 60% and 85%. Above that, people compete for desks.
  • Desk-sharing ratio. Employees per available desk. Most companies running hot desking sit between 1.3:1 and 2:1. Find yours by comparing headcount to peak attendance, not to total staff.
  • Space utilization. How the floor is actually used over time. It tells you where people gather, which desks sit cold, and what you can cut or repurpose.
  • No-show rate. Booked desks nobody shows up for. High no-shows waste capacity and hide real demand. Check-in requirements and auto-release rules bring it down.
  • Peak-day patterns. Tuesday and Wednesday are the busiest days for most offices, and Friday runs 30% to 40% below peak. Plan seat counts around the peak, not the average, or busy days turn into a scramble.

OfficeRnD Workplace reports on all of this: desk occupancy, who sat where, and how usage trends over weeks. That turns floor-plan decisions from guesses into evidence, and it’s how you keep the office right-sized as habits change.

Hot desking etiquette: dos and don’ts

New habits take time. A short how-to guide, plus clear etiquette, helps people settle in faster. Here’s what to cover for managers and employees.

Dos for managers

Address hot desking anxiety

Hot desking causes real stress for some people. In one survey of UK office workers, not knowing where they’d sit each day was the single biggest stressor, and the ability to pre-book a seat was what most wanted to fix it.

Meet that head-on with clear communication, training, and a booking tool that removes the daily uncertainty.

Use suitable software

Put hot desking software like OfficeRnD Workplace in place so people can book and manage desks easily, and so you get real-time data on how desks are used.

Get the right equipment

Make sure people have what they need to work anywhere: laptops, docking stations, monitors. Here’s a list of the best hot desking accessories.

Have a plan in place

Write down the guidelines, policies, and procedures. Communicate them clearly, and keep supporting people as they adjust.

Don’ts for managers

Don’t overlook employee preferences

Factor in job roles, work styles, physical needs, and personal preferences so the policy is fair and inclusive.

Don’t forget privacy and security

Shared desks and devices raise real concerns. Provide privacy screens, secure devices with passwords, and set clear security protocols.

Don’t ignore feedback

Ask people how it’s going and act on what they say. Check in regularly so small issues don’t fester.

Don’t forget to communicate changes

Policies evolve. When they do, tell people. Silent changes breed confusion.

Dos for employees

Respect your colleagues’ space

Don’t move or use other people’s things without asking. Leave shared areas clean.

Be on time and use the booking system

Respect the booking system and show up for what you reserve. Here’s an article on hot desking software if you want the detail.

Be mindful of others

[Image: office environment]

Keep the noise down. Take loud calls to a booth or meeting room, and skip the music on speaker.

Be flexible

Lean into hybrid work and stay open to change. Different desks, different neighbors, different days.

Don’ts for employees

Don’t leave a mess

Clear your desk, bin your trash, wipe up spills. The next person inherits whatever you leave.

Don’t dominate the space

Don’t camp on a high-demand desk all day if others need it. Share it fairly.

Don’t eat lunch at your desk

Strong smells and crumbs bother the next person. Eat in the kitchen or a break area.

Don’t claim a desk permanently

The whole point is flexibility. Don’t leave your things on one desk to mark it as yours. Take them with you or store them.

Tip: the fastest way to make etiquette stick is to put it in a short written policy people can find. Cover booking rules, clean-desk expectations, and noise, and keep it to a single page.

How to set up hot desking in your office

Here’s a step-by-step for getting started. We used a very similar guide to set up our hot desking.

1. Evaluate your space

Work out how much usable space you have and how many people it holds. Factor in noise, natural light, and proximity to common areas.

2. Create a hot desking policy

Set out the process: booking rules, equipment use, cleaning responsibilities. Communicate it clearly before launch.

3. Invest in the right technology

The right software is what separates a smooth rollout from a chaotic one. If you’re weighing options, our roundup of top-rated hybrid work tools compares the leading platforms. OfficeRnD Workplace gives you desk booking, room booking, floor-plan maps, and the analytics to manage it all.

4. Create a flexible layout

Choose furniture that moves. Lightweight desks and mobile workstations let you reconfigure the floor as needs change.

5. Provide the resources people need

Charging stations, printers, docking stations, monitors: make sure people can walk up and work.

6. Launch, then measure and adjust

Review the metrics above, gather feedback, and tune seat counts and zones. Treat the setup as something you refine, not something you finish.
