Name: 7 Strong Employee Motivators That Improve Office Attendance
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: The way we work keeps shifting, and where people work has become one of the most contested questions on any HR or facilities team’s desk.
Post body:
The way we work keeps shifting, and where people work has become one of the most contested questions on any HR or facilities team’s desk.

Fewer of us bump into each other in the break room, chat over coffee, and swap commute stories. More of the day runs through video calls, Slack, and email.

Remote work has clear upsides, but some employees worry a return to the office will cost them the flexibility they’ve built their lives around. Employers, meanwhile, want more in-person time and often meet resistance when they ask for it.

There’s a workable middle ground.

This article covers seven motivators that get employees to choose the office, with a focus on the collaboration and social connection that in-person time makes possible.

Quick Summary: Here are several questions we’ll answer:

  • Should you bring employees back to the office?
  • What are the benefits and drawbacks of employees being in the office?
  • What are some motivators for employees to work from the office?
  • How can you get employees excited about working from the office?

An office motivator is any incentive, amenity, or workplace condition that makes an employee choose to come in, rather than a mandate that forces them to. The distinction matters, because the data on forced attendance isn’t kind to employers.

Should you bring employees back to the office?

There’s no single right answer, and the current numbers show why.

As an executive, you know there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to a company and its culture. Some employees do their best work in an office. Others prefer to work remotely, or on the go.

The pressure to return is real. According to CBRE, 37% of companies were enforcing office attendance requirements in 2025, more than double the 17% who did so in 2024. But enforcement and attendance aren’t the same thing. Employees still push back, and forced mandates carry a cost: Pew Research Center found that 46% of workers who can work from home say they’d be unlikely to stay at their current job if their employer no longer allowed it.

At the same time, people do value the office. Many miss the social side of in-person work, the spontaneous conversations, and the collaboration that’s harder to replicate on a call. What they want is a say in when they come in.

Listen to your employees and weigh their concerns before setting policy. If you’re considering bringing your team back full-time, think hard about both sides of the decision.

4 benefits of employees returning to the office

Remote work is here to stay, but in-person time still delivers things that are hard to get any other way.

More opportunities for collaboration

Collaboration is where in-person work earns its keep. Working together in the same room makes communication and teamwork easier.

Research backs this up. Face-to-face requests are 34 times more effective than the same requests sent by email.

When employees share a space, they can bounce ideas around, brainstorm, and work through problems together. With OfficeRnD Workplace’s meeting room booking system, booking a room for your team takes a few clicks. That means more time collaborating and less time hunting for an open space.

Camaraderie and a sense of belonging

The office is where people meet, collaborate, and build relationships. Being there in person helps employees feel like they belong to something bigger than their own to-do list.

Belonging isn’t a soft nice-to-have. In McKinsey’s Great Attrition research, 51% of employees who had left a job cited not feeling a sense of belonging at work as a reason for quitting. Connection keeps people around.

Separate work from personal life

A physical line between work and home can lead to a healthier balance. That’s especially true for people who are always on the move, traveling for work or working remotely.

If you have an office space in your home, it’s easy to stay pulled into work when you should be focused on family.

It also makes it harder to switch off at the end of the day. Instead of relaxing at night, an employee might be replaying how their boss will react if a report isn’t done by morning. That helps no one.

Better resources

In the office, employees have access to better equipment and facilities. If they need a good monitor, a fast printer, or a quiet room to finish a task, the office often beats home.

This matters most for work that needs specialized software or hardware people don’t have at home.

Some companies also provide free food, which is a small perk that makes coming in more appealing than staying put all day.

4 challenges employees face when in the office full-time

Full-time office work has real downsides that employers should account for.

Commute time

Returning to the office means commuting, which takes time and money.

Long commutes can add stress and fatigue to the day, which can drag on productivity and work-life balance.

Distractions

Offices get noisy. Interruptions from colleagues and phone calls make it harder to focus and finish deep work.

Higher costs

Renting space, paying utilities, and stocking supplies cost businesses money. They also add to employee expenses through commuting and parking.

Difficulty with work-life balance

Commuting to and from work, dealing with office distractions, and long hours can make balance hard to hold. When employees are overworked and stressed, their physical and mental health suffers, leading to burnout and less creativity and motivation.

Meeting in the middle with hybrid work

In-person work brings clear benefits. Office-only work brings clear costs. Hybrid work gives you both.

The research supports it. PwC’s Workforce Radar Report, based on 13 months of research and a survey of over 20,000 people, found hybrid workers report the highest levels of satisfaction, and more than three-quarters feel like they belong, ahead of both fully on-site and fully remote workers. A hybrid model lets people balance face-to-face interaction with the flexibility of working from home.

That balance helps employees, and it can lift productivity and save businesses money.

Hybrid work software such as OfficeRnD Workplace helps teams close the gap, with features built for communication, connection, and collaboration.

Its collaborative scheduling features make it easy for employees to plan in-person time and come to the office for the moments that matter.

The software simplifies desk and meeting room scheduling, so double bookings and missed meetings stop being a problem.

7 return-to-office employee motivators

Getting people to come in is hard when they can work from their own kitchen table. Here’s what actually draws them back for in-person collaboration.

Appealing office spaces

A comfortable, functional, well-designed workspace pulls people in. Invest in ergonomic furniture and hot desks so the space is genuinely nice to work in.

Office design isn’t a vanity project. A June 2025 Crown Workspace survey of 1,250 workers and decision-makers found 91% would come into the office more often if the space better met their needs. Make the office somewhere people want to gather, socialize, and work together.

With OfficeRnD Workplace’s desk booking software, employees can find and book the right desk for the day. They can also invite teammates to sit nearby, which encourages collaboration and casual interaction.

Sense of community

Social connection is one of the strongest reasons people show up. Design your office to make that connection easy, and the office becomes a place people want to be.

OfficeRnD Workplace makes it simple to manage space for social events, break rooms, game areas, and team-building activities. It also shows who’s coming in for happy hours, game nights, or potlucks.

Flexibility

Give people a say in when they come in. Run surveys and use the feedback to set the right hybrid work policies. When employees have more control over their schedules, you build trust and a calmer work environment.

Perks and incentives

Perks can tip the decision to come in. Snacks and drinks in the break room, gym memberships, commuter benefits, or the occasional catered lunch all help. Free or subsidized meals in particular rank among the most-wanted office amenities in recent surveys.

Celebrating milestones and achievements

Build a culture that marks personal and professional wins. Company-wide events, team outings, or personalized rewards for hitting milestones give people a reason to gather in person.

Personal growth and development opportunities

Chances to learn and grow make people feel invested and valued. Offer training programs, mentoring, or tuition reimbursement for further education. In-person mentorship in particular is hard to replicate on a call, and it’s one of the clearer reasons for early-career employees to come in.

User-friendly technology

Tips to get employees excited about being in the office

A few practical moves make a real difference.

Explain why

People are more willing to come in when they understand the point. Be clear about what in-person time delivers: better collaboration, networking, and social connection. Connect the office to their goals and the company’s success. Mandates without a reason tend to breed resentment, not attendance.

Listen to feedback

Ask what people want to see: more natural light, better seating, upgraded technology. Then act on it.

When you implement suggestions, you show employees their opinions count. That builds a sense of ownership in the office. While you’re at it, work on becoming a better collaborative communicator.

Get creative with work arrangement options

Flexibility motivates people. It consistently ranks among the top reasons workers take a new job.

Offer a mix: flexible schedules, remote days, and some in-office time to get the benefits of working alongside your team.

That’s why hybrid works. It supports a good work-life balance, lifts productivity, and lets companies use less office space and spend less on overhead.

Name: Do Companies Save Money With Remote Employees? [2026]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, many businesses moved to remote work for safety reasons. Restrictions have long since eased, and the question that stuck around is a financial one: does keeping people out of the office actually save money?
Post body:
Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, many businesses moved to remote work for safety reasons. Restrictions have long since eased, and the question that stuck around is a financial one: does keeping people out of the office actually save money?

Plenty of employees have settled into working from home or on a hybrid schedule and don’t want to give it up. Employers, meanwhile, want to know what the arrangement does to the bottom line. So, do companies save money with remote employees?

Quick answer: Yes. Companies save money with remote and hybrid employees mainly through lower rent and utilities, reduced travel and relocation costs, and smaller bills for cleaning, security, and food. Global Workplace Analytics estimates a typical employer saves about $11,000 per year for each person who works remotely half the time. Many companies also report higher productivity and better retention.

Remote work is an arrangement where employees do their jobs outside a central office, usually from home, either full time or as part of a hybrid schedule that splits the week between home and the workplace.

Here’s where the money goes, and where it stops going once people work from home at least part of the week.

Do companies save money with remote employees? Short answer: yes

Studies consistently point to cost savings when employees work remotely. Running an office five days a week, all year round, is expensive.

First, you rent a building. Then you buy office supplies, stock food and coffee, and pay someone to clean. If employees relocate to your premises, you cover that too.

Switching to hybrid or remote work removes the overhead behind many of these fixed costs. Global Workplace Analytics estimates that if everyone with a work-from-home-compatible job did so half the time, U.S. employers would save between $10,400 and $13,200 per employee per year across real estate, absenteeism, turnover, and productivity. Here are the main line items.

Rent and utilities

The more people you have on-site, the more square footage you pay for.

Prime office space isn’t cheap. Annual occupancy costs in Manhattan reached over $169 per square foot in the second quarter of 2021. When a meaningful share of your team works from home part of the time, you can move to a smaller footprint and pay less rent.

Real estate is usually the biggest win. IBM cut real estate costs by $50 million through remote work, and average real estate savings from full-time telework run around $10,000 per employee per year.

Rent isn’t the only cost. A fully on-site workforce needs a desk, chair, and computer for everyone. Those purchases add up fast.

Remote workers using remote spaces, or a hybrid model, mean you buy less furniture and fewer supplies while keeping enough for the people who come in a few days a week.

A smaller office also means lower electricity bills, and fewer people on-site means smaller internet and water bills.

Travel and relocation expenses

Video conferencing has replaced a lot of business travel. Employees meet clients, customers, and colleagues online instead of getting on a plane.

Relocation is another saving. Nortel estimates it saves $100,000 per employee it doesn’t have to relocate.

Cleaning and security services

Fewer people in the office means companies pay less for cleaning, and often less for security too.

Food and beverages

Remote work cuts spending on coffee, snacks, and refreshments for meetings, and the same goes for on-site cafeterias. You also save on food storage, dishes, and cutlery.

Companies also see more profitability with remote workers

Saving money is only half the story. Remote and hybrid work can also lift profit. Here’s how.

Increased productivity

Workers tend to be most engaged when they spend a good part of the week working remotely, roughly three to four days out of five.

Engagement pays off. Gallup’s research finds that the most engaged teams are 18% more productive and 23% more profitable than the least engaged, and they see measurably better output.

There’s real-world evidence too: Global Workplace Analytics reports that American Express’s remote workforce produced 43% more than its office-based staff.

Read more about remote work productivity.

Increased employee retention

Retention is often where flexible work pays for itself. 46% of companies that allow telework say it has reduced attrition, and 72% say it has a high impact on employee retention.

Keeping your best people isn’t only good for morale, it’s cheaper. Replacing an employee can cost anywhere from one-half to two times that person’s annual salary. See more hybrid work statistics for context.

Less absenteeism

Here’s a number that surprises people: 78% of workers who call in sick aren’t actually ill. They’re dealing with stress, family issues, or personal needs. Unscheduled absences cost employers about $1,800 per employee per year.

Telework programs cut unscheduled absences by 63%, largely because flexible hours let people run errands or handle appointments without burning a whole day.

Giving employees control over their own schedules also signals that you trust them to do the job wherever they are. That tends to produce a happier, healthier, more productive workforce.

Larger talent pool

Companies used to hire only from their local area, or pay to relocate someone from farther away.

Remote-first hiring removes that limit. You can recruit from a much wider geography and find a better match for the role, without asking anyone to move.

Remote work also opens roles to people with disabilities, widening the pool further.

So yes, flexible working carries real benefits for employers.

Costs and drawbacks of remote work

Remote work isn’t free of downsides. A few to plan for.

Data security issues

Remote work requires investment in technology such as video conferencing and project management tools.

Those tools carry security risk, as years of high-profile breaches show.

Companies also have to train employees on security so that people using company apps or equipment at home still take precautions, such as VPNs, when they’re outside in-office IT protections.

Collaboration concerns

In Buffer’s 2022 State of Remote Work report, a small majority of employees said they felt less connected to coworkers after shifting to remote work.

There’s also a risk of an “ingroup” and “outgroup” forming when some people work remotely and others are on-site.

You can support in-person collaboration with the right tools, such as OfficeRnD Workplace and its collaboration features. OfficeRnD Workplace is workplace management software that helps teams coordinate who comes in and when, so office days are worth the trip.

Read our case study on how Tavistock enabled in-person collaboration while adopting a hybrid model with OfficeRnD Workplace here. They cut real estate costs in the process.

Occupational safety and health administration issues

Employers may be liable for accidents in a worker’s home, under Section 1904.5(b)(7) of the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) rules. A few examples from OSHA itself:

“If an employee drops a box of work documents and injures his or her foot, the case is considered work-related. If an employee’s fingernail is punctured by a needle from a sewing machine used to perform garment work at home, becomes infected and requires medical treatment, the injury is considered work-related.”

OSHA doesn’t consider incidents like these work-related:

“If an employee is injured because he or she trips on the family dog while rushing to answer a work phone call, the case is not considered work-related. If an employee working at home is electrocuted because of faulty home wiring, the injury is not considered work-related.”

Keep up with occupational and safety laws in your country to make sure everything is above board.

Remote work also has tax implications worth checking, especially for employees working across state or national lines.

Save even more money with OfficeRnD Workplace

Do companies save money with remote employees? Yes. The savings show up in rent, utilities, travel, and overhead, and many companies also report higher profitability and stronger retention.

Remote work isn’t for everyone, though. Some people want to be back in the office, others want a couple of remote days a week. A hybrid arrangement usually gives you the best of both.

Name: The Truth About Hybrid Work Burnout [And How To Avoid It]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Employees split their weeks between the office and home, and hybrid work is now the default for most people who can do their jobs remotely. It gives them the flexibility and autonomy to manage their schedules — that is, when it works.
Post body:
Employees split their weeks between the office and home, and hybrid work is now the default for most people who can do their jobs remotely. It gives them the flexibility and autonomy to manage their schedules — that is, when it works.

As good as hybrid work is, it can lead to burnout if it isn’t managed well.

This guide covers what causes hybrid work burnout, what business leaders can do to fix it, and how to set up arrangements that give employees the benefits of hybrid work without the exhaustion.

Quick Summary

  • Hybrid work burnout usually comes from poor management and unclear expectations, not the model itself.
  • Employees who don’t have structure around their schedules and feel disconnected from key decisions are more likely to burn out.
  • Business leaders should involve staff in scheduling decisions while building a culture of connection, health, and well-being.

What is hybrid work burnout?

Hybrid work burnout is the chronic exhaustion, disengagement, and reduced performance that builds when employees split time between the office and home without clear boundaries, structure, or support.

Hybrid work is a working model where employees spend part of the week in a workplace and the rest working remotely, usually from home. It gained traction during the pandemic and has since settled in as the standard arrangement for desk-based work.

Burnout is common across every work model. Eagle Hill Consulting found that 57% of hybrid workers report burnout, compared with 61% of fully remote workers and 55% overall. The pattern in the data is consistent: location matters less than workload, boundaries, and the quality of management.

Prevalence doesn’t make burnout inevitable. Here are the main causes, and what to do about each.

Hybrid work can disrupt a settled routine

Switching between office days and home days means switching contexts, commutes, and childcare arrangements from one day to the next. That constant adjustment blurs the line between work and personal life.

The blurred boundary is one of the most cited causes of hybrid burnout. In Owl Labs’ 2025 State of Hybrid Work report, 90% of workers said their stress was the same or worse than a year earlier, and the overlap between home and work is a common reason why.

Employees can feel disconnected from key decisions

In-person teams coordinate easily. Bringing remote colleagues into the loop takes more deliberate effort. It starts with small exchanges and minor details, but as people get used to who’s briefed and who isn’t, ingroups and outgroups can form.

Over time, remote workers may be left out of bigger conversations and key decisions, creating a sense of disconnection from the organization.

Left unaddressed, this can lead to what Harvard Business Review describes as a “dominant class” (those who feel central to the organization) and an “underclass” (those who feel peripheral and disconnected from their work). That divide feeds burnout.

Unlimited schedule freedom can backfire

The instinct is to give people total control over their schedules. The data points the other way.

Gallup found that employees who set their own hybrid schedules are more likely to report burnout, fatigue, and worse work-life balance than those on team-set schedules. Relative to team-decided arrangements, employees who control their own cadence are 76% more likely to name burnout or fatigue as their biggest challenge.

The takeaway isn’t less flexibility. It’s shared structure. Gallup found that hybrid work models work best when teams, not individuals, decide the rules, and that people are more productive and less anxious when teams set shared norms. This can happen with any hybrid work model, so the fix applies broadly.

Unclear expectations create anxiety

When people don’t know when they’re expected in the office or what “good” looks like on a remote day, the uncertainty itself becomes a stressor.

Managers set the tone here, and many aren’t giving clear guidance. In Microsoft’s Work Trend Index, 81% of employees said it’s important that their managers help them prioritize their workload, but less than a third (31%) said their managers had ever given clear guidance during one-on-ones. Without that clarity, employees carry the weight of figuring out priorities on their own.

The pace and volume of work keep climbing

Hybrid work didn’t reduce the workload. If anything, the always-on culture stretched the day further.

Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index, based on a survey of 31,000 workers across 31 countries, found that 68% of employees struggle with the pace and volume of work, and nearly half (46%) report burnout as a result. The workday also runs later: Microsoft found that hybrid workers are more likely than remote workers to experience evening hours as a source of stress rather than quiet catch-up time.

Meetings pile on top of the workload. Microsoft’s telemetry shows employees are interrupted every 2 minutes on average by a meeting, email, or notification, and nearly half of employees (48%) say their work feels chaotic and fragmented. That fragmentation leaves little room for focused work, which is where burnout takes hold.

What can business leaders do to reduce hybrid work burnout?

Most burnout isn’t caused by hybrid work itself but by poor management and weak communication.

Leaders can prevent or reverse it by doing a few concrete things.

Let teams set the schedule together

Designing a hybrid setup that works for everyone takes coordination, which is hard for organizations used to working face-to-face.

Involving teams in the decision makes it easier and builds trust. It also produces better well-being outcomes than either top-down mandates or pure individual choice.

Gallup found that hybrid schedules are now split roughly evenly between employees who set their own (34%), those whose manager decides (33%), and those set by the team or employer. Teams that agree the rules together report the fairest, most collaborative outcomes, and 91% of employees whose schedule is decided by their team view the policy as fair, matching the satisfaction rate of those with full autonomy. The structure is what protects against burnout, without giving up flexibility.

Build connection between hybrid workers

Give your team the tools they need to connect.

Check in with employees regularly. Share information and keep everyone updated on company policies and procedures, whether they’re in the office or remote.

This closes information gaps and helps prevent ingroups and outgroups from forming.

Team-building exercises keep remote and in-office workers connected. Hold virtual company events, pair up colleagues who don’t usually work together, or bring the whole team in on the same day for a shared lunch.

The manager is the biggest single factor. Gallup found that 70% of the variance in team engagement is influenced by the manager, so supporting managers directly is one of the highest-return moves a leader can make.

Create a culture of health and well-being

Look at whether your culture supports or undermines well-being.

Small structural changes help. In one survey, 36% of employees wanted daily breaks and a monthly “self-care” day, and 34% wanted a weekly meeting-free day. Employees say these things make them more productive, so they pay off both ways.

Don’t overwork people. It’s the fastest route to chronic workplace stress. Set boundaries between work and personal time, and hold to them.

Employees who feel supported stay more engaged and productive, and you keep your best people.

Name: Does Hybrid Work Increase Stress? [A Definitive Answer]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: For many workers, the prospect of shifting to hybrid work is full of promises of work-life balance.
Post body:
For many workers, the prospect of shifting to hybrid work is full of promises of work-life balance.

Spend only two or three days at the office and work the rest of the time from home!

Reduce your commuting time!

Get out of bed 30 minutes later than usual!

Enjoy a flexible work schedule!

Have more time to spend with your family!

With true benefits like these, hybrid work does sound ideal — and it can be. But if it isn’t managed well, it can affect employee stress levels, because hybrid work introduces a new working format that may be unfamiliar and require a whole new way to think about your work day.

So: does hybrid work increase stress? It doesn’t have to — as long as you have the right policies and technologies in place.

There’s an art and a science to implementing hybrid work in a way that keeps your employees happy, in a good mental state, and motivated to keep doing good work.

This article covers how to prevent stress from building up in employees who work in hybrid environments.

Quick Answer:

Hybrid work by itself doesn’t increase stress. The split between home and office is a working format, not a stressor. What raises or lowers stress is how the model is managed: clear policies, the right tools, and respect for boundaries. A 2025 study of 4,002 hybrid workers across the US and UK by International Workplace Group found 70% experienced fewer stress-related health conditions and 80% reported better work-life balance and reduced anxiety.

But to get those results, work through the following eight mitigation tips:

  1. Set clear work-from-home policies.
  2. Respect employees’ work preferences.
  3. Use the right hybrid work management software.
  4. Encourage employees to have a dedicated workspace at home.
  5. Honor employees’ work/life boundaries.
  6. Encourage breaks.
  7. Conduct frequent, friendly check-ins.
  8. Offer an informal digital meeting space.

These tips and other information on whether hybrid work increases stress are covered below.

The hybrid work experience paradox

Companies and employees are still weighing hybrid work’s advantages and disadvantages, even though it’s now the dominant setup for people who can do their jobs remotely.

Many workers simply love hybrid work. They like the flexibility and report that it gives them less stress than other arrangements.

Gallup’s 2025 data shows that among US employees in remote-capable jobs, 51% work hybrid, about 28% are fully remote, and 21% are fully on-site. Those splits have barely moved since 2022, which tells you hybrid isn’t a transitional phase. It’s the operating model.

Preference runs the same way. Roughly 6 in 10 remote-capable employees say they’d choose a hybrid arrangement, and the ideal for most sits at two to three office days a week.

Despite that enthusiasm, other research shows hybrid work can still leave employees stressed — and the reasons are usually about management, not location.

Owl Labs’ 2025 State of Hybrid Work report, based on 2,000 full-time US workers, found that 9 in 10 employees say they’re stressed at work, and for 39% of them it has gotten worse over the past year. Stress shows up across every work model. The top drivers workers named were lack of career growth (50%), limited flexibility (47%), worry over job stability (47%), and having their activities monitored (47%).

Check out this article if you want more hybrid work stats.

So if employees love hybrid work, especially compared with entirely in-person arrangements, why is stress still so common? The answer is what happens around the format: unclear boundaries, weak communication, and thin management support. We’ll get into that below. First, some context on workplace stress in general.

What is work-related stress?

Work-related stress is the harmful physical and emotional response that happens when the demands of a job don’t match a person’s ability to cope with them.

The European Agency for Safety and Health at Work frames it as a negative psychological state that arises when work pressures become excessive and prolonged relative to a person’s perceived ability to cope.

The traditional workplace contributes plenty of it.

Starting the day with a rush to get out the door, caring for dependents, and slogging through traffic jams or the daily grind of a crowded commute is just the first source of stress.

Once at the workplace, common stressors include:

  • Unclear directions or processes
  • Conflicts with coworkers or supervisors
  • An unhealthy or unsafe work environment
  • Not feeling adequately compensated for the work done

So if working partially from home removes the morning commute and eases other pressures, does hybrid work increase stress or reduce it?

Types of employee stress related to hybrid work

Hybrid work reduces some stressors outright, such as the daily commute or being physically present in an unhealthy workspace.

Here’s the catch:

The other stressors on that list — unclear directions, interpersonal conflict, feeling underpaid for the value you bring — don’t disappear when someone works from home.

In many cases, a hybrid environment not supported by clear hybrid work policies exposes a real gap in off-site communication or in operations and processes.

Even with its benefits, hybrid employees report new challenges that can cause stress over time:

  • Distractions at home (spouse/partner, kids, pets, deliveries, etc.)
  • Difficulty staying disciplined or motivated
  • Fear of covert electronic monitoring by supervisors seeking to maintain control
  • A sense of becoming disconnected from coworkers (this can be triggered by generational differences)
  • Lugging equipment, such as a laptop, back and forth between work and home
  • Technology challenges such as lacking adequate equipment, the right software, or company network access at home
  • A slow or unstable internet connection
  • Feeling like you’re always working, or that your work life is seeping into your home life
  • Difficulty connecting virtually with one’s boss, team, or department
  • Feeling like it’s harder to take time off when you’re not in the office

The blurred line between home and work deserves a closer look, because it’s one of the most consistent stress signals in current research. Owl Labs found that only 27% of hybrid workers say they have a clear start and end to their workday, compared with 64% of in-office workers. When the day never really ends, checking email and chat at all hours becomes the norm, and that “always-on” pattern is what tips flexibility into fatigue.

Surveillance is the other one worth naming. In Owl Labs’ 2025 data, only 19% of workers said their company isn’t using employee tracking software, and having their activities monitored ranked among workers’ top concerns. Monitoring tends to erode trust, and low trust is a stress multiplier.

The good news: employers can address most of these contributors through good hybrid work management (more on that below).

But first, what’s the impact of going hybrid on employers?

Employer stress related to a hybrid workplace

Employees aren’t the only ones facing new stress from hybrid work. Employers, managers, and supervisors also have to adapt to this way of working and prevent burnout.

Their stressors look a little different, but they’re tied directly to how employees experience stress:

  • Staying on top of employee engagement and productivity when the team isn’t always present
  • Juggling meetings when key employees aren’t in the workspace
  • Investing in, mastering, and maintaining new technologies to keep the hybrid workforce connected
  • The sunk costs of empty offices
  • The effect of empty desks on employee morale

Managers carry a real load here. Gallup found that where teams, not individuals, set the hybrid rules, people are more productive and less anxious. That points to a fix worth stealing: let teams agree on shared norms rather than leaving each person to guess.

To minimize hybrid work stress, it helps to understand how potential stressors affect different personality types. That makes managing a hybrid workforce, and finding solutions, much easier.

How hybrid work affects different personality types

There’s no one best personality type for hybrid work.

Any personality type can do well in a hybrid environment because the format is flexible by design. The trick is to account for each employee’s strengths and needs when you manage the team.

There are many personality frameworks, but for brevity we’ll use the DiSC® model. Many companies use DiSC in hiring to gauge how well an applicant fits the role and the company.

DiSC works with four profiles: Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, and Conscientiousness. Each responds differently to workplace stress, and you can adapt the hybrid environment to their strengths.

Dominance

A person with a high D score wants to make things happen, ideally in no time.

As the typical drivers in the workplace, D-types love action and thrive in creative tension. They handle stress better than most and generally do well in a flexible environment.

So throw the Ds into hybrid work head-first. Most will be eager to take on the new challenge.

Influence

The i-types love the social side of life. They’re enthusiastic, optimistic, collaborative, friendly, and convincing.

Their greatest fear is loss of influence. Being thrust into an environment where social connections thin out can cause them a lot of stress.

So make sure your i-types have ways to stay connected in a hybrid setup so they don’t lose their social moorings.

Steadiness

Those with a high S-score enjoy collaborating. They tend to be calm, consistent, patient, and predictable, and they like stable, routine work.

S-types fear a loss of stability. A hybrid arrangement can stress them simply because it uproots fixed patterns and demands more flexibility.

So go easy on the S-types. Reassure them that new processes will soon settle. And if they struggle with the change, give them the option of staying put.

Conscientiousness

C-types are knowledge-oriented, factual, and methodical. They demand accuracy and use their analytical skills to get things done the right way.

C-types may resist processes that seem random to them, such as changing desks every day. But once they understand the rationale, they tend to do well in hybrid arrangements.

So help the C-types see the concrete benefits of hybrid work. They may well become your best advocates.

With this extra effort, each type will feel supported as they settle into hybrid work.

8 tips to reduce hybrid work stress

Keeping personality types and different stress responses in mind, here are eight ways to manage potential hybrid work stress.

1. Set clear work-from-home policies

For many companies, policy still lags behind practice. That gap creates stress-inducing situations where employees aren’t clear about what’s expected of them.

So before going hybrid, write a straightforward work-from-home policy that applies to everyone. Where you can, let teams shape the specifics: Gallup’s data shows shared, team-level norms lower anxiety more than top-down rules.

Here are two free ebooks on developing a hybrid work model:

  1. Hybrid Work For Dummies, OfficeRnD Special Edition
  2. Guidelines and Policies for Optimizing Your Hybrid Workspace

2. Respect employees’ work preferences

Not everyone takes well to hybrid work. Some simply don’t like it, even if they could manage it.

To keep your workforce happy, don’t pressure people into hybrid work when it clashes with their circumstances.

Instead, run an employee-centric workplace strategy that lets workers shape their own arrangements.

3. Use the right hybrid work management software

Coordinating hybrid schedules gets complicated fast, but workplace software takes the manual work off your plate.

OfficeRnD Workplace gives HR, facilities, and IT teams desk and meeting-room booking, scheduling, and workplace analytics in one place, so people come to the office for the moments that matter without the coordination headaches.

Watch a 1-minute video on desk booking and more:

4. Encourage employees to have a dedicated workspace at home

Help your employees get set up remotely with recommendations for a good home office.

Provide the equipment you’d give them in the office, such as a large monitor and an ergonomic chair.

Check out this article on the top hot desking accessories.

Set up a system to reimburse home office expenses such as pens, printer ink, and copy paper. Nobody should have to come begging for basics.

5. Honor employees’ work-life boundaries

Set clear guidelines for when people at home can and can’t be contacted for work, so they don’t feel always on call. This matters: only about a quarter of hybrid workers report a clear end to their day, so the boundary won’t hold itself.

Encourage the “turn off notifications” feature in whatever communication tools the company uses.

6. Encourage breaks

Breaks reset the mind and body during the day.

Remote workers tend to take fewer of them. Some feel guilty stepping away from the computer for anything more than a bathroom break.

So reassure your remote employees that breaks are fine. Encourage them to get out of the chair and go outside for some movement and fresh air.

7. Conduct frequent, friendly check-ins

Since disconnection from coworkers is a real risk, have supervisors touch base regularly with remote workers.

Do it not just over messaging or email but in person, via phone or video, and show interest in the person’s life beyond the job.

8. Offer an informal digital meeting space

Isolation is a well-documented risk of remote work. Owl Labs found that among workers who feel left out of meetings, hybrid and remote workers make up a real share of the group, and connection ranks high on what employees say they miss.

To counter it, give employees a space such as Zoom or a team chat channel where they can touch base informally, the way they would at the office. You can also organize virtual team-building activities.

The final verdict: does hybrid work increase stress?

Hybrid work can raise stress for some people, mostly through blurred work-life boundaries, adapting to new technology, and feeling cut off from colleagues. It can also lower stress by adding flexibility, reducing commuting time, and improving work-life balance.

Which way it goes comes down to management. Employers control most of these stressors through policies and tools designed to make hybrid work easier for employees and managers alike.

Author: asen-stoyanchev

Post body:
Introducing an office hoteling policy into your workplace is a wise decision, especially if you’re looking for a way to reduce company costs.  

The only issue is knowing how to get started. 

This article will provide a comprehensive guide of everything you need to know in 2023, including a list of essential factors your office hoteling policy should contain and how to choose the right software to help reduce time and confusion.

Quick Summary:

Office hoteling is a flexible work style that allows employees to reserve available desks or specific office spaces. Companies considering using office hoteling will need to put the right policies in place that every employee must follow in order for such an arrangement to succeed. This includes hygiene protocols, proper labeling systems, a booking procedure, and an eligibility checklist to find out which types of workers an office hoteling policy will extend to. Successful office hoteling leads to increased productivity and reduced costs, among other benefits.

Let’s dive in. 

What Does “Hoteling” Mean in an Office Setting?

Office hoteling is an alternative work arrangement that allows employees to reserve a desk or office space based on availability. Similar to a traditional hotel, workers are expected to book a desk in advance, usually through a software program.

As employees continue to request work options outside of the nine-to-five model, the pressure for companies to adopt alternative work strategies is quickly increasing.   

And the demand for this model has held steady. 52% of remote-capable US employees now work in hybrid arrangements, and 88% of US employers offer at least some hybrid options as of early 2026.

Average office utilization sits at 50–60% globally in 2025, which means a lot of desk space goes unused under traditional assigned-seating models. Office hoteling addresses that directly.

As a related resource, check out our article on this effective hot desking policy template.

What Types of Businesses Need an Office Hoteling Policy?

83% of workers prefer a hybrid arrangement combining remote and in-office days, according to Owl Labs’ 2025 State of Hybrid Work report. That number puts hoteling within reach of almost any company.

This means that most companies should at least consider transitioning. However, the need is more pressing for some businesses than others, including the following:

  • Businesses running a hybrid work model with variable in-office attendance.
  • Companies that have recently downsized or are planning to reduce their real estate footprint.
  • Start-ups that are still establishing how and when people come in.
  • Enterprises with multiple office locations and employees who travel between them.

What Should an Office Hoteling Policy Template Include?

Before introducing an office hoteling policy in your workplace, it’s essential to create ground rules that all employees must follow.

#1 Hygiene Policy

Shared workspaces need explicit cleaning expectations. The flu can stay infectious on hard surfaces for up to 48 hours, so desks used by multiple people throughout the week carry real transmission risk if protocols aren’t enforced.

Enforcing a hygiene policy is a great way to keep shared workspaces as clean as possible. 

Here are some procedures you could include in a hygiene policy: 

  • Disinfect regularly touched items, such as computer mice, keyboards, and screens, after each use. 
  • When they’re ill, employees must report their symptoms and refrain from entering the office space. 
  • Hand sanitizer should be provided at each workstation. 
  • All workers should wash their hands regularly and avoid touching their faces. 

#2 Labeling System

Having a labeling system ensures organization and clear communication among employees. For instance, you could use the following:

  • Color-coding: For example, you could use green labels to indicate collaborative spaces. 
  • Employee names: You could place name labels outside a workspace to let the other employees know that the space is occupied — and by whom. 
  • QR codes: These can indicate what type of space the room is, when it’ll be available, and how many people are allowed to use it at one time. 

#3 Booking Procedure

A booking procedure allows employees to search and reserve a workspace in advance for a specific period. It also helps ensure no double bookings are made, and spaces don’t become overcrowded.

Effective booking systems include the following features: 

  • Reservations: Employees use office hoteling software to book a desk for the day. Usually, a calendar and floor plan view display the locations and availability of desks.
  • Confirmation: An employee receives an automated email confirmation that includes the booking’s date, time, and duration — as well as an access code if required. 
  • Checking in: Each person must check in upon arriving at their desk. You may have employees check in at reception, scan a QR code, or enter their access code. 
  • Checking out: This can be done easily with hybrid work software that has a desk booking system, such as OfficeRnD Workplace. 

Don’t make your booking procedure overly complicated. Everyone must understand and be able to access the system at all times for office hoteling to work. 

#4 Eligibility Checklist

An eligibility checklist identifies which people an office hoteling policy applies to. 

This is especially useful when introducing the policy, as it promotes awareness and increases fairness in booking practices. It also helps identify requirements from workers, such as completing training. 

Some factors to consider include the following: 

  • Will the policy extend to part-time workers?
  • Can all jobs within your company be completed under this flexible work model? 
  • Will employee performance impact ongoing involvement? 

4 Benefits of Office Hoteling

Office hoteling can improve how employees work individually and as a team. Here are four examples of how it can benefit your company:

  • Improves space utilization: Most offices sit at 50–60% average occupancy. Hoteling raises that figure by redistributing available desks based on actual attendance, not headcount. Desk booking systems contribute to a 35% increase in space efficiency for companies adopting flexible work models. 
  • Cost efficiency: 55% of organizations actively cut their real estate footprints in 2025, with portfolio optimization now the top stated objective for corporate real estate leaders, according to JLL. A hoteling model with a seat ratio of 0.7 (70 desks per 100 employees) on a hybrid team of 500 people can reduce desk count by 150 – translating to roughly $1.4M in annual space savings at average US per-seat costs. 
  • Accommodates hybrid and remote workers: Office hoteling gives remote employees a reliable way to book a desk when they need to come in for focus work, team meetings, or access to equipment they don’t have at home. They know they’ll have a spot. That certainty matters. 
  • Allows for flexibility: Gallup’s 2025 data shows satisfaction peaks when employees spend roughly 3 days in the office and 2 at home. A hoteling system supports exactly that pattern by letting people book when it makes sense for their schedule, rather than showing up and hoping a desk is free.

For more insights about office hoteling, check out our article on the difference between hot desking vs. hoteling vs desk sharing.

How to Effectively Apply an Office Hoteling Policy

The following four steps will show you how to create a functional, practical, and intuitive hoteling policy.  

#1 Provide the Right Tools

Each employee must have access to the tools they need to do their job. 

This includes both software and hardware, such as 

  • A computer and monitors 
  • Printers 
  • Communication software, like Slack 
  • Microsoft Office 
  • Chrome
  • hoteling software (more on that in a minute)

#2 Create a Variety of Workspaces

Don’t make every desk identical. Employees come in for different reasons: focused work, collaboration, video calls, workshops. Your space should reflect that.

The idea behind office hoteling is to create diversity, so don’t fall into the trap of making all workspaces identical.

  • Assess employee needs and preferences to determine what types of workspaces are needed. For example, collaboration spaces are typically more valuable in advertising agencies than conference rooms. 
  • In each space, use versatile furniture that can be reconfigured as needed. 
  • Don’t be afraid to experiment with different lighting and acoustics. 

#3 Start Small

Before applying a hoteling policy to the whole office, it’s a good idea to “patch test” with a small group. This will help you clarify any issues and determine whether hoteling would be a complement to your work culture. 

Some things to look out for in the testing stage include the following: 

  • Drops in productivity levels. 
  • Technology or access issues. 
  • Reoccurring distractions. 
  • Employees’ emotional responses. 

Check out our valuable resource on the most important hybrid work KPIs for more info.

#4 Consider Storage Solutions

Storing personal items can be frustrating when employees don’t have a designated desk. 

That’s why having various storage stations throughout the workplace where personal items can be locked away is vital.  

Some examples include lockers, storage cabinets, rolling carts, and personal storage bins. You’ll need to ensure these are available if you’re setting up office hoteling.

How to Choose the Right Desk Hoteling Software

Choosing the best desk-booking software can determine whether an office hoteling policy will succeed.

A multi-functional software can increase efficiency when booking desks, reduce the administrative burden, and ensure employees can voice concerns.

Unreliable software with limited functionality, poor user experience, or slow response times, on the other hand, is likely to irritate employees.

Some aspects to look for in desk booking software include mobile accessibility, interactive floor plans, a simple interface, and in-app communication ability.

Helping thousands of businesses to manage the hybrid work model effectively, OfficeRnD Workplace anticipates the needs of hybrid employees and employers to an impressive degree.

It provides a straightforward user interface, a presence tracking system, advanced workplace analytics, and everything you need to manage a hybrid workplace successfully.  

The following are some notable inclusions of OfficeRnD Workplace: 

  • Intuitive desk and meeting room booking system on a beautiful and interactive floor plan
  • Option to sync calendars 
  • Can book from anywhere 
  • Interrelated SSO and seamless integration with Microsoft and Google tech stack.
  • QR code presence tracking system

Click here to book a live demo and see what OfficeRnD Workplace has to offer.

How AI Is Changing Office Hoteling in 2026

AI has moved from a feature on product roadmaps to something that actually changes day-to-day hoteling management. Here’s what it does in practice.

Predictive desk allocation

AI-powered systems analyze past booking behavior, team schedules, and occupancy patterns to predict which desks will fill on a given day. They surface availability recommendations before employees even open the app, cutting booking time and reducing no-shows.

Smart no-show management

There are systems that automatically release desks when employees don’t check in by a set time, making the space available for walk-ins without any manual intervention from facilities teams. This is a material improvement over reminder-based systems, where someone still has to process the release.

Collaborative scheduling

AI can suggest the best days for team members to come in together based on individual preferences, meeting patterns, and team anchor days. Instead of a manager coordinating via Slack, the system recommends a day when 80% of the team is already planning to be in, then prompts the rest to book nearby desks.

Occupancy heat maps and space rightsizing.

AI-driven analytics give facilities managers a running picture of which zones get used, at what time, and by whom. JLL’s 2025 data shows that 90% of organizations track utilization, but only 7% rate their data quality as excellent. AI-assisted analytics close that gap by cleaning and interpreting sensor data automatically, rather than relying on monthly manual reviews.

Reverse hoteling

What’s really cool is that some tools now support reverse hoteling: employees with assigned desks can mark their seat as available on days they’re working remotely, automatically adding it to the bookable pool. The desk returns to them when they’re next in. This is especially useful for hybrid teams where certain roles are in-office more than others.

How Do You Measure the Success of Your Hoteling Program?

Most hoteling programs launch without a clear definition of what success looks like. That’s a problem simply because without data, you can’t tell whether the policy is working or just generating complaints. Track these KPIs from day one:

  • Average and peak occupancy: Target 45–65% average, with peaks manageable without employees hunting for desks.
  • No-show rate: Keep this under 10–12% with auto-release rules. Above that, your booking window is probably too long.
  • Time-to-seat: How long does it take an employee to arrive and confirm a desk? Under 2 minutes is the target.
  • Seat ratio: Desks per eligible employee. A ratio of 0.7 is common for hybrid teams that come in 2–3 days per week.
  • Employee satisfaction (eNPS): Survey monthly for the first quarter. Problems surface fast here before they show up in utilization data.
  • Booking lead time: The median time between booking and use. Very short lead times may indicate employees distrust availability and book last-minute out of anxiety, not preference.

Use your chosen platform’s reporting tools to pull these automatically. Manual tracking through spreadsheets doesn’t scale past 50 people.

Moving offices can be daunting, especially considering the numerous details and logistical challenges involved. 

From coordinating with your staff and IT department to ensuring that the new space is ready for occupancy, there are many factors to keep in mind. 

It’s crucial to create a comprehensive office move checklist when changing locations, as this helps avoid unnecessary stress and ensure that the move goes smoothly. 

This article will provide you with a step-by-step guide to planning and executing a successful office move. Whether you’re moving to a new office or renovating your current office space, this business relocation checklist will help you stay on top of everything that needs to be done.

Quick Summary: We’ll delve into the following aspects of an office move: 

  • Creating an office move timeline (with an example)
  • Packing and labeling
  • Preparing your work area (and why flexible workspaces work best)
  • Communicating with onsite and remote employees throughout the move
  • Budgeting and cost control
  • Setting up your IT infrastructure with minimal downtime
  • Preparing your hybrid workplace
  • Where to update your business contact information
  • Running necessary training sessions
  • Testing and troubleshooting
  • Celebrating your big move

9 Things to Consider for a Successful Office Move

From IT infrastructure to employee communication, here are nine things to consider for your office move.

1. Timing and Logistics

Timing is critical when it comes to an office move because you want to minimize the disruption to your business operations. 

A well-planned move will ensure that your onsite and remote employees can continue to perform their jobs without any significant downtime. This means scheduling the move at a time when it will have the lowest impact on your business operations.

You’ll also need to coordinate with movers, vendors, and onsite and remote working employees to ensure that the moving process goes smoothly. 

If you’re moving into a new office space, it’s essential to know how long it will take for your furniture and equipment to arrive. These time estimates will help ensure everything is set up in time for your employees to move back into the office, whether they’ve been working from home or on-site.

2. Packing and Labeling

From desk chairs to office plants, packing up everything is arguably one of the most tedious aspects of an office move. As such, having a well-defined packing and labeling system is essential for a smooth transition.

The right labels will help ensure that all items are organized and accounted for, reducing the risk of damage or loss occurring during the move. Clear and descriptive labeling also makes it easier to unpack and organize items in the new office space, saving time and minimizing confusion. 

Lastly, labeling can help movers or employees identify fragile equipment that requires special handling to safely transport it.

3. IT and Technology

Moving IT equipment requires special attention. Safely disconnect and pack computers, servers, and other devices to prevent damage during transportation. 

It is also essential to securely back up all data and files and ensure their successful transfer to the new location. 

With hybrid work, consider the impact of the move on remote employees’ access to technology — you’ll need to provide the necessary support to maintain seamless connectivity.

4. Office Setup

Whether you’re renovating your office space or moving to a new office, deciding on your office setup is a big deal. As you visualize your office layout, consider the many benefits of hybrid work and a flexible work environment — the office of the modern era.

According to a McKinsey survey, 35% of workers work from home full-time, and 23% do part-time. And this hybrid work trend shows no signs of slowing down.

The culture of hybrid work comes with many advantages, from increased flexibility and productivity to a more collaborative environment. 

Learn how OfficeRnD’s hybrid workplace management software can help your team take full advantage of these benefits in your new and improved office space.

5. Communication and Coordination

Throughout your move or office renovation, ensure everyone knows what’s going on at all times. Without clear guidance, employees may feel left in the dark, which can lead to confusion and frustration. 

Not only will effective communication help minimize disruptions and delays, but it will also foster a sense of teamwork within the organization. 

OfficeRnD Workplace’s nifty collaborative features can help foster communication and employee engagement throughout your move. From knowing who will be in the office to syncing your schedules, our hybrid workplace software gives your team the tools they need to stay in the loop.

Learn more about how OfficeRnD can help solve the many challenges that come with hybrid work by watching this short video.

6. Budgeting and Cost Control

Cost management during an office move is critical to ensuring that the move is financially feasible and doesn’t exceed the organization’s budget. 

Stary by researching what others have paid for a move of similar size and scope. This can provide valuable insights into the expected costs and help identify potential cost-saving opportunities. 

Next, compare quotes from different moving companies and ensure that the services offered match the organization’s needs. Pose questions like:

  • Does the quote include simply moving boxes or packing, too? 
  • Will your team unpack the boxes themselves, or the moving team unbox everything and set up the workstations?

Clearly defining these costs from the beginning will help you avoid unexpected expenses and get the best value for your money.

7. Safety and Security

Safety and security are top priorities during an office move. To ensure the building is secure during your move, follow these tips:

  • Ensure that all doors are locked when you leave for the day.
  • Lock up any valuables in a safe and secure location.
  • If you have access to CCTV cameras in your building, ensure they are working properly so you can monitor them from home if necessary (or delegate someone else to do it).
  • Consider taking some extra precautions with expensive and valuable equipment, such as computers and servers.

8. Unpacking and Setting Up

Setting up a new workspace can be a stressful and tiring process, so here are some tips:

  • Set up the furniture and equipment first, and ensure your team’s personal belongings are in place.
  • Arrange files and documents next. Take care of the paperwork by putting it where it belongs (and ensuring nothing gets lost).
  • If your organization is adopting a hybrid work model or remote workspaces, set up the necessary technology and equipment to support these arrangements. This may include video conferencing equipment, cloud-based file storage, and other remote collaboration tools.

9. Testing and Troubleshooting

After an office move or renovation, it’s easy to overlook something that might cause problems later on in the move. To keep this from affecting your team’s work processes, give everything in the office a trial run.

  • Test the network connectivity to ensure that all devices can connect to the internet and communicate with each other. This is particularly important for hybrid work, where employees may work remotely or use different devices.
  • Test all audio and video equipment, including conference room systems, webcams, and microphones. This is critical for hybrid work environments in which video conferencing is becoming increasingly important.
  • Test the security systems, including access control systems, surveillance cameras, and alarms. This is particularly important if your organization deals with sensitive data or has compliance requirements.

Office Move Timeline

An office move can be a complex process with many moving parts. To ensure that everything goes smoothly, create a timeline that outlines important dates, key milestones, and tasks to complete leading up to and after the move. 

Here’s an example of a timeline for an office move.

6–12 Months Before the Move

  • Determine the scope and budget of the move
  • Assign a project manager to oversee the move
  • Research and select a moving company
  • Conduct a space planning analysis to determine the layout of the new office
  • Review lease agreements and negotiate any necessary changes

3–6 Months Before the Move

  • Notify employees of the move and provide them with regular updates
  • Create and distribute a moving checklist for employees
  • Purchase new furniture, equipment, and office supplies
  • Order new business cards, signage, and marketing materials with the new address
  • Schedule IT and phone system installations in the new office

1–3 Months Before the Move

  • Begin packing non-essential items
  • Notify vendors, customers, and partners of the move and update your contact information
  • Schedule a walkthrough of the new office with the moving company
  • Confirm the move details, including timing and logistics, with the moving company
  • One month before the move, spend some time setting up your hybrid workplace – floorplans, resources, and integrations and test it out with several users.

1–2 Weeks Before the Move

  • Pack any remaining items, and label boxes with the contents and their destination
  • Disassemble furniture and equipment as necessary
  • Coordinate with the moving company to ensure that all items are packed and ready to go
  • One week before the move, spend some time guiding the adoption of the hybrid work tool. Onboard employees, so they can be prepared when the time comes.

Moving Day

  • Supervise the move to ensure that everything is loaded properly
  • Complete a final walkthrough of the old office to ensure that nothing has been left behind
  • Supervise the unloading and unpacking of items in the new office

1–2 Weeks After the Move

  • Unpack any remaining items and set up any new furniture or equipment
  • Test the IT and phone systems in the new office
  • Conduct a post-move evaluation to identify areas for improvement
  • Celebrate the successful move with employees and stakeholders

Office Move Checklist for Hybrid Working

Each office move or renovation comes with its own set of challenges and considerations. However, there are some key things that you should always consider to ensure a successful transition. 

To help guide your move or renovation, we’ve compiled an office move checklist covering everything from budgeting and planning to unpacking and troubleshooting. We’ve also included some questions and suggestions to ensure you’re covering all the bases.

Label Your Boxes

Use packing tape to seal the boxes securely, and label them with their contents and destination. This way, what’s in each box at the new office is clear. Consider using a color-coding system to streamline this process in the new office.

Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Two teams arrive at the same room at 10 am. One of them booked it three weeks ago in a shared calendar. The other wrote it on a whiteboard by the kitchen. Somebody moves to a corridor.
Post body:
Two teams arrive at the same room at 10 am. One of them booked it three weeks ago in a shared calendar. The other wrote it on a whiteboard by the kitchen. Somebody moves to a corridor.

Sounds familiar, right?

Most free spreadsheets stop that from happening twice. This meeting room booking template in Excel goes further: it records whether anyone turned up, then tells you what your rooms are doing with the rest of the week.

Same file, same formulas, no macros. Pair it with our desk booking template in Excel if you need both, then use our RFP template when you’re ready to compare proper tools.

What’s in the file

Six tabs, in the order you’ll use them.

  • Start Here. Setup in 4 steps, plus the signs you’ve outgrown a spreadsheet.
  • Setup. Your rooms (up to 12), their seats and equipment, and your people (up to 30). Entered once. Every other tab reads from here.
  • Bookings. One row per meeting, up to 200 rows. Date, room, start, end, organizer, attendees. The Status column flags clashes as you type.
  • Day Board. Pick a day, see every room half hour by half hour, and who has it.
  • Room Week. Pick a room, see its whole two weeks in one screen.
  • Dashboard. Utilization by room, by day, by weekday and by time slot. No-show rate. A report on whether your rooms are the right size.

The limits, stated plainly: 12 rooms, 30 people, one office, 200 bookings across 10 working days, and a bookable day of 16 half-hour slots. Past that, look at meeting room booking software instead.

How to use the meeting room booking template in Excel

Fifteen minutes in total, start to finish.

1. Make your copy

In Google Sheets, use File, then Make a copy, so it saves to your own Drive. In Excel, download the file and put it on SharePoint or OneDrive if more than one person will edit it. Emailing the file around is how a booking system dies in week 3.

2. List your rooms and your people

Open Setup. Type your room names, the floor or zone, how many people each room seats, and what’s in it. Video conf, whiteboard, huddle, focus room.

Fill in the Seats column. It drives the room right-sizing report on the Dashboard, and it’s the number most people skip.

Then add your people. Those names fill the dropdowns on the Bookings tab.

Set your bookable day while you’re there. The default runs 9:00 to 17:00, which gives every room 8 bookable hours a day. Change the start time and all 16 half-hour slots move with it.

3. Set your start date

Set “Bookings start” to a Monday. Every date on every other tab updates from that one cell. Leave it alone and it defaults to this week’s Monday.

4. Log one row per meeting

Go to Bookings. Add the date, room, start time, end time, who booked it, what it’s for, and how many people are coming.

Use a clean time format, 14:00 or 2:00 PM, and keep it consistent down the column.

Two columns then do the checking for you:

  • Status reads OK, or Conflict if another meeting wants the same room at the same time. It also flags Check times when the end is before the start, and Outside range when the date falls outside your two weeks.
  • Room fit reads Over capacity when more people are coming than the room seats, and flags a booking as much bigger than needed when a meeting takes at least double the seats it uses.

The Day Board shows you where a conflict sits, so you can move one of the two meetings 30 minutes and be done.

5. Mark what actually happened

The next morning, go back to yesterday’s rows and set “Took place?” to Yes or No-show.

This is the step people skip, and it’s the step that makes every number on the Dashboard mean something. Two minutes a day.

Who owns the file

One person, named, with a backup. Office manager, workplace coordinator, or whoever already fields the “is the big room free?” question.

In Google Sheets, give the owner Editor rights and everyone else Commenter rights if you want bookings requested rather than made. Room names change more often than people expect, and one person keeping the Setup tab current is what stops the rest of the file drifting.

What your dashboard is telling you

Fourteen numbers sit across the top of the Dashboard. Six of them decide what you do next.

  • Room utilization. Hours booked against rooms multiplied by bookable hours. Under 40% across ten days and you have rooms nobody wants, or rooms nobody can find. Over 80% and people are giving up and taking calls at their desk.
  • No-show rate. Booked, and nobody came. Above 10% and your busy days look busier on paper than they are.
  • Clashes. Should be 0. Anything above that is a rule problem, not a spreadsheet problem.
  • Empty seats per meeting. Average seats in the booked room minus average attendees. This is the number that tells you what to do with your floor plan.
  • Oversized bookings. Meetings that took at least double the seats they needed.
  • Busiest weekday. Your peak. Nobody experiences an average.

Below those, four tables do the thinking.

Utilization by day gives you the 10 working days in a row, with a bar per day. The shape of your week averages Monday to Friday across both weeks, which is the table to screenshot for your leadership team.

Utilization by room ranks every room by hours booked, with its seats and average attendee count next to it. Who books the rooms lists your people by meetings, hours, and no-shows, which settles arguments about who is holding the big room every Thursday.

Are your rooms the right size?

The right-sizing block splits your two weeks into 6 counts: meetings for 1 to 2 people, meetings for 3 to 5, meetings for 6 or more, bookings in a much bigger room than needed, bookings with more people than seats, and bookings where nobody turned up.

Most offices run the same pattern. A pile of 1-to-1s and 2-person calls, a solid middle of 3-to-5 team meetings, and a handful of larger sessions that fail whenever the big room is taken.

Two people sitting in a room built for 12 is the commonest kind of waste in an office, and it’s invisible until you count it.

The market has been moving the same way. JLL’s 2026 Global Occupancy Planning Benchmark Report records private offices continuing to decline while phone booths, focus rooms and small meeting rooms take their place, and makes the point that knowing whether those rooms work needs space-level utilization data rather than building-level badge counts.

At 12 rooms, this template is that data. If your 1-to-2 count is high and your empty-seats-per-meeting number is 6 or 7, you don’t need a bigger office. You need to turn one large room into two small ones.

Where the fight for rooms actually happens

The Dashboard’s time-slot table breaks your bookable day into half hours and shows the share of rooms in use at each one.

Almost every office finds the same shape. Microsoft’s Work Trend Index research on the infinite workday found that half of all meetings land between 9-11am and 1-3pm, that Tuesday now carries 23% of the week’s meetings against Friday’s 16%, and that 60% of meetings are ad hoc, with 1 in 10 booked right before it starts.

Room shortages are a problem with about 4 hours of the day, on about 3 days of the week.

Our own office says the same thing from the other direction. We run OfficeRnD Workplace on our own floor, and across the year to July 2026 our Tuesday utilization was 71.5% against Friday’s 37.2%.

The same meeting rooms serve nearly twice as many people on a Tuesday as on a Friday. The full year-by-year breakdown sits in our desk booking template article.

Two things follow for your rooms.

First, a room no-show costs more than a desk no-show.

In our own office, 9.2% of desk bookings were auto-canceled because nobody checked in. A missed desk booking wastes one seat.

An abandoned booking on an 8-person room blocks 8 people from meeting, usually at 10am on a Tuesday, which is the exact hour and the exact day when nothing else is free. That’s what the “Took place?” column is for, and it’s why a room no-show rate above 10% is worth acting on before you go looking for more space.

Second, recurring meetings run against the grain of hybrid attendance.

74.6% of the office attendance we measured was booked one-off, week by week, rather than on a repeating pattern. Standing meetings do the opposite: they repeat forever, and in a two-week grid you retype every one of them each fortnight. Log the recurring set first, then add the ad-hoc bookings on top.

If you ever need to calculate how much office space you need, check out our office space calculator.

How this template compares to other free ones

Most free meeting room templates are a weekly grid with a booking table under it. This one goes further in 6 places.

Typical free templateThis template
FormatsGoogle Sheets only, or Excel onlyExcel and Google Sheets, one file
Email gateOftenNo
Rooms1 room per viewUp to 12, all visible on one board
Conflict detectionManual check, or a basic flagAutomatic, plus wrong-time and out-of-range checks
Capacity checkingNoneFlags over-capacity and oversized bookings
No-show trackingNonePer booking, with a rate on the dashboard
Utilization reportingNoneBy room, by day, by weekday and by half-hour slot
ViewsOne weekly gridAll rooms for one day, plus one room for two weeks

The right-sizing report is the part with the most money attached. A template that stops double bookings saves an argument. A template that tells you 3 of your rooms only ever hold 2 people tells you what to do with your next fit-out.

Excel or Google Sheets

Every function in the file (COUNTIF, COUNTIFS, SUMIF, INDEX, MATCH, SUMPRODUCT) works in both. Choose on how your team works.

Several people booking at onceNeeds SharePoint or OneDriveWorks out of the box
Offline accessYesNo
Booking from a phoneWorkable, not comfortableBetter
CalendarOutlookGoogle Calendar
Version historyManual, or via OneDriveAutomatic
Conflict checks and dashboardSameSame

Short version: Sheets if more than 3 people will touch the file in a day. Excel if you’re the only editor, or if IT keeps everything inside Microsoft 365.

Where the spreadsheet stops working

The file is honest about its ceiling. Here are the signs you’ve hit it.

  • More than about 12 rooms, more than one floor, or more than one office in the same file.
  • People double-book because they booked before somebody else’s row appeared.
  • Rooms sit empty because nobody cancels a meeting they no longer need.
  • You want months of utilization history rather than a rolling two weeks.
  • Desks, parking or visitors need booking alongside the rooms.
  • Somebody has to walk the floor to find out whether the 11am in Everest actually happened.

Meeting volume is part of why this arrives faster than teams expect. Organizations have seen a 12.9% rise in the number of meetings per employee since 2020, and none of that growth lands evenly across the week.

There’s also a quieter problem. When we polled our audience, 30% were on hybrid work software, 11% ran bookings on a spreadsheet, and 17.4% had built something in-house.

Answers from the same company often disagreed, because different teams were running different systems. If sales books rooms in Outlook and engineering keeps a sheet, you have three booking systems and none of them can tell you how full the office was on Tuesday.

Also, here’s an image showing the main pros and cons of using a meeting room booking excel sheet.

What this looks like in meeting room booking software

Every tab in the template exists because software does the same job on its own. Here’s the mapping.

Day boardInteractive floor plans with real rooms in real positions

The automatic release is the piece a spreadsheet can’t reproduce. Our 9.2% figure came from one setting: check-in required, auto-cancel on miss. In a spreadsheet, that same result takes a person walking the floor.

Naming your rooms well helps more than it sounds, too. Our list of meeting room name ideas is there when you get to it, and better room data usually ends in a smaller office footprint.
