Name: 7 Proven Hybrid Work Tips for Employees [2026]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Hybrid work is a flexible arrangement where employees split their time between a physical office and a remote location, usually home, on a structured or self-directed schedule.
Post body:
Hybrid work is a flexible arrangement where employees split their time between a physical office and a remote location, usually home, on a structured or self-directed schedule.

It’s now the default for most office-based roles. As of Q2 2026, 52% of remote-capable U.S. workers are hybrid, 26% are fully remote, and 22% are fully on-site, and these figures have held relatively stable since 2022. Workers want it to stay that way, and many will change jobs to keep the flexibility.

While this shift had been building for years, COVID-19 sped it up. Hybrid work gives employees the flexibility to move between the office and home based on the work in front of them.

That flexibility comes with new challenges. You have to stay productive no matter where you work from, and you have to protect the line between work and life when both happen under the same roof. The good news is that a few habits make the switch far easier.

Here are seven hybrid work tips for employees to help you stay productive and protect your work-life balance.

7 practical hybrid work tips for employees

The productivity question is largely settled. Hybrid work does not hurt productivity when managed well, hybrid employees often report higher engagement than fully on-site workers, and although remote workers spend slightly fewer hours on the job than before the pandemic, this has not translated into reduced output. Management quality, not work location, is the primary determinant of team productivity.

Rather than removing the office from the equation, hybrid work keeps the human connection that fully remote work makes harder to find.

For you, that means finding ways to do your job well and hold onto a good work-life balance. The tips below are built to do both and to clear the friction that sometimes comes with hybrid work.

#1: Set appropriate boundaries

One of the hardest parts of hybrid work is the stress that comes from blurring the line between home and work.

It leads some people to work longer hours and take on more than they did when they went into the office every day. That’s why boundaries matter. The risk is real: employees with fully self-determined hybrid schedules are 76% more likely to say burnout or fatigue is their greatest challenge compared with employees whose schedule is set by their manager or team.

Start with boundaries for yourself. Setting a schedule that separates work from home is a challenge, but one worth taking on. If you get to choose when you work at home, those hours don’t have to match your old office hours.

Even when you work independently, show up to meetings on time. Daily check-ins help too. Take a moment after work to ask yourself:

  • Did I have too much work to complete today?
  • How stressed am I feeling now?
  • How do I feel about what I managed to accomplish today?

If you notice you’re stressed, not getting enough done, or taking on too much, adjust so it doesn’t repeat. Boundaries aren’t something you set once and forget. Reflecting helps you find what works and change what doesn’t.

#2: Establish a dedicated work area

Based on research by Stanford University, only 49% of American employees have a dedicated work area in their homes. The rest work from bedrooms or shared spaces that change from day to day.

A spot at home that’s only for work can lower stress, cut frustration, and help you finish the workday faster.

Choose a long-term space where you can focus on work instead of everything else going on at home. A few things to consider as you set it up:

  • Pick a dedicated work area, whether that’s an extra room, a garage, a shed, or any convenient space.
  • Use a table or desk at work height, which is 29 inches from the floor to the surface.
  • Choose a good monitor (or two to three) set at a height where your eyes are around 25% below the top of the screen.
  • Get a proper office chair. Adjustable height, lumbar support, rolling, and seat pan tilt all make the space more comfortable.
  • Add good lighting, with overhead and indirect sources that prevent glare on the monitor.
  • Make sure you have a reliable internet connection.
  • Sort out the rest of your kit, such as a mouse, keyboard, headset, and microphone. You don’t want to be scrambling for something mid-meeting.

If you often work somewhere other than home, these tips still apply. Consider a travel setup for hotels, coffee shops, coworking spaces, and other places you get work done.

#3: Become a communication and collaboration master

Clear communication and intentional collaboration are the skills that set you apart in a hybrid environment. They matter more than ever: nearly half of hybrid workers report that their team has never discussed a formal or informal plan for collaborating effectively. Don’t wait for your team to fix that. Model it.

Five tips to help:

  1. Communicate your availability clearly: Share your schedule so teammates know when they can reach you for meetings and when to contact you.
  2. Get good at video conferencing: It keeps you connected when you’re remote and helps build stronger relationships and improve communication. Learn how to run Webex, Google Meet, and Zoom well.
  3. Refine your communication skills: Be clear and concise whether you’re in the office or remote, and actively listen. Sharpening your presentation skills and writing better email will carry you a long way.
  4. Learn the collaboration tools your team uses: Project management software and file-sharing platforms keep track of tasks, deadlines, and progress. Common picks include Asana, Trello, Google Docs, Slack, and Zoom.
  5. Be responsive: It’s easy to drift from your team when remote. Check your email and messaging apps regularly, and respond promptly to your team members and managers.

#4: Stay flexible

In a hybrid workplace, you need to be flexible. Things change as they progress, and you want to be ready.

Schedules might shift, or you could be asked to learn new tools, such as desk booking software or a meeting room booking system.

Keep an open mind and be willing to try new things in the office and at home. A few ways to build that flexibility:

  • Build a more flexible mindset. Change is part of the job, so rigidity costs you.
  • Switch your routine on occasion by altering your schedule or work style.
  • Add flex time to both your work and personal schedule.
  • When you see an issue coming, handle it early.
  • Accept that nothing stays the same forever.
  • Seek out learning opportunities and expose yourself to new things.

Flexibility builds trust with your team and managers, and trust is where the model lives or dies. Only 54% of managers who supervise remote workers strongly agree that they trust their teams to be productive when working remotely, and just 57% of employees strongly agree that they feel trusted by their manager. When you’re flexible and reliable, you earn more autonomy.

#5: Prioritize self-care

In a hybrid setting, separating work from personal time is hard, especially at home. That’s true whether you’re new to hybrid work or years into it. When you move to hybrid or change how you work, your wellbeing has to come first. It’s not soft: 76% of hybrid workers cite improved work-life balance as a top benefit of the model, and protecting that balance is on you as much as your employer.

There are plenty of ways to do it.

  • Set boundaries: Define when your workday begins and ends, and stick to it. This separates work from personal time and frees you to focus on self-care in your off hours.
  • Schedule self-care: Make time for what nourishes you, whether that’s exercise, meditation, or a hobby you enjoy.
  • Practice mindfulness: Manage the anxiety that comes with too much work and learn to switch off. Deep breathing and short meditations help. The Calm app is one option, and 10 minutes a day is enough to start.
  • Take regular breaks: Sitting at a computer all day drains you, so get up and stretch your legs.
  • Maintain social connections: Stay in touch with friends, family, and colleagues to cut isolation and loneliness.
  • Go for a walk to reset. Even a couple of minutes of stretching between meetings helps.
  • Drop the pursuit of perfection. Changing your whole routine is rough, but it gets easier as you keep at it.

For more on self-care and building it into your life, watch the video below:

#6: Embrace the technology

One of the best things you can do to make hybrid work easier is get comfortable with the tools.

Technology holds hybrid work together. You need to be able to use the tools that help you collaborate, run video calls, and get work done efficiently.

Here’s a list of the most common tools required for hybrid work. Skip this step and you’ll fall behind coworkers who didn’t, and staying productive gets harder.

On the office side, one tool does a lot of the heavy lifting. OfficeRnD Workplace lets you book a desk or a meeting room, see who’s in on a given day, and plan your office days around the people you actually need to see. If your employer runs it, use it to make your in-office time count.

#7: Stay organized

The last tip is about organizational habits. Moving into a hybrid model can be jarring, and a lot of people end up disorganized, especially at home.

Disorganization breeds anxiety and slows your workflow. A few ways to fix it:

  • Use a cloud drive so you can move between the office and home without missing a beat. You can reach documents from anywhere, start something at home and finish it in the office, and keep a backup of your work. Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, and Dropbox are all solid choices.
  • Simplify your home workspace. Stacks of books, documents, and manuals create clutter. If you haven’t used something in months, move it out of your office space.

Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Hybrid work has settled into the operating model for most desk jobs. As of 2026, even cautious voices in the business world treat it as the default rather than an experiment.
Post body:
Hybrid work has settled into the operating model for most desk jobs. As of 2026, even cautious voices in the business world treat it as the default rather than an experiment.

Hybrid work is a model where employees split their time between the office and a remote location, usually spending part of the week in each.

The numbers back up its staying power. Gallup’s 2025 data shows that among remote-capable U.S. employees, 51% work hybrid, about 28% are fully remote, and 21% are fully on-site. Those splits have held steady since 2022, which tells you hybrid isn’t a phase companies are waiting out.

You’re here for the quotes, though, not the stats. Here’s what some of the world’s top business leaders and analysts have said about hybrid work, and what their words reveal about how they read this way of working.

First, a quick distinction.

What’s the difference between hybrid and remote work?

People often use hybrid and remote work interchangeably. They overlap, but they aren’t the same.

Both involve employees working outside a traditional office. The difference is how much time an employee is physically in the office. Hybrid work mixes in-person and remote days, while remote work happens entirely outside a physical office.

12 hybrid work quotes from those on the front lines

Here are 12 hybrid work quotes to educate and inspire anyone curious about how this model actually plays out.

#1 Miroslav Miroslavov, CEO and Co-founder, OfficeRnD

Hybrid work doesn’t happen by chance, and you need to be intentional, proactive, and thoughtful to make it work properly. It’s not easy but is doable and the outcomes can be massive!

Miroslav Miroslavov is the CEO and co-founder of OfficeRnD. OfficeRnD builds tools that help landlords, operators, and companies manage flexible and hybrid workplaces. Miroslav is also among the most distinguished hybrid work influencers.

#2 George Penn, Managing Vice President, Gartner

Success in a hybrid work environment requires employers to move beyond viewing remote or hybrid environments as a temporary or short-term strategy and to treat it as an opportunity.

George Penn holds a management position with a global team of executive advisors and researchers in Gartner’s HR practice. Gartner helps executives and their teams make faster, smarter decisions about company priorities.

Gartner helps organizations cut through the flood of information to find clarity based on peer and practitioner research, leading to decisions that drive stronger performance. Penn supports HR operational issues and talent management, helping companies address workforce challenges.

#3 Sir Richard Branson, Virgin Group

First and foremost, I believe in flexible working. It is important that employers appreciate their employees’ work-life balance and give them the flexibility to work around their personal lives.

Innovator. Pioneer. Entrepreneur. Adventurer. These are just some of the words that describe the man behind Virgin Group. The group’s holdings span travel, telecommunications, health, banking, music, and leisure.

Virgin has more than 40 companies in over 35 countries worldwide, many of which embrace the hybrid work model.

#4 Peter Yobo, Partner at Credera

Communication is key for employers, millennials, and others who want to transform and shape work flexibility. We need to empower our leaders to have those conversations, and our leaders empower the managers to provide those opportunities for their people within the teams.

Peter Yobo is a partner, product, and Atlanta market leader with Credera. Credera is a digital consulting firm delivering technology solutions, strategy, and innovation to a range of clients.

Yobo joined Credera in mid-2022 to help clients solve critical challenges and bring value to stakeholders and the markets those clients serve. He is a public speaker on topics such as “3 Steps to Greatness.”

#5 Rahul Goyal, Managing Director at ADP

While hybrid working can represent the best of both working worlds, this shift could require an investment in more sophisticated technology.

Rahul Goyal is the managing director of ADP India Private Ltd. ADP specializes in HR outsourcing, payroll outsourcing, consulting, and HR automation.

#6 Michelle Obama, Former First Lady

Flexible work makes employees loyal.

Michelle Obama was the first African American First Lady of the United States.

She is also an attorney and an acclaimed author, and an advocate for the arts, education, and nutrition.

#7 Goncalo Silva, CTO at Doist

Even when I worked in an office, I would often bring work home with me. When I started working remotely, it was just a recipe for disaster. Over time, I’ve found two things to be very important. This is a bit cliché, and everybody says this but it’s really true. Rest is very important. And time off is very important.

This quote comes from Goncalo Silva, the CTO at Doist. Doist creates apps and workflows that measure productivity and organize work and life. Doist has been an asynchronous, remote-first workplace since its founding in 2010.

#8 Stephanie Ruhle, Journalist

Work-life balance is not just a buzzy, self-help term that real business people laugh at. You need it.

Stephanie Ruhle is an MSNBC anchor, NBC News senior business correspondent, and the host of The 11th Hour. She has interviewed political, business, entertainment, and sports figures across her tenure at MSNBC.

She is active in women’s leadership development and founded the Corporate Investment Bank Women’s Network.

#9 Elon Musk

Remote work is no longer acceptable.

In June 2022, Musk sent a memo to Tesla’s executive staff signaling the end of remote work for the company’s employees.

In the email, which later leaked, Musk said that anyone who refuses to work at least 40 hours per week from the office should leave the company. He added that employees who disagree with the decision should pretend to work somewhere else.

Later, Musk took a more divisive workplace policy approach.

#10 Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta

Hybrid work is the perfect solution for companies looking to create a more productive, flexible, and engaged workforce.

Mark Zuckerberg is the founder and CEO of Meta, formerly Facebook.

Meta’s management team adopted remote work early in the shift. Zuckerberg spends much of his time working away from Silicon Valley.

#11 Larry English, Author of Office Optional

To start building your remote culture, establish and share some basic rules. The first and most important rule is mutual trust between the company and its workers. The rules after that? As few as possible.

Larry English is the cofounder and president of Centric Consulting. Centric was built as a fully remote company designed to promote employee and client happiness.

Centric now has offices in 12 US cities and India. It’s among the many companies that adopted a hybrid work model and never looked back.

#12 Alex Turnbull, Founder of Groove

Successfully working from home is a skill, just like programming, designing, or writing.

Alex Turnbull is the founder and CEO of Groove, which gives startups and small businesses a more efficient way to handle customer support. Its app offers a shared inbox, knowledge base, and reporting.

Check out what more executives are saying about the future of hybrid work here.

What are the four work modes that make hybrid work succeed?

One of our favorite quotes on this list comes from George Penn of Gartner. Gartner identified four work modes that organizations should invest in equally to make a hybrid environment work.

Synchronous

  • Working together, together: teams are in the same location and meet in that shared space.
  • Working together, apart: teams work in separate locations but meet virtually to stay aligned.

Asynchronous

  • Working alone, together: teams share a workspace but don’t work at the same time.
  • Working alone, apart: teams are in different locations, and individuals do deep-focus work remotely.

Gartner’s point is that most companies overinvest in the synchronous modes, defaulting to meetings, and underinvest in the asynchronous ones. Its research found that asynchronous work matters just as much for team innovation, yet few organizations build for it.

How software makes the four modes work

Intentional hybrid work needs coordination, and that’s where tooling earns its keep. OfficeRnD Workplace lets employees book desks and meeting rooms, see who’s in the office on any given day, and plan their onsite time around the teammates they want to see.

That last part is what turns a policy into a working routine. When people can coordinate their in-office days around each other instead of showing up to a half-empty floor, the synchronous modes actually deliver on their promise, and the analytics show you which days and spaces are being used so you can right-size your office.

Name: Ex-FlexJobs Marketing Director On Hybrid Work, Return To The Office And Being Lost At Sea
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Michael Gutman is an interesting person.
Post body:
Michael Gutman is an interesting person.

Besides being a recognized remote and hybrid work expert and educator, he’s also a former marketing director of FlexJobs – one of the leading platforms for finding flexible jobs.

In his early 20s, Mike had a lucrative career in Silicon Valley that he ditched to travel the world and shape his core values.

And he’s had many crazy experiences while visiting some of the world’s weirdest places.

Having consulted hundreds of companies on implementing the hybrid work model, Mike knows a thing or two about succeeding in today’s evolving workplace landscape as a business leader.

Hybrid work is a model where employees split their week between the office and a remote location, usually home, instead of working from one fixed place.

Luckily he agreed to share his vast experience and knowledge with our audience.

What follows is a compelling interview with the man himself, where we talk about:

  • Hybrid work and what it takes to succeed if you’re just starting out
  • What are the best online resources to learn more about the hybrid work model if you’re a beginner
  • The most common challenges that leaders face when adopting a hybrid working model
  • The return to the office and how leaders should approach it
  • The fast-paced life of a keynote speaker and hybrid work consultant
  • Michael being robbed at gunpoint and walking a puma through the Bolivian jungle

And much more.

Read on.

Would you please introduce yourself to our audience and let us know what you do for a living?

I’ve led remote teams since 2008 and since 2013 I have been helping teams adopt flexible and remote work strategies. My roles have ranged from heading up customer success at a remote collaboration tool company to leading the marketing and partnerships efforts at FlexJobs, to building remote learning and development experiences for adults looking to upskill into tech.

Currently, I am consulting and coaching leadership teams on implementing measurable remote work strategies, speaking at workforce development conferences, and authoring remote work courses on Linkedin and other platforms. My remote work courses have reached over 1 million learners to date.

How did your career start and why did you choose this path?

I’ve been working remotely since 2007 and I’ve always supported having access to work flexibility. But back in 2013, I had an “Aha!” moment.

At that time I was running a social enterprise focused on helping companies engage in corporate social responsibility. Part of the work involved teaching K-12 students about energy conservation and sustainability.

It was my belief that if we can change one person’s behavior to consume less and recycle more, we can make incremental changes in the world.

However, the model I was working with did not scale. We could only hold so many workshops and change so many people’s minds.

My mindset shifted to ask the question… how do we layer a sustainability model on top of behavior that people already want?

My answer was remote work. People want it.

The behavior reduces consumption from office space, fuel emissions, and general infrastructure. It is a behavior that does more with less and people are pushing for it. So I dove in and have been on a mission to help connect people and companies to the value of flexible and remote work ever since.

What was it like to be a Marketing Manager in Silicon Valley?

To be honest, it never aligned with the answer to the question “What do you want to be when you grow up?”

That being said, there were many aspects that I enjoyed. I was learning a lot, making good money, working with clients I never would have encountered, and managing large budgets. But at the end of the day, I realized I needed to make a career shift and align my work with my values.

Back then I was in my 20’s so I was still trying to determine what my values were.

(Maybe we never fully know) So I took a career break to figure out where I wanted to pivot. I did some traveling and lots of fierce introspection and realized I wanted to be intentional about helping humanity and the planet in some way.

And here we are today!

What was your biggest challenge as a director of marketing at “FlexJobs”?

I was at FlexJobs from 2016-2019. Our mission was to help increase the number of flexible jobs available so people could live better lives.

My biggest challenge (and opportunity) was to show people that flexible or hybrid jobs were real, and show companies that offering work flexibility could be a viable strategy for productivity and profit.

Remember, before the pandemic, the number of remote and flexible jobs out there was slim compared to on-site, 9-5 jobs.

Our approach was a methodical and strategic process that took time.

One of the silver linings of the pandemic is it gave people and companies a glimpse into what flexible and remote work could feel like and how to manage it properly. Which achieved the mission of connecting people and companies to flexible work in a matter of months.

How did you decide to become a remote and hybrid work consultant and speaker?

People just started asking me for help.

I have been living, breathing, and working to support remote work since 2013, and working remotely even longer. I’ve spoken to countless leaders at Fortune 100 companies, government agencies, start-ups, nonprofits… all people trying to get remote work dialed in for the communities they work with.

So I have a diverse perspective on how different stakeholders approach remote and flexible work.

So over time, people looked to me for my expertise. There is a big need for expertise from people who have been at this for a long time. To meet that need I am now giving keynotes on remote and flexible work and helping leadership teams dial in the employee experience for their employees.

What are the three most important things that leaders should know about hybrid work before adopting the model within their organization?

First, leaders should be asking what each employee needs to be successful. Each employee will have different needs. From home office set-ups to communication preferences, to work-life balance, to optimizing productivity, to health and wellness.

The list goes on. Also, people managers also need training to be successful in this environment. And if you don’t know what people need, you can’t support them.

Second, leaders need to measure the success of their program. You can’t optimize what you can’t measure.

Third, ensure whatever model you adopt is a flexible model.

The landscape of our work and lives is changing and if you create a rigid model that does not have room to evolve, it will break.

How should leaders better educate themselves on the topic of hybrid work, especially those who are new to the concept?

For leaders who are just learning about hybrid work, there are plenty of resources available. A simple google search will yield many results. Below are some specific resources I recommend.

  • There is the Hybrid Work For Dummies, OfficeRnD Special Edition.
  • I teach a 30 min rapid course people can access. It is called the Essential Remote/Hybrid Training For Managers Of All Levels. As a remote work consultant, I also offer live coaching and workshops. Feel free to reach out at SucceedRemotely.com
  • Gallup published a study on the advantages and disadvantages of hybrid work, and it keeps a running read on where the model stands now.

Additionally, I recommend all leaders chat with their colleagues or people in their professional networks about their experience. Ask people what is working for them, what they have learned, and what their best practices are. If you are a leader working in a hybrid environment, I also recommend asking the people you supervise this one powerful question.

“What does an ideal hybrid work experience look like for you and how can I help you with that?”

Based on your experience, what are the biggest challenges that leaders face when trying to implement the hybrid work model?

The biggest challenge for leaders is that they often feel like they have to have all the answers to support remote or hybrid work experiences, just because they are in leadership positions.

I tell new clients that they are never going to get their hybrid or remote model right straight away.

It is just impossible to please everyone. With that in mind, I suggest that a new model should be rolled out in phases.

The first phase should be informing the initial plan. So what I suggest is asking teams what an ideal hybrid model looks like, and then trying to roll out the first phase of the implementation strategy that tries to align with the feedback.

Then build in feedback loops to evolve the plan over time in the following phases.

Companies can also fall into the trap of having a communications strategy that promises hard and fast deadlines for their plan. They should keep their communications strategy flexible as well so as to never overpromise.

Gallup’s own data backs the case for letting teams shape their own approach. When a team decides its hybrid schedule together, 91% of employees call the policy fair, compared with 73% when leadership decides it for them.

What approach should employers take to bring employees back to the office and is the return to the office dead?

I always encourage a people-first approach. Ask your people if they want an office, and if so, what for. Then craft an office experience that aligns with the culture of the team. Maybe they want to use it for collaboration days, professional development time, or creative time.

Most people don’t want to be forced back in to be heads down at their desks. They could do that at home and be more productive.

So it comes down to being intentional and being able to justify why your return to office policy exists.

If you can’t justify why you are forcing people into the office, people will start to resent the policy over time.

The numbers say the same thing. Despite the wave of return-to-office headlines, Gallup finds 51% of remote-capable U.S. employees still work hybrid, and hybrid workers are in the office about 2.3 days a week, up only slightly since 2022. A blanket five-day mandate runs against where most of the workforce actually sits.

What’s the most valuable insight about hybrid and remote work you’ve learned after consulting clients?

Simply put, people want choice. The choice to choose when, where and how we get work done.

The biggest question leaders have is how they can manage choice and autonomy at scale.

This can be done by moving to a results-centered performance management strategy. Where you know if productivity goals are being met, regardless of when, where, and how.

Now, the million-dollar question: What’s the future of hybrid work?

This is too big of a question for me to predict. I only have a small sliver of insight. From a remote and hybrid perspective, I believe that remote work is here to stay.

As future generations grow more and more into leadership positions, we will see more and more distributed work.

For example, I didn’t have a cell phone or email until I was 18. Generations who are connected to the globe as children will know how to communicate and collaborate from anywhere better than we can currently. I believe these generations will pave the way for reducing the friction of remote and hybrid working.

The data so far agrees with Mike. Gallup’s work-location figures have held roughly steady since 2022, which suggests hybrid has settled into a durable model rather than a phase on the way back to the old office.

You’re an avid traveler. What’s the weirdest place you’ve ever been to?

Hmmmm…. I’ve been through a lot. Here are some of the strangest experiences off the top of my head.

  • I’ve been lost at sea in a small boat, in a rainstorm, at midnight in Panama.
  • I’ve walked a puma through the Bolivian jungle for 12 miles a day for a month at an animal refuge in Bolivia.
  • I’ve been robbed at gunpoint
  • Survived giardia
  • Lived in a garage in a yoga community
  • Been inked by an octopus
  • and was forced to pay the police the equivalent of $100 for crashing a motorcycle…

…and I survived to tell the tale.

Where can people find you online?

I encourage people to connect with me on Linkedin or to send me a note through my website SucceedRemotely.com

Running hybrid work day to day

Mike’s advice lands better with a system behind it. OfficeRnD Workplace gives HR, facilities, and IT teams the tools to run a hybrid office: desk and room booking, attendance data, and week-by-week visibility into how the space actually gets used. That’s the measurement Mike points to when he says you can’t optimize what you can’t measure.

How does hybrid work success actually look in practice? It’s less about the number of days in the office and more about giving people clear expectations, the right tools, and a reason to show up when they do.

This article covers what hybrid work success takes, then walks through six companies that made the model work.

We’ll look at:

  • How these organizations approach hybrid work
  • How the right hybrid work software removed workflow friction and improved day-to-day operations
  • What changes they made to run the hybrid model well

And more.

Hybrid work is a working model where employees split their week between a workplace and a remote location, usually home, instead of being in the office five days a week. Hybrid work success means that split runs smoothly: people collaborate in person when it counts, work focused hours at home, and managers can see how office space is actually used.

The stakes are real. Hybrid is now the default for people who can work remotely. Gallup finds that six in 10 employees with remote-capable jobs want a hybrid arrangement, about one-third prefer fully remote work, and fewer than 10% prefer to be on-site.

What is needed for hybrid work success?

According to a Forbes article on hybrid workplace mistakes, the “hybrid workspace is about enabling as much productivity as possible without costing our employees too much personal time, sacrifice, or ability to control their workday.”

Even with the flexibility that hybrid work models offer, a few practices separate the companies that make it work from the ones that struggle:

  1. Get employees on board early. Communicate transparently, clearly, and often. Give managers what they need to answer their teams’ questions.
  2. Invest in the right tools, technology, and equipment. Use tools that support productivity and communication, work across devices, and are mobile friendly. Use hybrid work management software that integrates with your existing tech stack. Give your employees the equipment for a healthy home setup, from larger monitors to supportive chairs. Designing your hybrid office well matters too.
  3. Keep a positive, engaged, and collaborative culture that centers on employee experience. Ask for feedback and act on it.
  4. Check in with the whole team regularly. Schedule calls, video meetings, or in-person progress reviews so you can see how well the model is working.
  5. Offer continuing education for employees, team leads, and managers. Make sure everyone knows about upcoming learning opportunities, and meet different needs with different formats.
  6. Track goals and other performance metrics. Keep the dialogue open, build development plans, and track progress against them.

Examples of hybrid work success stories

Here are six companies that put a hybrid model in place and made it stick. Each one hit a different problem, from scaling across countries to squeezing more collaboration out of fewer desks.

#1 Müller Group

  • Industry: Food service; manufacturing and distribution
  • Number of employees: approximately 31,700
  • Location: 22 offices across Europe and the UK
  • Hybrid mix: 100% hybrid; 3 days in the office

Müller is a family-owned company that operates internationally with annual sales of 7.0 billion euros. It manufactures well-known brands across dairy, fish, deli, sauces, dressings, and services. Before Covid, Müller ran a 100% in-office policy.

Like many others, the company went fully remote during the pandemic. It kept growing and needed to house new staff as employees returned, so it moved to a hybrid model. Corporate employees now come in three days a week.

Booking rooms and resources is easier too, because the software integrates with their existing Microsoft Teams and Outlook, which keeps collaboration in tools people already use.

Most meeting rooms are now booked directly from Microsoft Teams or Outlook, without the need for yet another app.

Managers also use the analytics to make better calls on office resources, which lowered costs and improved efficiency. What makes the model work is how well Müller manages a growing shared-desk setup across 22 locations. You can read the whole story here.

#2 Tavistock Restaurant Collection

  • Number of employees: 1,575
  • Location: United States
  • Hybrid mix: 100% hybrid

Before Covid, Tavistock was 100% in the office. When the pandemic slowed fine dining, the company needed to cut costs by shedding unnecessary office space.

Its hybrid work policy asks employees to be in the office Tuesday through Thursday.

Tavistock shared office space with its private equity parent company, which made reserving desks and rooms cumbersome.

That friction pulled the corporate team’s attention away from supporting restaurant-level staff. Managing corporate apartments added another layer of complexity.

The fix: Tavistock adopted OfficeRnD Workplace, which gave the operations team better support.

Because the software integrates with Microsoft Teams, employees can sync calendars and reserve spaces without leaving the app. That made offices and apartment space easier to manage.

Tavistock needed a solution that integrated fully with their existing MS Teams app. Easy adoption mattered so HR could stay focused on restaurant operations.

OfficeRnD Workplace delivered that: integration with Microsoft Teams that lets employees book desks and rooms inside the app and see who else is coming in, which supports face-to-face collaboration and business growth.

The software also let Tavistock manage multiple locations and office neighborhoods in a single system.

The result: more in-person collaboration and lower real estate costs. Read the full story here.

#3 plentymarkets

  • Number of employees: 250
  • Location: Germany and Romania
  • Hybrid mix: 100% hybrid with a 16% desk-to-employee ratio

Another story that shows how much the right software matters when moving to hybrid.

Based in Germany, plentymarkets connects online and offline trade processes and changes how products are sold.

Its multi-channel approach helps merchants manage sales faster while serving more than 50,000 users daily. The cloud-based system keeps online and offline processes working together.

During Covid, the company moved from a Monday-to-Friday model to fully remote. It now runs a 100% hybrid model where employees choose when to work from the office.

The company has 250 employees and only 40 office seats, so returning to work became a logistical headache for everyone.

Managers struggled to bring people in for collaboration and productivity. They needed a technical solution to manage the crunch.

That’s where OfficeRnD Workplace came in.

The software helped plentymarkets optimize an office footprint that ran at a 16% employee-to-desk ratio. For every 4 office employees, they had one desk.

It also integrates with their existing tech stack, so booking desks and rooms happens inside the apps people already use.

The in-app survey tool helped the company stay compliant with strict German health regulations. Management also uses the surveys to track employee NPS, a useful hybrid work metric.

According to Lucas Wöhrl, director of operations at plentymarkets, OfficeRnD Workplace let them track expected versus actual hybrid usage across the organization. That shaped decisions and helped them manage office resources more efficiently.

Since rollout, employees have come back to socialize and collaborate, which lifted engagement and productivity.

Building flexible workplace policies got easier too. Office maps and schedules in the app keep calendars in sync, which improved how teams work together.

#4 IES

  • Number of employees: 272
  • Location: Glasgow and Dublin
  • Hybrid mix: 40/60 remote to office

Integrated Environmental Solutions (IES) has built a 25-year reputation in global performance-based building analysis.

IES is home to one of the largest physics analytics teams in the world, backed by expert consultancy and a dedicated R&D department that keeps its tools current.

Before Covid, IES was 100% in the office. During the pandemic, it went fully remote.

No one expected getting people back to be hard, but two years of remote work changes a lot.

Resources needed managing, budgets needed revising, and the company needed systems that let employees collaborate well when they were in.

The management had three main challenges:

  1. Bring the workforce back for collaboration while keeping the flexibility people wanted.
  2. Track hybrid work performance and see office usage for future planning and expansion.
  3. Make the back-to-office policy work across multiple offices in several countries and cities.

Fast adoption, an easy-to-use product, and a personalized onboarding process from the customer success team brought employees back for face-to-face collaboration sooner than expected.

IES also needed logins and workflows to stay simple, which it handled with OfficeRnD Workplace integrations and SSO.

#5 Slack

Slack develops real-time collaboration software: messaging, file sharing, video and voice calls, and more, used by organizations worldwide.

Its messaging platform is one of the tools that made distributed work practical for a lot of teams.

Before the pandemic, Slack was an in-office company. In June 2020, it announced a permanent work-from-home option while keeping its offices open.

Slack also opened many new roles to remote candidates and encouraged people to work hours that fit their lives, in support of better work-life balance.

Instead of enforcing rigid schedules, Slack’s managers use “core hours,” usually up to four hours a day when workers are available for collaboration. That leaves time for focused, meeting-free work.

They also run a “no-meetings Fridays” policy so employees can protect time for creative work. Leadership actively works to avoid proximity bias, one of the common pitfalls of hybrid work.

Cal Henderson, Slack’s CTO and co-founder, has said:

We will be mainly using offices for collaborative work and social interaction.

He expects most employees to come in several times a year to socialize or collaborate rather than daily.

Slack employees report feeling engaged wherever they work, with outcomes measured by results rather than hours at a desk.

#6 Work Better

Work Better is a modern coworking space in Europe and one of the most popular in Sofia, Bulgaria.

Work Better runs a hybrid model successfully and has seen real benefits from it, with OfficeRnD Workplace doing a lot of the heavy lifting.

43 companies work there in a hybrid model, and 90% of Work Better’s clients use OfficeRnD Workplace to manage their work.

By combining physical and digital workspace offerings, Work Better built an environment that fits the different ways its members want to work.

That lets people pick their own mix of remote and in-person time, which helps both productivity and flexibility.

The payoff has been real. By removing geographic limits, Work Better widened its reach and member base.

Name: 9 Expert Hybrid Work Tips For Managers [#3 Is Crucial]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Among US employees whose jobs can be done from home, hybrid work is now the default. Gallup’s workforce data shows 52% of remote-capable US employees work hybrid, 26% work fully remote, and 22% are fully on-site. Compared with 2019, when about a third of remote-capable workers had any hybrid arrangement, the shift has been fast and it has held.
Post body:
Among US employees whose jobs can be done from home, hybrid work is now the default. Gallup’s workforce data shows 52% of remote-capable US employees work hybrid, 26% work fully remote, and 22% are fully on-site. Compared with 2019, when about a third of remote-capable workers had any hybrid arrangement, the shift has been fast and it has held.

Hybrid work is a model where employees split their week between a workplace and a remote location, usually home, instead of coming into the office five days a week.

This article covers nine practical hybrid work tips for managers, based on our work with thousands of organizations that went hybrid over the past few years. These are the same tips we follow in our own company to make hybrid work.

Quick summary: Here are the nine tips that leaders should follow to manage a hybrid workplace successfully:

  1. Create opportunities for employee engagement
  2. Set clear objectives
  3. Select the right hybrid work software
  4. Offer regular feedback
  5. Test drive useful technology
  6. Be strategic about your hybrid work policy
  7. Use employee check-ins
  8. Build intentional collaboration
  9. Avoid bias

Most companies now offer some form of flexible work, and managers have to adapt. It comes down to creating boundaries between home and work, working with people across locations, and communicating well.

Managers need to support team members in this environment. Systems, practices, and processes have to fit the way people work in a hybrid workplace.

Here’s what you need to know as a manager to make that work.

9 hybrid work tips for managers applicable in every organization

#1 Create opportunities for employee engagement

One of the most repeated stories about employee engagement is when President Kennedy asked a janitor at NASA what he was doing, and the janitor replied, “I’m helping to put a man on the Moon“.

Keeping the workforce enthusiastic and absorbed in the work they’re doing matters just as much in a hybrid workplace as in a traditional one. It can also reduce absenteeism.

Employees don’t need to be in the same building, city, or state to engage with each other and build their emotional commitment to the company and its goals.

As a manager, make sure employees:

  • Have all the necessary resources and tools available
  • Receive recognition when they do a good job
  • Know exactly what you expect of them
  • Have opportunities to grow and learn
  • Feel their opinions matter to you

This isn’t the easiest thing to implement, but that doesn’t make it any less important. Put in the work and the results last. Also, learn how to work with generational differences in your workplace.

#2 Set clear objectives

For employees to do a good job, they need to know what you expect. For a manager, that means setting clear objectives and key results.

It also helps when workers understand how their work fits into the organization’s goals as a whole. This is about more than setting goals once a year.

Aim for continuous performance management with regular reviews. Businesses change quickly, so employee targets need to stay flexible. Managers have to spot priority changes and know when to move in a different direction.

It helps to learn how to set smart goals. Here are some good examples of smart goals for work.

#3 Select the right hybrid work software

The right hybrid work software is essential, and picking it can be hard when so many solutions exist.

First, the most important feature is the ability to book desks and meeting rooms from anywhere. You can’t run desk hoteling or hot desking properly without it.

Second, as a manager, you need accurate data to run your hybrid workplace well. A clear view of your team’s office visits and space usage lets you shape your workplace strategy with evidence instead of guesswork.

That’s why your solution should include workplace analytics that track metrics like the monthly, weekly, and daily usage of your desks and spaces. Attendance clusters midweek, so peak-day desk demand, not average headcount, is what you plan around.

Third, most of us are already drowning in apps, and being told to learn one more is frustrating.

Instead of an app people have to learn from scratch, pick software that works inside the tools you already use, like Microsoft Teams and Outlook or Slack. A free desk reservation tool such as OfficeRnD Workplace does exactly that.

That way employees book desks and meeting rooms without leaving their favorite applications. OfficeRnD Workplace is desk and room booking software that runs inside Teams, Outlook, and Slack and gives managers the office usage data to plan around. See how it combines these features at OfficeRnD Workplace.

Check out the short video below to see the tool in action.

#4 Offer regular feedback

Another tip is to give feedback often. Whether things are going great or a little off-kilter, feedback tells employees how they’re doing. Scheduling it regularly keeps it from slipping when something else comes up.

Instead of a single annual review, check in throughout the year.

Regular reviews can motivate employees to do even better and improve team engagement. Managers have to be able to change direction when needed to hit the mark.

Continuous performance management is a big part of this. It makes both employees and managers accountable for what’s happening. HR watches the major trends while managers keep things on track day to day.

Gallup’s research is blunt about why this matters in hybrid teams: managers tend to communicate less often as people spend more time remote, yet hybrid engagement can beat on-site engagement when managers check in multiple times a week. The communication has to be deliberate.

#5 Test drive useful technology

Get in there and use the technology yourself.

Some useful tools for hybrid workplaces are:

  • Desk and meeting room booking software
  • Microsoft Teams and Outlook
  • Trello
  • Zoom

A new work environment means new processes and systems, so understand them well enough to offer support and training. That’s part of driving innovation in the workplace.

As a manager, you should be able to run an online review or set up a video conference without fumbling.

Train your team on the right tools for hybrid work, and revisit processes that changed when you went hybrid.

Help everyone get comfortable with new technology, and learn the best ways to manage from a distance. That’s what makes a good manager now: being effective in any environment.

#6 Be strategic about your hybrid work policy

A full return to the office five days a week isn’t the direction most companies are heading. Structured hybrid has become the standard, so bring people into the office with a clear plan and keep rethinking your policies.

There are two approaches, mandate and magnet, and mixing them often works best.

With a mandate approach, workers are required to come into the office a set number of days per week. The most common structured pattern now is three days in the office, two remote.

The magnet approach moves away from forced days and instead makes the office a place people want to come to for collaboration and socializing. And collaboration helps businesses grow.

Think about what people actually want to come together for, then make sure the office offers that.

Use what you already know, or ask your workers directly. Make the office somewhere people want to meet up and work together.

#7 Use employee check-ins

Managers often assume remote work is going fine. Check-ins tell you whether that’s true.

But what are employee check-ins exactly?

Check-ins are regular one-on-one meetings where managers discuss goals, objectives, and results without turning it into a formal performance review or micromanagement.

They build two-way communication and keep you aware of what’s happening with your team. Weekly check-ins are a good way to get project updates and surface challenges. They only help if you listen and then act on what you hear.

As a manager, resolve issues and make sure your hybrid team members feel ready to move forward. Help with career progression and find opportunities for people to develop. That’s what makes workers feel valued and connected, and it contributes to a better work ethic. Regular communication is a big part of it.

#8 Build intentional collaboration

Every successful executive knows collaboration matters.

Good collaboration happens when team members connect, learn about each other, and work toward shared goals. That’s harder when some people are remote, but it’s still possible.

It can start with something as simple as having people use their cameras in online meetings.

When workers can see each other, it builds connection and lowers the barriers between people in different locations. Even non-work calls can get people excited about working together.

Planning time to collaborate in person is worth it for engagement, productivity, and team culture. Many tasks work fine at home, but some go better with other people in the room.

Let people plan to come in for the work that benefits from a group, and collaboration follows.

How do you get your team to visit the office more often? Attract them rather than force them.

Work on turning your office from a space into a place people want to come to. Refresh parts of the workspace and add amenities like green spaces, cafés, or quiet areas.

To go further, survey your workers about the amenities and dedicated areas they’d want, then act on the answers. Here’s a useful list of hybrid work questions to ask.

#9 Avoid bias

The last of the nine tips is bias. No manager wants to treat office workers and remote workers differently, but it happens.

Proximity bias is the one to watch. Many leaders unconsciously favor the people physically closest to them over those at a distance.

SHRM’s survey of 817 supervisors shows the scale of the problem. Two out of three supervisors admitted they see remote workers as more replaceable than on-site workers, and 42% said they sometimes forget about remote workers when assigning tasks.

Don’t be that manager. Be aware of proximity bias and push against it. Pay attention to everyone, not just the people in the same building.

Redirect your focus to people contributing from other locations. Do it consistently and it changes the tone of the workplace. When it’s clear you value all work equally, people feel comfortable working from wherever suits them.

Show that everyone is working toward the same goals, whatever their location.

Name: Free Desk Booking Template in Excel [Plus Google Sheets]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Most desk booking spreadsheets tell you what people booked. This desk booking template in Excel also tracks who turned up, which is where the difference between a tidy sheet and a useful one sits.
Post body:
Most desk booking spreadsheets tell you what people booked. This desk booking template in Excel also tracks who turned up, which is where the difference between a tidy sheet and a useful one sits.

It’s one file, free, and it works in both Excel and Google Sheets. Six tabs: your desks, a 2-week booking grid, a check-in log, a day-by-day floor view, and a dashboard that calculates your utilization and tells you how many desks you actually need.

We built it after looking at 12 months of our own desk data: 12,829 bookings in OfficeRnD’s office, all requiring check-in. What that year showed us is in the second half of this article, so you can hold your own numbers against a real hybrid office.

What’s in the file?

Six tabs, in the order you’ll use them.

  • Start Here. Setup in 4 steps, plus a short list of the signs you’ve outgrown a spreadsheet.
  • Setup. Your desks (up to 30) and your people (up to 40), entered once. Every other tab reads from here, so you add a desk in one place, and it appears everywhere.
  • Bookings. A 2-week grid, Monday to Friday. Pick a name from the dropdown to book a desk. If somebody ends up booked at two desks on the same day, the cell turns red.
  • Check-in. The tab that does the work. Each morning you mark Showed or No-show against yesterday’s bookings. Amber means booked but not yet checked in.
  • Day View. Pick a day and see the whole floor: who’s sitting where, which desks are free, who didn’t show, and a list of everyone in that day.
  • Dashboard. Utilization by day and by weekday, peak against average, no-show rate, and a desk requirement calculated from your busiest day.

The limits, stated plainly: 30 desks, 40 people, one office, 10 working days at a time. Past that, look at desk booking software instead.

How to set up your desk booking template in Excel

Twenty minutes, start to finish.

1. Make your copy

In Google Sheets, use File, then Make a copy so it saves to your own Drive. In Excel, download the file and save it to SharePoint or OneDrive if more than one person will edit it.

2. List your desks and your people

Open Setup. Type your desk names into the desk table: D1, D2, or whatever your office already calls them. Add a zone (North, Quiet, Focus) and a note about what’s on the desk. Dual monitor, standing, dock. People pick desks on those details, so it’s worth the 5 minutes.

Then add your people. Those names fill the dropdowns on the Bookings tab.

3. Set your start date and your buffer

Set “Bookings start” to a Monday. Every date across the grid updates from that one cell.

Set your peak buffer. 15% is a sensible default: it’s the spare capacity you want on your busiest day so that the last 2 people in still find a seat. This number drives the desk recommendation on the Dashboard.

4. Book desks, then record check-ins

Click any cell in the booking grid and pick a name. Blank means the desk is free.

The next morning, open Check-in and mark who showed up. This is the step people skip, and it’s the step that makes every number on the Dashboard mean something. Ten minutes a day, walked from the door to the far wall.

Who owns the file

One person, named, with a backup. Office manager, workplace coordinator or people ops. Their job is to keep the desk list current, record check-ins, and settle clashes.

In Google Sheets, give the owner Editor rights and everyone else Commenter rights if you want bookings requested rather than made directly. In Excel, use SharePoint or OneDrive and skip email attachments entirely. Version control by email is how a booking system dies in week 3.

What your dashboard is telling you

Six numbers sit across the top. Here’s what a bad one looks like.

  • Average daily utilization. Booked or occupied desks against desks available, averaged across the 10 days. Under 40% and you’re paying for space nobody wants. Over 85% and people are hunting for seats.
  • Peak day utilization. Your busiest day. This is the number that decides whether the office feels workable, because nobody experiences an average.
  • Peak vs average. The multiple between the two. Anything above 1.5× means your week has a strong shape and you need to plan around the peak.
  • No-show rate. Bookings where nobody turned up, as a share of recorded check-ins. It’s calculated on check-ins you’ve actually logged, so a half-filled log still gives an honest number. Above 10% and your busy days look busier on paper than they are.
  • Desk to people ratio. How many people share each desk today.
  • Desks you need. Busiest-day demand plus your buffer, rounded up. Compared against the desks you have, so it comes out as a surplus or a shortfall.

Below those, two tables do most of the thinking: utilization day by day, and utilization by weekday averaged across both weeks. The weekday table is the one to screenshot for your leadership team.

How your numbers compare to a real hybrid office

We use OfficeRnD Workplace to run our office, so we pulled a full year of data from it. 8 July 2025 to 7 July 2026. 12,829 desk bookings requiring check-in, 8,467 confirmed booking occurrences.

Here’s what to hold your dashboard against.

Your dashboard saysOur office, one year
Average daily utilization62.8% (median 66.7%)
Peak vs average1.9× (Tuesday 71.5%, Friday 37.2%)
Days above 80%About 1 working day in 5
No-show rate9.2% of bookings auto-canceled at check-in
Booked desk-days released early34%

Tuesday runs at nearly twice Friday

Monday, Tuesday and Thursday each average 70 to 72%. Wednesday sits at 64%. Friday comes in at 37.2%, barely half of any other weekday.

An office sized for our 63% average would be under pressure every Tuesday and half empty every Friday. Roughly one working day in five goes above 80%, and our busiest days of the year hit full capacity.

This matches what the benchmarks show. CBRE’s 2026 Global Workplace & Occupancy Insights puts global average office utilization at 53% for 2025, up from 38% the year before, with peak utilization averaging 80%. The gap between the two numbers is the entire planning problem.

So when your template’s weekday table shows a 2× spread, that’s normal. Plan for the busy end of it. Our office space calculator works the same way, and there’s more detail in our guide on how much office space you need.

Three-quarters of attendance gets decided week by week

74.6% of our confirmed attendance came from one-off bookings rather than recurring ones. People decide each week whether coming in is worth it, usually because a specific colleague or meeting will be there.

This is why the booking grid needs to be easy to read and easy to change. Recurring patterns cover a quarter of the picture. The rest is people looking at who’s in on Wednesday and deciding on Tuesday night.

The Friday paradox

Friday produced the strangest finding of the year. It has the highest share of recurring bookings of any day (30%), and it’s also the least reliable day of the week.

39.2% of Friday bookings end up canceled, against 32 to 34% on other days. Friday’s no-show rate is 11%, the highest of the week, compared to 8.2% on Tuesday.

The people who book Fridays are regulars, and they’re the most likely to bail. Standing Friday reservations quietly decay into empty desks. If your check-in tab shows the same thing, you’ve found the day where your booking rules need the most teeth.

One in three booked desks gets released before it’s wasted

Of those 12,829 bookings, 66% were confirmed, 24.8% were canceled by the employee ahead of time, and 9.2% were auto-canceled because nobody checked in.

Read together: a third of booked desk-days went back into the pool before they were wasted, and nearly 1 in 10 bookings would have been a desk sitting empty all day with somebody’s name on it. In our office that’s 4 to 5 desks recovered every working day, or about 8% of daily capacity, from a single policy setting.

Without check-in, our reported utilization would be inflated by desks nobody sat at, and anyone looking for a seat on a busy Tuesday would see a floor plan full of empty “occupied” desks.

Your template can’t auto-release anything. What it can do is show you the size of the problem, so you know what a check-in rule is worth before you go looking for one.

The mandate sets the floor, the week sets the shape

Our hybrid policy asks for 8 office days a month. Against roughly 21 working days, that’s an attendance floor of about 38%.

Friday utilization is 37.2%, sitting almost exactly on the floor. Monday to Thursday averages 69%, which is 1.7 to 1.9× above it.

Everything above the floor is voluntary. People cluster on the days their colleagues are in, and they do it consistently enough that the pattern held across a full year. If you’re writing or revising a policy, our hot desking policy template and our ebook on hybrid work guidelines both cover the mechanics. There’s wider context in our hybrid work statistics roundup.

How many desks do you actually need?

The Dashboard’s right-sizing block answers this from your own data rather than a rule of thumb.

It takes your busiest day’s demand, adds your peak buffer, and rounds up. Demand uses real check-ins where you recorded them and bookings where you didn’t, so the number gets more honest the more diligent you are with the check-in tab.

Two things worth understanding about it.

  1. It uses the busiest day, not the average. Sizing on an average produces an office that fails once a week.
  2. It counts people who showed, not people who booked. Those are different numbers, and our year of data puts the gap at 9.2%.

Desk sharing ratios have tightened as attendance has recovered. CBRE reports that 48% of organizations now target a sharing ratio between 1.01 and 1.49 people per seat, up sharply from 21% in 2024, and 87% now set explicit utilization targets. If your template suggests something in that range, you’re in step with the market.

Treat the output as a direction. Ten working days is too short a window to sign a lease on, but it’s long enough to know whether you’re 2 desks short or 10 desks over. More ideas on the operational side in our guide to hot desk management.

Five booking rules that keep the numbers honest

Rules make the difference between a spreadsheet people trust and one they ignore.

  • A 2-week booking window. Matches the template’s grid. Long enough to plan around a meeting, short enough that nobody parks a desk for a month.
  • One desk per person per day. The grid flags a double booking in red, but the rule is what stops it happening.
  • Cancel by 5pm the day before. Our data says employees canceled 24.8% of bookings themselves, which is where most of that recovered capacity comes from. Make cancelling easy and people will do it.
  • Check in by 10am. Without a rule, the check-in tab becomes optional and every number downstream stops meaning anything.
  • Clean desk at the end of the day. Shared desks stop being shared the moment somebody leaves a monitor stand and a family photo on one.

Set the rules once, write them down, and put them somewhere people see them. Policies like these also affect attendance and team productivity more than most managers expect.

Excel or Google Sheets

Same file, same formulas, and every function in it (COUNTIF, INDEX, SUMPRODUCT, MATCH) works in both. Your desk booking template in Excel behaves identically in Sheets, so choose on how your team works rather than on features.

ExcelGoogle Sheets
Several people booking at onceNeeds SharePoint or OneDriveWorks out of the box
Offline accessYesNo
Mobile bookingWorkable, not comfortableBetter
CalendarOutlookGoogle Calendar
Backup and version historyManual or via OneDriveAutomatic
Check-in trackingSameSame
Utilization dashboardSameSame

Short version: Sheets if more than 3 people will touch the file in a day. Excel if you're the only editor, or if your IT policy keeps things inside Microsoft 365.

Where the spreadsheet stops working

This template is honest about its ceiling. Ours covers 365 days and 12,829 bookings. Yours covers 10 working days and whatever somebody remembered to type in.

Signs you’ve reached the limit:

  • More than 30 desks, more than one floor, or more than one office on the same file
  • Somebody has to walk the floor with a laptop every morning to fill in check-ins
  • Meeting rooms, parking or visitors need booking alongside the desks
  • You want months of history, not a rolling two weeks
  • Different teams have quietly started using different systems
  • Booking clashes happen weekly
  • Your desk count has to be defensible to finance rather than estimated from 10 days

The last one matters more than it sounds. A 2-week sample tells you your week has a shape. It won’t tell you what next year’s floor plan should look like.

There’s one more limit that shows up in bigger companies. When we polled our audience on social media, 11% said they ran desk booking on a spreadsheet and 17.4% had built something in-house.

Around 30% were on desk booking software. The split matters less than what sat behind it: answers from the same company often disagreed, because different teams were running different systems. If your finance team books desks in Outlook and your engineers share a sheet, you don’t have a booking system. You have three, and none of them can tell you how full the office was on Tuesday.

Hybrid working itself has settled into something worth measuring properly. The randomized trial by Bloom, Han and Liang, published in Nature in 2024, found that hybrid work cut quit rates by a third with no drop in performance. That’s a working arrangement to manage well, and managing it well means knowing who’s in the building.
